articles.title_original: Superbrewed Food expands beyond bulk protein with postbiotic launch
articles.content:
"We’re seeing tremendous interest in natural ingredients that can bring digestive and immune-support functionality into supplements and everyday functional foods," says CEO Bryan Tracy.
Superbrewed Food —a startup best known for producing single-cell protein via biomass fermentation—has launched Thryvia , a low-dose “postbiotic” ingredient made from the same protein-rich bacterium and positioned to support digestive and immune health.
The Delaware-based firm, which began commercial production in Europe earlier this year with manufacturing partner Döhler, is best known for SB1, a whole-food protein ingredient made from a non-GMO bacterium and designed for use at 10–20 grams per serving.
Thryvia, which has a slightly different formulation, is intended for much lower inclusion rates of around 200mg per serving across capsules, powders, gummies, bars, foods and beverages. Superbrewed has also brought in nutraceuticals industry veteran Michael Bush as chairman of the board.
“This isn’t a move away from the protein opportunity,” cofounder Bryan Tracy told AgFunderNews . “Customer interest and demand for our postbiotic cultured protein (SB1) remain strong. The constraint is capacity: raising the capital required to build substantially beyond what our Döhler partnership can currently produce remains a real challenge.
“We’ve developed Thyrvia as a postbiotic with functionality at much lower inclusion levels, which addresses a different customer need and value proposition. We can support multiple significant customer launches and their growth with our existing production footprint rather than waiting for a major capacity expansion.”
The timing is also compelling, he claimed. “We’re seeing tremendous market interest in natural ingredients that can bring digestive and immune-support functionality into supplements and everyday functional foods. Thyrvia gives us a highly differentiated way to address that demand.”
“As someone who has spent years in the microbiome space, I know exactly what it takes to bring a category-defining ingredient to market — and Thryvia has that potential.” Michael Bush, co-chairman, Superbrewed Food; former president and CEO, Ganeden
Unlike probiotics, which are live microbes that can only be used in a limited number of food and beverage applications, postbiotics are inert. This means they can be used in a wider variety of products that don’t need refrigeration or special processing conditions to maintain their viability.
They are sometimes heat-treated or ‘inactivated’ probiotics, but can also be byproducts of fermentation such as metabolites. Postbiotics already on the market include ADM’s heat treated version of its BPL1 probiotic , and Cargill’s Epicor yeast fermentate .
Thryvia is produced from a heat-killed, non-viable Clostridium tyrobutyricum strain that secured a GRAS “no questions” letter from the FDA in 2024 and is shelf-stable at room temperature, explained Tracy.
“Because Thryvia is non-viable, its functionality does not depend on maintaining live-organism viability through manufacturing, distribution and shelf life. This gives brands broad formulation flexibility across capsules, powders, gummies, bars, foods and beverages—including shelf-stable and UHT-processed formats—as well as pet nutrition.”
He added: “One of the most interesting opportunity spaces is products that are difficult or impossible to formulate with traditional probiotics or prebiotics. Probiotics can introduce stability, processing and cold-chain constraints and generally won’t survive processes such as UHT.
“Prebiotics can require multiple gram-level inclusion, which can create formulation and sensory challenges. Thyrvia is compatible with demanding food-processing conditions and shelf-stable even in UHT applications and we’re actively working towards multiple customer launches.”
According to Tracy, Thyrvia is distinct in the market as its “bioactivity comes from proteins that are part of the biomass. Several postbiotics in the market are based on beta-glucans, metabolites, and secondary metabolites. I’m not aware of postbiotics in the market that are based on proteins.”
But what evidence is there to support gut health or immunity claims, and won’t large customers want to see published human clinical studies before they make any claims on pack?
According to Tracy, in vitro testing on Thyrvia demonstrates selective activation of receptors that trigger signaling pathways involved in innate immunity, inflammation, and maintenance of the gut barrier.
Animal studies in turn provide “translational evidence of intestinal and host-response activity,” says Tracy, while a four-week consumer perception study found self-reported improvements across multiple measures of digestive comfort.
Additional human studies are “ongoing,” he claimed. “Human evidence is absolutely required, with the level of rigor required depending on the specific claim a customer intends to make.”
Consumer perception studies can tell you whether people actually experience a meaningful benefit, which can be sufficient to make a claim in some cases, he said. Mechanistic and translational studies, meanwhile, help us understand the biology and establish plausible modes of action.
“But substantiating specific structure/function claims [such as supports gut health] ultimately requires appropriately designed well-powered, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled human trials. We are building this complete evidence package now.”
He added: “That commitment to evidence should be familiar from SB1: we sponsored two human clinical trials and have supported several third-party functional evaluations. We intend to build the Thyrvia evidence base just as seriously.”
For potential customers, the postbiotic message is resonating, said Tracy, who claimed that Superbrewed’s bacterium meets the definition of ‘postbiotic’ laid out in an ISAPP (International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics) consensus paper (‘a preparation of inanimate microorganisms and/or their components that confers a health benefit on the host’).
“A majority of potential SB1 [protein] customers are also very interested in Thyrvia. That overlap makes sense: digestive and immune support can be highly complementary to protein nutrition, particularly as brands increasingly look beyond macronutrients toward broader functional benefits.”

articles.title_original: Guest article: The field day is the new term sheet; how growers are vetting ag robotics for real-use application
articles.content:
"The field day tells us whether or not they’ll stay in business for the long run," says Connie Bowen at Farmhand Ventures.
Connie Bowen is founding general partner at Farmhand Ventures , an early-stage impact investment firm that invests in agricultural technology focused on farmworker well-being, economic viability, and climate resilience. Hannah Johnson is founder of Hannah Johnson & Co . and industry lead at UC ANR Innovate . Together, they operate UC ANR Innovate’s Connect program, a series of selective, free field days designed to get startups with real solutions in front of California’s farming industry.
The views expressed in this article are the authors’ own and do not necessarily represent those of AgFunderNews.
On August 6, more than 250 growers, investors, and startup teams from the US, Brazil, and Europe converged on a Connect field day to watch advanced physical AI technology take on one of agriculture’s hardest crops to automate: leafy greens. It was the sixth Connect field day we’ve hosted in just two years, with more on the calendar this fall and into 2027.
There are many factors to evaluate when investing in a startup. Most investors will agree that team is one of, if not the, most critical and controllable factors to analyze in making an initial investment decision. Markets shift, products fail, co-investors and customers change their minds, and at the end of the day, the people are left to navigate changing tides. Unfortunately, it can be really hard to evaluate teams. Founders are always on their best behavior while courting investors, and they’re almost always going to make introductions to customers and partners with whom they have strong relationships. External reference checks can help, but we’ve found something better – pressure testing in the field.
Over the past two years, we’ve been working together to develop and implement the University of California Ag & Natural Resources (UC ANR) Connect program. Startups apply, get vetted by growers and researchers, go through virtual prep, then demo live at one of several field days hosted across California.
And what we notice after every cohort, in spite of all the vetting and prepping of these companies throughout the program, is that the field day tells us whether or not they’ll stay in business for the long run. The signals and data points that come from a company’s participation in a field day are invaluable in vetting teams, and too many investors are missing them.
And the stakes are real. The founders who nail these signals don’t just leave with good feedback — they leave Connect with commercial contracts in hand. The ones who don’t, leave with a list of what to fix before the next one.
We immediately clock how a startup staffs the event. When a company sends enough technical staff to answer growers’ specific questions, that tells us they value the opportunity and can support the work behind it. When one overwhelmed rep shows up, we ask why: they may be resource-constrained, or they may not understand what the opportunity demands.
Afterward, we watch what happens next. Do they follow up with growers who asked questions, send the data they promised, and thank the host farm or research station? Those small acts are predictive because companies that treat a field day as a one-and-done PR stop rarely treat customers differently after the sale.
The clearest signal is care: does the team ask growers real questions and listen to the answers—or do they see acreage instead of a person carrying the weight of feeding people for a living?
We get it — the economics still have to pencil, and none of these soft cues catalyze an exit on their own. But if the “there” doesn’t strengthen our food system or solve a real grower’s problem, we don’t care how good the math is. The win is short-lived, for all of us.
We want more investors to see what we’re seeing — and act on it before the next cohort proves us right. We think you’ll be more successful, and agtech — and agriculture — will be better off too. With our next Connect field days already on the calendar for this fall and 2027, the smartest diligence you can do this year might be a day in the field.

articles.title_original: Pairwise sees ‘dramatic uptick’ in CRISPR licensing as gene editing moves beyond row crops
articles.content:
Pairwise has seen a “dramatic uptick” in licensing deals for its gene editing platform over the past 12-18 months and now has 25 licensees
Gene editing is rapidly expanding beyond row crops into specialty crops, animals, and microbes, says Pairwise , which has seen a “dramatic uptick” in licensing deals for its Fulcrum platform over the past 12-18 months and now has 25 licensees covering more than 30 species.
Unlike transgenic plants —which are classified as GMOs as foreign DNA from another species is introduced—gene editing involves tinkering with species’ native genes, which eases the regulatory pathway in a growing number of markets and can deliver speed and precision, two potential gamechangers in breeding, says COO Ian Miller, PhD.
“We’re really enthusiastic about the direction that the regulatory environment is going worldwide,” adds Miller, who says Pairwise is seeing growing interest in Europe now that the EU has enshrined a new, simpler regulatory framework for plants made using new genomic techniques.
“I think there’s an understanding that in many cases, what comes out from gene editing is equivalent to conventional breeding because we’re working within the plant’s own genes. The beauty of gene editing is that if it sits somewhere in the gene pool, you can bring it to bear for a problem.”
Founded in 2017 by ag biotech veterans Tom Adams PhD, and Haven Baker PhD, alongside CRISPR pioneers and scientific founders Feng Zhang PhD, David Liu, PhD, and J. Keith Joung PhD, Pairwise has some high-profile collaborations with industry heavyweights such as Bayer and Corteva on row crops, spanning everything from short-stature corn to soybeans with reduced susceptibility to Asian soybean rust.
However, its Fulcrum CRIPSR gene-editing platform is now attracting interest from a far wider range of companies, researchers, and nonprofits working on everything from cassava and cacao to insects, vegetables, ornamental horticulture, microbes used in ag biologicals, and livestock, says Miller.
“I would say behind those 25 [licensees], I would say, we have at least as many more that are in various stages of discussion. We’re also working with a big CPG company that I can’t disclose yet.”
The breadth of those licensees gives Pairwise a window into where agricultural gene editing is heading.
Agragene , for example, is using Fulcrum to work on sterile insects for pest control; Genus is working in animal genetics; and CSIRO—Australia’s national science agency—has a license covering livestock, aquaculture, microbes, and plants.
Other licensees include vegetable seed company Enza Zaden and leading ornamental horticulture player Ball , while Mars has licensed the technology in cacao. Pairwise is also working with the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) in yam and has licensed its technology for other staple crops including cassava, cowpea and rice.
“I think if you look at the scope of the licensees there, it can go everything from yield to disease to composition,” says Miller. “We have other folks interested in biofuel.”
For Miller, this breadth suggests there is considerable pent-up demand for genetic tools outside the handful of crops that have historically attracted most breeding and biotech investment. “It tells us there’s a lot of untapped potential.”
The easiest way to think about Fulcrum is to liken it to a word processor, Miller tells AgFunderNews :
“We have Ctrl F to find the spot in the DNA to make the edit, and then we have tools that do everything from hitting the delete key [nuclease editing, typically cutting DNA to knock out or inactivate a gene responsible for an undesirable trait] to changing a letter [base editing, which chemically converts one DNA base into another without making a double-strand break].
“Then we have find and replace [templated editing, which uses a DNA or RNA template to rewrite a targeted stretch of DNA with a specified new sequence].”
Pairwise routinely carries out multiplex editing internally and has performed as many as 17 simultaneous edits.
Notably, Pairwise is trying to capture that opportunity by licensing a broad suite of gene-editing tools through a single platform rather than requiring users to assemble separate licenses from multiple IP holders, he explains.
“You don’t have to get multiple licenses. We’re offering one-stop shopping. We license one stack, one royalty rate, which is competitive with what single licenses are charging folks in other spaces. The idea is whatever’s the right tool for the job, people should use. We want to reduce that friction and make it easy for people to innovate.”
The business model typically includes a modest upfront fee, maintenance fees and royalties if a licensee ultimately commercializes a product. Pairwise can also provide limited technology transfer for customers that need help getting started.
Two areas Miller sees as particularly attractive are perennial and specialty crops, where lengthy breeding cycles can make conventional crop development especially slow.
The attraction of gene editing in perennials is partly speed, he says. “We can do things in a single generation that would take years and years and years to create. If you’re working in a tree in a breeder, and it takes you 5-10 years to do a cross, that limits your ability to innovate.”
Blackberries are a case in point. A genetically complex perennial crop, they can be slow and challenging to improve through conventional breeding. Through gene editing, Pairwise has been able to develop varieties with a more compact architecture to triple plant density per acre, coupled with seedless and thornless fruit.
“So the blackberry we’re commercializing ourselves with our partner Plant Sciences Genetics . They were the ones who did the original breeding on the variety that we edited on top of, but we’re actually the one taking that one to market, and we now have commercial growers for the compact variety in Colombia.
“The pitless variety is in field trials right now,” adds Miller, who says Pairwise also has a partnership with Sun World International working on a pitless cherry .
Miller does not see gene editing replacing conventional breeding, however. Rather, editing can create precise genetic variation that breeders can then work with, while conventional breeding remains useful for “moving large numbers of genes around.”
As work moves well beyond corn and soy, there’s less data to work with, acknowledges Miller, who says many crops have received a fraction of the genetics research invested in the major commodities.
“Clearly, there’s been a lot less investment in some of these crops, particularly when you think about stuff that impacts the global South,” says Miller. But biological mechanisms can be conserved between species, he notes, enabling researchers to apply knowledge generated in better-understood crops to new ones.
Pairwise’s work with IITA on yam provides one example. The partners are exploring a more compact plant architecture, drawing on Pairwise’s broader work on dwarfing and compactness in other crops, which creates a “flywheel effect” that increases the odds of success in subsequent projects, says Miller.
“What we’re focused on is developing understandings of the networks of genes that produce traits. So dwarfing architecture is something we’ve spent a lot of time understanding, and so things may not be exactly the same from one crop to the next, but we do now have a much better understanding of those pathways.”
There are limits, however. Editing tools can make increasingly sophisticated changes, but companies still need to understand which genes and gene networks control a desired trait, which is the biggest challenge with complex traits such as drought, heat or salinity tolerance.
Ultimately, Miller sees Pairwise’s pipeline as evidence that CRISPR’s next phase in agriculture could look substantially broader than its first.
“I’m wildly enthusiastic, and I think we’re in a great spot. What the shape of our pipeline tells you is that the opportunities for CRISPR in the future aren’t just focused on corn and soy.”

articles.title_original: Quorn Foods’ UK retail recovery gathers pace, but foodservice ‘likely to get worse before it gets better’
articles.content:
Quorn's new protein bites reach a new set of consumers and command higher price points and margins, says the alt meat firm.
Meat alternatives maker Quorn Foods is beginning to emerge from a prolonged slump, with sales growing modestly in Q2 and margins rebounding as restructuring measures and a stronger performance in UK retail offset weaker sales in foodservice.
The firm—which is owned by instant noodles giant Monde Nissin —said its protein segment comprising the Quorn and Cauldron brands generated revenues of ₱7.38 billion ($120 million) in the first half of 2026, up 2.2% on a constant-currency basis vs the first half of 2025.
Core net income was ₱106 million ($1.7 million), vs a ₱215 million ($3.5 million) core net loss in H1 2025, said CFO Nick Cooper on the firm’s earnings call.
“We see growing momentum in UK retail, and I expect the second half of the year in UK retail to be as strong as, or even stronger than the first half. But at the same time, we have a lot of work to do in foodservice, and that will be a drag in the second half of the year, and is likely to get worse before it gets better.”
CEO David Flochel highlighted the early performance of recent launch Protein Bites, which Quorn has placed both in meat-free fixtures and food-to-go sections in UK retail, and is now introducing into the foodservice channel:
“It’s early days, but the rate of sale is very good and very promising to a point that has been helping us to unlock even further distribution for the second half of the year. This is a key driver of the continuous double-digit growth in snacking that we’ve been enjoying in Q2,”
The format is particularly attractive because it can reach consumers beyond the traditional meat-free category while commanding higher price points and improving margins, added Monde Nissin CEO Henry Soesanto.
“We are seeing these new [snacking] products [such as Protein Bites] building good potential, playing into new convenient retail formats for single consumption, catering to a much wider audience even beyond the UK and Europe. We also believe that this is a scalable new part of the portfolio, where taste, convenience, and health are rewarded with higher price points, which will be accretive to the gross margin of the protein portfolio as a whole.”
Quorn has made meaningful progress on two of the three pillars of its “Transform to Win Together” plan: fixing UK retail and rebuilding gross margins through supply-chain improvements.
However, sales in the foodservice channel, which accounts for 18% of the protein business, fell 5% in Q2, a “disappointing” result, said Quorn Foods CEO David Flochel, a CPG industry veteran brought into the business in 2024 to lead a turnaround.
Quorn is now applying the same “back-to-basics” approach in foodservice as the team has deployed in UK retail and seeks to diversify beyond education and healthcare into higher margin business and industry channels, said Flochel. It is also unlocking new opportunities through Protein Bites and its blended meat offering enabling foodservice partners to combine meat and mycoprotein to create hybrid products, which are now gaining traction in several markets.
“In the long term, I remain convinced and confident that we can drive positive contribution and growth for that [foodservice] channel. However, in the short term, there’s still a lot to be fixed.”
Looking ahead, CFO Nick Cooper cautioned that the improving sales trajectory will not be linear: Q2 benefited from a relatively weak prior-year comparison, while higher input costs due to the Iran war are expected to hit gross margins more heavily in Q3 and Q4.
Nevertheless, management expects further supply-chain savings to offset much of that pressure, said the firm, which has gone through several rounds of restructuring and layoffs as part of an “organizational right-sizing” process over the past couple of years.
High in protein and fiber and low in saturated fat and calories, Quorn mycoprotein is an edible filamentous fungus called Fusarium Venenatum first discovered growing in soil in Buckinghamshire in the UK in the late 1960s and grown at a commercial scale using a controlled fermentation process in large steel tanks.
Launched in the UK in 1985, Quorn was introduced to the US in 2002. Its parent company Marlow Foods was acquired by Monde Nissin—one of the leading consumer packaged foods companies in the Philippines— in late 2015 for $831 million. Cauldron Foods, a UK-based brand founded in the early 1980s, was acquired as part of the same deal.
According to Monde Nissin’s 2025 annual report , the UK accounted for 79.1% of sales in its meat alternatives business in full-year 2025, with 5.5% coming from the US and the remainder from the Republic of Ireland, mainland Europe, Southeast Asia, and Australasia.
In UK grocery retail, Cauldron was the #6 alt meat brand with a 3.5% value share in 2025, while Quorn was No. 1 with 27.8%, according to Circana data cited in the report.

articles.title_original: dsm-firmenich takes Protopia yeast protein to industrial scale, targets fishmeal and whey
articles.content:
Protopia could generate a novel revenue stream for Indian ethanol producers who are sitting on significant underutilized capacity.
dsm-firmenich is preparing to move its Protopia single-cell protein into industrial-scale production, with a 120,000-liter fermentation run planned later this year, and plans to move into a larger facility in Europe in 2027.
Single-cell protein (fermenting microbes and harvesting the whole biomass) has attracted growing interest as a more efficient way to produce large volumes of protein but many startups have struggled to translate bench scale yields into competitive economics at industrial scale.
dsm-firmenich is betting that a highly optimized yeast strain, flexible low-cost feedstocks, and superior yield and productivity can close the gap.
Its “feedstock agnostic” strain of torula yeast can feed off ethanol, methanol, acetate, sugar, molasses or other substrates and deliver 2-3x the productivity of most liquid biomass fermentation systems, enabling it to compete head on with fishmeal in aquaculture and whey in human nutrition, claims the firm.
It could also generate a novel revenue stream for Indian ethanol producers who have rapidly expanded production capacity to meet government biofuel mandates but are now sitting on significant underutilized capacity, director of single cell protein Karim Kurmaly, PhD tells AgFunderNews .
The initial plan is to produce sufficient quantities to prove out the bioprocess at scale and provide enough product to enable market testing, says Kurmaly, who is based in the Netherlands. The longer-term plan is to expand via a licensing model whereby local production partners would make and sell the protein, while dsm-firmenich would supply the strain, process technology, know-how, and tech support.
The torula yeast in question has a long history of use in foods in multiple geographies including the EU, notes Kurmaly. What’s new is that dsm-firmenich has optimized a strain and fermentation process so it can be produced as a ~70%-protein, neutral-tasting ingredient at inclusion levels high enough to function as a primary protein source.
According to Kurmaly, dsm-firmenich has produced batches for customer trials in a 15,000-liter fermenter and plans to move to a 120,000-liter fermenter later this year. After that, the plan is to move into a facility, most likely in Eastern Europe, with access to both bioethanol and beet sugar, where it aims to produce about 2,000–10,000 tons/year.
The aim is to produce around 400–500 tons from the middle of next year onward to seed the market and support customer trials, while simultaneously working on licensing agreements in three countries.
Unlike many startups in the single cell protein field, dsm-firmenich has extensive experience in biomanufacturing at an industrial scale, says Kurmaly. “We started in reverse order: if this is the COGS, how do we get there?
“We optimized the process tech and the strain to get higher yields and significantly higher productivity. We also had to make the strain versatile enough to be feedstock agnostic.”
The company has explored continuous fermentation but concluded that semi-continuous operation works better on cost and overall performance, particularly because contamination in a fully continuous process can result in a much larger loss, he claims.
Protopia contains a minimum of 70% protein, with a full complement of essential and structural amino acids, and a protein digestibility (PDCAAS) score of around .94–.96, almost on a par with animal protein.
For aquaculture and pet food, downstream processing is relatively straightforward: dewatering, pasteurization and drying. Food applications require additional processing to make the material pumpable before spray drying, with particle size adjusted according to the intended use. But none of this requires exotic equipment, stresses Kurmaly.
“The strain is the magic, not the facility, not the steel and the concrete.”
As the underlying yeast has a long history of food use, Protopia can already be used in the US and EU without requiring a GRAS notice or EU novel food authorization. However, dsm-firmenich is separately assessing regulatory requirements in markets including India and Brazil.
Labeling will vary by geography but will likely be something along the lines of “yeast protein” or “fermented yeast protein.”
In Europe, dsm-firmenich is working with the top three players in the aquaculture sector, the top five in the pet food sector, and the top five in the food sector, claims Kurmaly, who says inclusion rates can go up to 10–12% inclusion in human foods without negative impacts on taste and up to 20% in salmon diets.
For the aquaculture market, the key opportunity is salmon production, where producers are grappling with rising fishmeal prices and concerns over availability. These have been exacerbated this year with El Niño disrupting Peru’s anchovy industry, says Kurmaly.
“Today 65% high-quality fish meal is around €3,000/ton and we can compete at those levels. Providing it doesn’t drop below €2,000/ton, we’re okay.”
Trials with aquaculture companies show Protopia can serve as a 1:1 replacement of fishmeal, where producers are laser focused on nutritional content and security of supply, he explains.
In pet food, palatability is the #1 issue along with price, with independent kennel trials showed Protopia outperforms competing proteins, he adds.
For human food, Protopia is supplied as a fine off-white powder with a slight savory note if eaten on its own. Interest is coming from a wide range of foods from snacks to meat alternatives, with customers interested in its functional properties (gelling, emulsification), nutrition, and sensory advantages over plant proteins, which come with off tastes, says Kurmaly.
“There is no smell, no aftertaste, and no grittiness, so it also lends itself well to smoothies and milk alternatives” at a time when the price of whey protein has “skyrocketed to $25 to $28 per kilo, and that’s if you can get it,” he adds.
India makes “very little cheese in comparison to the mountains we have in the Americas and Europe,” adds Raman (Chandru) Chandrasekar—managing director at UK-based Sustein Ltd, which works on sustainable protein and bioeconomy projects.
“And because most of the cheese is paneer, you don’t really get much whey protein out of it, so India imports almost all of its whey and prices have gone way up. Proptopia is a suitable replacement nutritionally and it’s also very similar in color.”
Chandrasekar—who grew up in India but is now based in the UK—sees India as a particularly attractive market for Protopia given its protein deficit and surplus ethanol capacity.
Potential applications range from mass-market protein fortification of noodles, breads, chapatis and snacks through to more functional uses in premium beverages, he says.
The aim is to co-locate a Protopia fermentation module with an existing ethanol or sugar producer, using its feedstock, utilities and effluent infrastructure, while bringing in major food companies as off takers. A Protopia plant consuming 100,000 liters/day of ethanol could produce around 16,000 tons of Protopia annually.
“The ethanol industry has invested in nearly $5 billion worth of capacity to produce 20 billion liters,” says Chandrasekar. “But the government can only procure realistically half of that for E20, which is itself facing a huge backlash in India because the vehicles are not ready to go from E10 to E20.
“Protopia can utilize this ethanol as feedstock but also has the flexibility to use any source of sugars, methanol, acetate or any carbon source, really. So it’s a magical technology.”
While Quorn—which is produced via biomass fermentation—has been around for a while, he says, it lacks the protein content of Protopia and requires a cold chain, whereas Protopia can be stored for long periods as a dry powder at ambient temperatures.
“China has a strategic pork reserve; India could have a strategic protein reserve.”
Chandrasekar adds: “India currently imports almost all the yeast protein used in snacks and savory products, from a neighboring country where production is limited to 10,000 tons per year right now, and the companies probably have another 11,000 tons coming online in the near future. But 21,000 tons is just a drop in the ocean when you look at the unmet protein gap in India.
“If we just took the surplus ethanol and made Protopia protein from that, we could meet at least 40% of that demand gap.”
He adds: “Aquaculture and pet food are also growing in India and [for human food] the most popular snack is the instant noodle, which is often criticized for being just starch and junk food.” Adding Protopia would be a low-cost way of boosting the protein content of what has become a food staple without breaking the bank.
“So that’s a huge market that’s immediately open for innovation, and we are talking to some of the FMCG companies who are actively interested in this.”
But there are also opportunities in premium market segments, says Chandrasekar, who notes that Starbucks now offers a protein foam made from yeast protein on menus in India.
Ultimately, dsm-firmenich does not envisage owning dozens of Protopia factories but would instead supply what Kurmaly calls the “software”—the strain, process technology and application expertise—while partners supply the physical infrastructure.
Under this model, the licensee would manufacture and market Protopia under license and pay dsm-firmenich a royalty, with dsm-firmenich supporting both applications and go to market strategy to help partners secure offtake agreements.
The IP portfolio currently comprises 18+ patents spanning three areas: strain, process technology and applications, with additional filings in development.
The broader ambition is to build a repeatable licensing model around regions with either cheap feedstocks, existing fermentation infrastructure or low-cost renewable energy. Beyond Europe and India, Kurmaly highlights Brazil, China and the US as promising markets.

articles.title_original: Inside Nanovel’s bid to crack robotic citrus harvesting
articles.content:
In the US, says Isaac Mazor, “manual citrus harvesting costs around $42–43 per 900-lb field bin, versus $25-30 using our technology.”
Robots can now spray crops and zap weeds with centimeter-level precision. But ask one to pick oranges and the challenge is immediately apparent, says Israeli ag robotics startup Nanovel .
Citrus fruit can sit up to 1.5 meters inside dense foliage, requiring an autonomous harvesting system to identify fruit, leaves and branches in 3D, navigate through the canopy, move material out of the way and then harvest… all without damaging the fruit.
As a result, harvesting these kinds of specialty crops remains one of the toughest nuts to crack in ag robotics, says Nanovel founder and CEO Isaac Mazor.
Founded in 2018, Nanovel has spent several years refining a patented autonomous harvester with robotic arms designed to reach deep inside citrus trees, grip fruits with a vacuum gripper and cut their stems less than 2mm from the fruit before conveying them into bins.
The current model uses six telescopic arms operating simultaneously, coordinated by an onboard computer that uses computer vision and AI to map the canopy, allocate fruit between the arms, and avoid collisions. The computer is linked to a remote management system that supervises a fleet of ‘bots.
The vision system can select fruit by color and size, allowing growers to avoid harvesting fruit that would be rejected at the packing house, but does not yet do defect detection.
Following a seven-week trial at a leading grower in California last fall with the Citrus Research Board featuring a tractor-pulled version, the firm is now building a self-driving model.
Trials are planned with leading growers in southern Europe in 2027, with pilot deployments in 2028 and commercial deployment in 2029, says Nanovel, which has just secured a €2.5 million ($2.9 million) grant from the European Innovation Council (EIC) Accelerator program.
While high-tech harvesting might sound pricy, manual labor can account for 50% of production costs in citrus, where growers are highly dependent on seasonal labor, says Mazor.
“One of the reasons we picked oranges is that a substantial amount is grown in countries that are labor sensitive. Even in Brazil, where the labor cost is lower than in the US or Europe, they have severe logistic problems as the growing areas and the populated areas are very far apart and they have to move thousands of pickers back and forth and accommodate them.”
In the US, he says, “manual citrus harvesting costs around $42–43 per 900-lb field bin, versus $25-30 using our technology.”
But direct labor savings are not the only metric that counts, he says. Predictability is also core to the value proposition. Having a robotic harvesting fleet means a grower can schedule harvests without worrying whether enough seasonal workers will turn up. The ‘bots can also operate for longer periods and resume quickly after bad weather.
“The number one criteria is quality,” says Mazor. “If you don’t meet the quality, you’re out. But once you meet the quality, what is really important is the ability to plan ahead.”
While a robot cannot match the number of oranges that a human can easily pick from a tree, productivity matters more than pushing the machine to retrieve every difficult-to-see fruit, says Mazor.
“The optimal combination between autonomous and human harvesting is a machine that takes 70-80% of the fruit and then the rest we leave to the operator, who is an additional resource to pick the 10-15% of the fruit that are very difficult to cut.”
The aim is to triple or quadruple the productivity of one operator, rather than remove that operator altogether, he says. “We’re not offering a labor free solution. You can imagine a fleet of 10-20 robots and each one is escorted by an operator.”
The operator would also approve movements between picking positions, replace bins, clear occasional obstructions and decide when the robot should move on, he says, with training taking less than a day.
“Gen II is self-driving so the operator can stand at the back. The robot can move autonomously to the next station and the operator can pick the section that the robot just picked and get the leftover fruit.”
Longer term, Mazor hopes to generate a second revenue stream from data gathered during harvesting that can create high-res orchard maps capturing information such as fruit size and sugar content.
This could then be correlated with irrigation, chemical applications and other agronomic inputs.
Nanovel plans to sell the robots outright rather than offer harvesting-as-a-service, reasoning that large citrus growers can use the equipment for 8-11 months of the year and will therefore want to own the asset.
Each machine will likely have a selling price of around $400,000, with payback in under five years, a number Mazor predicts will go down as the machines improve.
“In Europe, in the last 10 years, they lost a lot of their agricultural labor and the average cost of labor is going up every year, so even if the payback is five years, it’s still appealing as otherwise they cannot pick the fruit. But of course we’re not sitting on our hands so our numbers will continue to improve.”
Nanovel envisages using manufacturing/assembly partners in markets such as California, Spain, Italy, Taiwan or Australia, combining a global component supply chain with final integration closer to customers to reduce shipping costs, says Mazor. “This is a big machine.”
The plan is to sell through local dealers/distributors, which would also provide maintenance and servicing supported by Nanovel subsidiaries in key markets.
Nanovel is deliberately focusing first on oranges and lemons, which Mazor estimates represent an addressable harvesting market of around $1.5 billion in its target geographies. After establishing the platform there, it could later move into clementines, avocados, mangoes and potentially other fruits.
In the short term, Nanovel is focusing on the US and southern Europe, where labor availability and costs make automation particularly compelling, although Mazor has also had inquiries from Argentina, Chile, Peru and Brazil.
Stepping back, Mazor is candid about the fact that the recent California trial was as much a learning exercise as a validation.
“What we have learned through this, of course, is that we have a lot to fix in terms of robustness and productivity. But we are also doing something new.”
While companies including Vision Robotics have developed robotic citrus harvesters, no one has as yet commercialized an autonomous fresh-market citrus harvester, he says.
“The number of harvesting robots for the fresh fruit market, rather than greenhouses or cultivated trellis type growing is very few. There are several [robotic harvesting systems] for apples, but these are often picked by twisting, not by trimming. When it comes to citrus, we are a pioneer.”
In the first four years, says Mazor, “It was just me and some engineers, and that means we have we able to get to this point with less than $10 million.”
And this pales in comparison to what some other ag robotics players have raised, he said. “[California-based ag robotics startup] Advanced Farm Technologies, which shut down last year, raised over $30 million [for its robotic strawberry and apple harvesting tech].”
The €2.5 million EIC grant also includes eligibility for an equity investment of up to €4.3 million, intended to anchor a planned funding round of around €8 million, he said.
With that additional funding, he predicted, the hope is that Nanovel “can go all the way to break even and make some positive cash.”

articles.title_original: Offbeast develops ‘world’s first’ beef-plant hybrid whole cuts
articles.content:
The hybrid meat product is enabled by a new manufacturing process designed to integrate into existing meat-processing lines, says Offbeast.
[Disclosure: AgFunderNews’ parent company AgFunder is an investor in Offbeast.]
Baltimore-based Offbeast has developed a manufacturing process designed to integrate into existing meat-processing lines enabling firms to create whole cuts of meat containing a 50:50 blend of beef and plant-based ingredients with a “continuous, muscle-like fiber structure.”
Blended meat is not in itself new. TVP (textured vegetable protein) is commonly used as an extender in processed meats such as burgers and sausages to save money and improve yield at low inclusion rates, while several startups now offer mycoprotein or plant-based solutions to create a new wave of 50:50 “hybrid” meats.
However, Offbeast believes it is the first to create hybrid whole cuts, says cofounder and CEO Insa Mohr.
“The product is enabled by a new manufacturing process designed to integrate into existing meat-processing lines. The technology can increase typical beef margins by two to four times while enabling a lower consumer price.
“I can’t tell you exactly how the process works because we’re filing a patent on it, but the basic rule for our process is that it has to fully work on off-the-shelf equipment; it’s basically the same technology we use for our plant-based stakes, which is already validated. Any company that has a meat sausage or burger line, or a plant-based meat sausage or burger line, can produce this product without any additional equipment.”
Offbeast’s “whole cut engineering” tech—originally developed for plant-based steaks—”transforms unstructured meat such as ground beef or beef fat, into aligned, muscle-like fibers,” explains the firm.
“A plant-based binder connects these fibers while simultaneously acting as an extender, reducing the amount of meat required while maintaining an authentic meat texture.”
According to Mohr, 16 out of 20 testers in a recent taste test rated the blended beef tips as “indistinguishable from conventional meat,” with texture receiving particularly strong feedback.
The tech has already been tested at production scale with capacity of up to three metric tons per shift at Offbeast’s pilot facility in Baltimore, says Mohr, who is now seeking partnerships with meat producers to bring blended whole-cut products to market.
“We are having confidential conversations, but the aim is to implement this with a large partner who already has distribution.”
The process can be used across a range of whole-cut formats, from beef strips and chunks to steaks, and can also be adapted to other types of meat, including pork, with no change to protein content, she claims.
While partners may be able to make a nutrition and sustainability argument for hybrid whole cuts, the primary drivers are economic, says Mohr: “Whole cut engineering is designed to create a compelling economic incentive for meat producers.
“We saw the focus of the meat industry moving a bit away from sustainability, so we are offering what we like to call ‘backdoor sustainability’ in that there is a strong financial incentive for companies [to do something that] is also sustainable.”
With a blended burger, “inexpensive meat and inexpensive plant ingredients are combined to create another relatively inexpensive product,” she adds. “Our technology is different because it can turn those same low-cost inputs into a significantly higher-value whole-cut product.
“It’s like surimi, which has been around since the ’70s, where they use fish paste blended with some other ingredients [to make imitation crab sticks], and that is a multibillion billion market today. So basically, we’re trying to do with beef what surimi did in the seafood market.”
According to Offbeast’s calculations, the resulting economics can increase margins while still allowing for a lower consumer price.
While Offbeast’s tech can produce steaks such as the one pictured above, the commercial focus will be on beef tips, rather than steaks sold in fine dining, says Mohr. “Beef tips are the lowest hanging fruit; it’s a cost sensitive use case. We’re taking unstructured meats and making them into structured meat, thereby kind of upscaling them.”
Founded by Insa Mohr and Jochen Mueller as Mooji Meats, the firm emerged from Y Combinator in 2022 pitching a high-throughput 3D-printing platform capable of turning plant proteins or cultivated meat cells into structured whole cuts.
It subsequently modified its approach to a proprietary “Cross-Fiber Assembly platform” and relaunched as Offbeast in January 2025. It is currently supplying plant-based steaks to foodservice clients and direct to consumer.
Based on a patent filing , its process starts with TVP, which is hydrated and broken down into small fibrous particles. These are incorporated into a protein dough, typically containing vital wheat gluten, that is formed into larger strands. The strands are then semi-aligned, layered with fat and juice, and compacted into a roast-like structure that can be sliced into steaks.
The idea is to create texture at multiple length scales: smaller fibers contribute chewiness, while the larger, imperfectly aligned strands mimic muscle bundles and give the finished product a more steak-like grain and directional bite.
Hybrid meats are gaining traction in several markets, with major supermarket chains in Europe including Lidl, Colruyt and Albert Heijn now experimenting with the products.
JOYN Foods has a blended meat solution (’50Cut’) featuring mycelium from edible mushroom strains, while Black Sheep Foods has developed a next-gen TVP from wheat and fava beans promising a superior bite, fat binding, and flavor carry that can be added at high inclusion levels in hybrid and plant-based systems.
While blended meat can help clients meet ESG goals and cut saturated fat and sodium while boosting fiber, the fact that it can also undercut beef on price is what ultimately seals the deal for customers, say the firms.
“It’s interesting because meat companies have been mixing extenders into sausages since the 70s, but suddenly we started calling it ‘hybrid’ meat,” says Mohr.
The current hybrid trend is arguably a little different as firms are blending meat with a wider range of ingredients at higher inclusion levels.
However, some of the change is also about how to frame the concept both to the industry and to end consumers, she says, noting that a “shiitake-infused” burger sounds more appealing than adding “meat fillers” to sausages.

articles.title_original: Millow raises $2.3m, gears up for commercial launch of minimally processed alt meat
articles.content:
“Installation is complete and we will run tests now, with first commercial volumes reaching customers in the coming months,” says CEO Fredrik Öhrn.
Millow —a Swedish startup producing minimally processed meat substitutes from oats and mycelium—has closed a €2 million ($2.3 million) funding round as it gears up for commercial launch.
The round was led by Magnus Emilson , founder of hospitality tech provider Visit Group and cofounder of hospitality group ESS Group, and supported by Jan Enhager , cofounder of nutrition firm Vitamin Well Group, plus other undisclosed investors.
The capital will fund expansion of Millow’s new production facility at a former LEGO production hall in Stenkullen near Gothenburg and the build-out of its commercial team for the Nordic foodservice market.
“Installation is completed and we will run tests now, with first commercial volumes reaching customers during the coming months,” CEO Fredrik Öhrn told AgFunderNews .
“We’ll operate three S-units [Millow’s proprietary fermentation units] with a combined capacity of roughly 430+ tons per year by the end of this year.
“We expect to reach around 90% utilization during late 2027 rather than running flat out from day one,” added Öhrn, a former Sodexo exec who joined Millow in March. “The building already supports three additional units, so doubling capacity doesn’t require a new facility.”
Millow is in talks with leading foodservice operators and distributors in the Nordics, with international interest growing in parallel, claimed Öhrn. “Jan and Magnus bring experience and a network we would otherwise spend years building. The job now is disciplined commercial execution.”
According to Öhrn: “The strongest pull right now is from foodservice; mince and some ready-made formats for public sector kitchens and restaurant chains, where our allergen-free profile and clean label solve many operational problems. Additionally, scope 3 requirements and CO2 emissions are becoming very important aspects for foodservice providers.”
The product also “blends extremely well with conventional meat, and we are having many conversations about that as well,” he added.
“With Vitamin Well we saw how fast a better product can move from niche to mainstream once the taste and the format are right. Foodservice protein is at that point now. Millow gives kitchens a clean-label product that does not ask them to change how they cook, and in my experience that is what decides whether a category crosses over .” Jan Enhager
Asked how the market is viewing Millow vs mycoprotein from firms such as Quorn, he said: “I’d say we are in a fundamentally different category. Quorn and ENOUGH Food use liquid fermentation and then run different downstream processing, [adding] binders and additives to become food. We use solid-state dry fermentation: mycelium grown directly on Swedish oats and psyllium so the output is the food: few ingredients, no binders, in a 16–24 hour production cycle with a fraction of the water and energy consumption.
“That translates to lower capex and a sustainable cost position that lets us compete for the long run in foodservice, with the ability to develop products rather quickly based on market demands.”
On protein content, he said: “We’re at 14% initially with the ability to increase up to 20%, plus 7.6% fiber, comparable to prepared meat dishes. In foodservice, honestly, nobody has said protein levels need to increase yet.
“Chefs care about taste, texture that survives boiling, frying and baking, allergen-free status and reliable supply. Nutritionists appreciate that it’s whole-food protein with all essential amino acids and improved iron bioavailability, not an extracted isolate.”
“I have spent decades building companies in technology and hospitality, and from the restaurant and hotel side I can see the demand for a protein like this coming. ” Magnus Emilson
While Millow is starting by fermenting oats and psyllium, its technology platform can ferment other plant-based materials, including food industry side streams, said Öhrn.
“It’s part of the long-term platform play. The clearest example is our work with an international industrial player on fermenting its side streams and residues. These types of collaborations can be structured toward a licensing model where partners run the technology locally and we would earn a fee per kilo.
“Some examples of side streams can be brewers’ spent grain, canola cakes from canola oil production, and okara from oatmilk production. The potential volumes are massive if we hit all the proper parameters in the fermentation and downstream process.
“That said, sequencing matters: first we prove the food business in the Nordics really works and the market likes the outcome, then we can take the next platform steps on our commercial journey.”
Millow’s technology is based on the work of Mohammad Taherzadeh, former professor of bioprocess technology at the University of Borås.
While several firms are growing fungal biomass to make meat analogs, Millow​​ adds mycelium to a plant-based substrate such as oats in a ‘dry fermentation’ process to create products with a ratio of around 50% fungi and 50% plants.
The fungi/oat combination can grow in any shape or form, depending on the shape and dimensions of the containers it grows in, without requiring expensive downstream processing, and has a balanced nutritional profile with protein, fiber, vitamins, and minerals.
While it sounds like tempeh, which is made via solid-state fermentation, Millow products have a meatier taste, bite, appearance and texture and don’t disintegrate when cooked in a sauce, claims the firm.
The product can be shipped fresh or frozen to food manufacturers and sold as a solo packaged product or combined in prepared meals.

articles.title_original: Swiss alt meat startup Planted scales fermented whole-cut platform, eyes B2B partnerships
articles.content:
“In Austria and Switzerland we’re the market leader and in Germany we’re the fastest growing player," claims Planted cofounder Pascal Bieri.
Swiss plant-based meat firm Planted is planning to double production capacity at its facility in Memmingen, Germany, to meet growing demand for steaks and other products made via its proprietary solid-state fermentation technology .
“We’re adding more capacity and taking our whole-muscle technology into new product categories, including cold cuts, where basically, you create a whole muscle that can be cut into thin pieces,” said cofounder Pascal Bieri, who would not put a figure on the capex involved.
The facility, which opened in 2025, puts extruded proteins through a solid-state fermentation process in chambers. This creates “huge, muscle-like pieces of meat that we then can form, cut, cure, and marinate,” said Bieri.
Extrusion provides the initial structure, while fermentation delivers additional texture, flavor and juiciness, added Bieri, who claimed the system was relatively capital efficient.
“We learned one thing going into the most difficult retail market in the world, Germany, which is that price matters. We never wanted to build a product that is solely used in Michelin restaurants. We wanted to reach everyone, so we only push technologies that can deliver on that.
“Our big goal vision, which we internally call ‘One Plus One Vision,’ is that we want to spend $1 on raw materials and another $1 on processing and packaging to produce one kilogram of meat for $2.”
The firm’s original facility in Kemptthal, Switzerland, handles extrusion, cutting, slicing, dicing, skewering, marinating and packaging for its core range, while the Memmingen site is focused on products made using fermentation.
Bieri added: “We’re making the steak and steak bites in Germany and very limited volumes of pastrami, which comes from the same muscle platform as the steak, it’s just cured differently and smoked differently. A minced meat that we’re launching soon is also coming off that platform, but we don’t have enough capacity to make as much as our customers would love.”
The Memmingen site currently produces about eight tons of product a day. Combined with the Kemptthal site, Planted makes around 20-25 tons a day with a 50:50 split between retail and foodservice.
Addressing recent media reports describing layoffs and internal dissatisfaction (anonymous sources described “total chaos,” a “culture of fear” and a “bad financial situation” on the Kununu review platform) Bieri said Planted had cut around 11% of its workforce over the past year.
“Certainly it’s not something you want to do, especially as a founder or manager but it’s a readjustment to the future,” said Bieri, who cofounded Planted in 2019 with Lukas Böni, Eric Stirnemann, Christoph Jenny, and Judith Wemmer.
“But we do try to have as many direct conversations as possible with everybody and our doors are always open. We have town halls with the whole company,” added Bieri, who would not comment on the firm’s runway, funding plans, or path to profitability.
The cuts reflected shifting priorities, technologies and geographic focus, and were concentrated in global management roles in Switzerland and in some markets where the business model is shifting.
Asked about the Netherlands, France and the UK, he said: “We have listings active at Tesco, Albert Heijn, and Carrefour, all of the big retailers in these markets. As we have scarce capacity, we have had to prioritize, so for us that was on DACH [Germany, Austria, and Switzerland]. But we do want to reach consumers all across Europe.”
Planted—which is backed by investors including L Catterton and Tengelmann Ventures —has historically sold products under its own brand. However, its fermentation platform could ultimately supply semi-finished products to local brands, manufacturers or butchers, said Bieri.
In France, for example, Planted is “exploring partnership opportunities” and new business models.
“I don’t think a better protein always needs to be branded,” said Bieri. “I don’t imagine a protein shelf being purple [the Planted brand color] across the world in 20 years. I think local brands prevail, local tastes prevail, and we do look at that very strategically.
“The question is with whom do we want to operate in certain market to maximize volumes and margins, for ease of doing business, and to make better local products for local consumers.”
He likened the model to supplying a carcass that can be processed differently in each market. Under such an arrangement, Planted would manufacture its fermented “muscle” in bulk, with local partners carrying out further processing and product development.
“Honestly I think I have a pretty good understanding of a typical German or Swiss consumer but I’m not necessarily [best-placed to] know what a consumer in northern Spain or southern France expects from a meat product,” he said. “I know what mistakes have been made by brands in the US that have come over to Europe with a totally un-European patty that never got any love here.”
The European plant-based meat market varies significantly by country but presents a very different picture from the struggling US category, where retail sales in particular have been declining precipitously in recent years, said Bieri.
In contrast, retail sales of alt meat in Germany grew 7.2% in the first quarter, while sales of Planted grew 49% driven by increased distribution and strong velocity, especially for the steak products, he claimed.
According to Bieri, alt meat sales in Austria and Italy are also growing, while Switzerland is broadly flat. Spain is declining and the UK remains “a bit difficult.”
He added: “In Austria and Switzerland we’re the market leader and in Germany we’re the fastest growing player and hopefully getting into a good challenger position.”
Planted has changed the names of its products in Switzerland following a court ruling preventing it from using terms such as “chicken” in plant-based product names, although it is still permitted to instruct consumers to “cook it like chicken,” he said.
“Actually, volumes have increased [since the label change], but we did adjust pricing downwards together with some of our partners so it’s hard to know [whether the name change had any direct impact].”
Despite recent challenges across plant-based meat, Bieri remains optimistic, although he expects further consolidation.
“I still truly believe the addressable market is the total protein market, and that the better technologies, the better unit economics, and the better products will prevail.”
Planted does not view itself as competing only within plant-based meat, he added, but within a broader protein market that will increasingly include animal, plant-based and cell-based products.
“Screw the ‘alt-protein’ [characterization]. The whole protein market will be so much more diverse in the future.”

articles.title_original: Prototype Ecorobotix ARA 1200 makes debut at ATH
articles.content:
Swiss manufacturer Ecorobotix is exhibiting a new 12-metre-wide ARA 1200 spot sprayer at the AgroTechniek Holland (ATH) trade fair.
Swiss manufacturer Ecorobotix is exhibiting a new 12-metre-wide ARA 1200 spot sprayer at the AgroTechniek Holland (ATH) trade fair. It is the first time the manufacturer has shown the machine to the public.
The Ecorobotix ARA 1200 on display at machinery trade fair ATH in Biddinghuizen is still at the prototype stage. Under the covers, however, the basic design is virtually final, although the cables, among other things, still need to be finished more neatly. Notably, the 12-metre-wide machine folds to a narrower transport width than the ARA 620.
The machine weighs 2,000 kg and has a wheel set at the rear. For transport, the centre sections fold upwards and the outer sections fold downwards. This positions the white protective cover on the outside and protects the spray nozzles underneath. The technology under the covers is identical to that of the already familiar 6-metre version. A new control box has now been added. Using load sensing, this box allows all hydraulic functions to be operated, such as folding in and out and locking the support wheels.
In addition to the ARA 1200 version, Ecorobotix is also introducing a 9-metre-wide version. The ARA 1200 will cost around €210,000. The ARA 900 will cost about €180,000. By comparison, the ARA 620 costs €134,000. The machines can be ordered, but are no longer available for delivery before next season. The available machines for that period have already sold out. Ecorobotix will deploy around 20 machines worldwide. According to the manufacturer, they are being rolled out to end customers at a steady pace so that service remains manageable.

articles.title_original: John Deere introduces AI assistant
articles.content:
John Deere is introducing a new AI assistant in John Deere Operations Center. The assistant, called JD, uses data on machines.
John Deere is introducing a new AI assistant in John Deere Operations Center. The assistant, called JD, uses data on machines, fields and operations stored in Operations Center to give farmers insight into the performance of their business.
The AI model is designed to function as a conversation partner for the farmer. JD is activated via a button in the Operations Center app .
From the app, users can ask questions about, for example, fuel consumption, machine performance and crop yields. JD analyses historical data available in Operations Center for this purpose. For example, the system can provide insight into fuel consumption over several years or help with a yield forecast. John Deere also cites determining the optimum harvest timing based on historical data as an application.
John Deere emphasises that users’ data remain under their control. The AI model bases its answers on the data available in the Operations Center account. The manufacturer says it does not sell farmers’ business data. Users also decide for themselves which third parties they share their data with and can stop that data flow at any time.
JD is now being tested with a limited number of users in the United States. John Deere wants to make the system more widely available later this year via Operations Center on the internet and mobile devices. Eventually, JD should also become accessible via displays in the cabs of tractors and other agricultural machines. It is not yet known whether JD will also come to the Netherlands.

articles.title_original: Odd.Bot gives Maverick weeding robot an upgrade
articles.content:
Dutch robot builder Odd.Bot is showing a new version of the Maverick weeding robot at the Agrotechniek Holland (ATH) trade fair.
Dutch robot builder Odd.Bot is showing a new version of the Maverick weeding robot at the Agrotechniek Holland (ATH) trade fair, from 16 to 19 September in the Dutch village of Biddinghuizen. The updated Maverick is equipped with a GPS system, and the control app has been renewed.
Maverick weeding robot uses the GPS system mainly as a check during operation. The robot recognises and drives over the ridges using a camera. Fundamentally, nothing has changed in this respect. The Maverick uses the GPS signal to check whether the machine has turned correctly on the headland and is driving in the right direction.
In addition, the user can set 2 separate geofences. These digital fences tell the robot where the field boundaries are. Robot builder Odd.Bot can set a second geofence in addition to the standard field boundary.
The second fence tells the robot within which area it is not allowed to turn. In the past, it has happened that the robot no longer saw any crop and thought it had reached the end of the field. As a result, the Maverick turned in the middle of the ridges. With the second fence, the robot can check whether it has already reached the end of the ridges or whether it still has to continue driving.
Odd.Bot has also updated the weeding robot’s control app. Here too, the further development relates to setting up geofencing, which is configured entirely via the app.
In addition, adjusting the robot is now easier. The parameters of the working area can now be set via the app. A number of other small improvements have also been implemented to improve ease of use.
The weeding units mounted under the Maverick operate independently of the robot. Each unit has its own camera and control software and, once connected to a 24-volt system, can be put to work immediately. Odd.Bot plans to sell the separate units to other manufacturers as well. Exploratory talks are under way between Odd.Bot and other market parties, but there is nothing concrete to report yet.

articles.title_original: Kubota launches WorkSmart Autosteer, bringing precision guidance to compact and utility equipment
articles.content:
Kubota Tractor Corporation has launched WorkSmart Autosteer, a precision guidance system built specifically for compact and utility equipment.
Kubota Tractor Corporation has launched WorkSmart Autosteer, a precision guidance system built specifically for compact and utility equipment. The system extends technology traditionally reserved for Kubota’s large ag tractors to a much broader slice of its equipment lineup, and it made its public debut at the Farm Progress Show in Boone, Iowa, in the United States.
Autosteer is the first product under WorkSmart, a new technology initiative Kubota describes as bringing factory-installed and retrofitted advancements to its equipment range while keeping the brand’s simplicity.
The system functions like an autopilot: it holds the steering line while the operator remains in control of the rest of the operation. Austin Hawkins, Senior Manager of Technology Sales and Marketing at Kubota North America, says the goal isn’t to take the operator out of the decision-making process, but to reduce fatigue and error, helping people cover more ground.
Most precision guidance products have historically been engineered for full-size row-crop tractors and sold as third-party retrofit kits. Kubota is taking a different route: WorkSmart Autosteer is engineered for the specific model it’s installed on, and can be sold, installed, serviced, warranted and financed through a single dealer.
Hawkins notes that autosteer technology was originally developed for large row-crop farmers, but has become increasingly complex and costly for smaller-acreage owners and other operators who don’t need features like section control or variable-rate application. WorkSmart Autosteer, he says, was built as a simpler, more affordable retrofit alternative for exactly that group.
Kubota’s own analysis of a typical operation points to several ways precision guidance pays off. Because the system holds the machine to a defined line, each pass registers consistently against the one before it – meaning seed, fertiliser and crop protection products land where they were planned, rather than wherever the previous pass happened to end.
That consistency also cuts down on overlap, the pass-to-pass duplication that manual steering tends to leave behind and that operations effectively pay for twice. Reducing it frees up more of the working day for new ground. Guidance also removes the operation’s dependence on an individual operator’s experience.
Kubota positions this as a single system that scales across an entire operation – from broadacre row-crop work to specialty crops, where consistent lines maintain row spacing, to turf and grounds maintenance, where the finished pattern is visible to anyone who looks at it.
Both tiers run through Kubota’s standard user interface and are designed to be approachable for first-time guidance users as well as experienced operators.
Authorised Kubota dealers can install the system in around two hours, including an operator training session. The system is managed through a free WorkSmart Autosteer app for iOS and Android, which also provides calibration guides, tutorials and troubleshooting videos, and lets users update and upgrade the system remotely.
WorkSmart Autosteer is compatible with select Kubota tractors, mowers and RTVs, and supports seeding and planting, tillage and cultivation, hay operations, spraying and spreading, mowing, road grading, and orchard and vineyard work.
The system carries a retail price of $6,000, excluding dealer installation, and is compatible with both new and used Kubota equipment. The system is available now through authorised Kubota dealers in the United States. No rollout dates have yet been announced for Europe, Australia or New Zealand.

articles.title_original: Voltrac moves Thor robot into pre-series production
articles.content:
Spanish agtech startup Voltrac has confirmed that its Thor autonomous electric robot is moving into pre-series production.
Spanish agtech startup Voltrac has confirmed that its Thor autonomous electric robot is moving into pre-series production. The company’s current Thor 2 model – recently demonstrated at a robotics event in Berlin – is described by its founders as a pre-serial vehicle, with the follow-up Thor 3 set to be the first production-ready version.
Voltrac plans to manufacture 96 units per year at its 1,200-square-metre factory in Valencia as a first phase, with longer-term blueprints targeting 1,000 vehicles per year. The Thor is not a converted diesel tractor with an electric motor dropped in. Voltrac built it from the ground up with autonomy as the starting point – and that distinction shapes nearly every engineering decision the company has made.
A conventional tractor carries a gearbox, oil filters, radiators, and a range of components that are prone to leaks and failures. Voltrac eliminated all of them. ‘By just removing them and electrifying, all we have is cables, instead of complex mechanisms’, company co-founder Francisco Infante Aguirre points out. The result is a machine with roughly 70 percent fewer components than a traditional tractor.
In place of a conventional drivetrain, Voltrac uses one electric motor per wheel – four in total – each paired with a reduction box. That configuration delivers 20,000 Newton metres of wheel torque. Four-wheel propulsion also means tight turning circles, which is relevant for orchard and vineyard work where headland space is limited and maximising planted rows directly increases yield.
If one motor fails, the other three carry on. ‘It’s a tool. It’s a workhorse. It has to carry on pushing’, according to Infante Aguirre. Repairs are designed to be done on-farm: each motor unit is accessible with two bolts, and Voltrac ships replacement units directly to the customer.
The Thor runs on hot-swappable battery packs that deliver up to 20 hours of uninterrupted operation. Rather than charging in the field, operators can carry a second set of packs and swap them out in minutes. Voltrac is also partnering with solar panel manufacturers to give customers a complete off-grid energy solution for charging.
Hydraulics are currently retained for implement compatibility, but Voltrac expects to phase them out as implements increasingly switch to electric power – eliminating fluid leaks on the field entirely.
One of the Thor’s central selling points for existing farm operations is its three-point hitch, which makes it compatible with any implement a farmer already owns. ‘For farmers, they don’t have to buy anything fancy or new’, Infante Aguirre explains.
The robot carries a dual compute module – one for functional safety, and one running a CPU-GPU combination for machine learning – along with stereo cameras front and rear and mono cameras on the sides. Every pass over a field can be used to monitor crop health, detect disease early, and optimise fertiliser and chemical inputs. The platform is also open to third parties: Voltrac allows external developers to run their own applications on the robot’s compute, effectively creating a marketplace for field-level tools.
Connectivity runs through dual SIM cards and a Starlink connection, with a remote teleoperator always available.
The key operational model is one operator supervising multiple vehicles across multiple fields simultaneously — rather than one person per machine. GPS precision sits at around 5 centimetres.
Voltrac produces the Thor in Valencia. Infante Aguirre: ‘The talent is here, the precision manufacturing is here. The know-how is here.’ With Thor 3 and serial production now the immediate target, Voltrac is moving from demonstration to delivery.

articles.title_original: French cooperative Océalia takes stake in weeding robot developer Cyclair
articles.content:
French agricultural cooperative group Océalia has acquired a minority stake in startup Cyclair.
French agricultural cooperative group Océalia has acquired a minority stake in startup Cyclair, backing the autonomous weeding robot developer as part of its Cap 2030 strategic plan. The investment, announced earlier this year, positions Cyclair’s mechanical weeding technology as a concrete alternative to chemical herbicides for Océalia's cooperative members across the French region Nouvelle-Aquitaine.
The robot is currently available in Western and Central Europe, North America, and Australia. Cyclair is already working on what comes next. Its development roadmap includes the addition of an electric weeding module, a crop health sensor, and a soil sensor – expanding the platform from a weeding tool into a broader agronomic data collection system.
For Océalia , the deal sits within its Sillon Responsable (Responsible Furrow) sustainability framework, which treats technology adoption as a long-term driver of commercially grounded, environmentally responsible farming. The cooperative is looking for solutions that reduce herbicide use without compromising farm profitability – and the economics of mechanical weeding at scale are central to that ambition.
Cyclair was founded in Pressac, in the Vienne department of France, by three partners with backgrounds in industry, robotics, and agriculture. Its GS and GW robot models are designed for open-field crops with row spacing between 30 and 90 centimetres, combining mechanical weeding, AI-based vision, and an optional targeted spot-spraying module.
Rather than relying on GPS, the robot uses a combination of cameras and LIDAR technology to identify crop rows directly, distinguish weeds from cultivated plants, and navigate around field obstacles – all without operator input. The system requires only field boundaries as input to begin operating autonomously.
The robot currently covers maize, sunflower, and rapeseed, with extensions to cereals, open-field vegetables, and specialty crops planned. Alongside weeding, it functions as an agronomic data collection platform, capturing leaf development metrics and feeding field-level monitoring through a dedicated application suite.
A central challenge for any mechanical weeding alternative is cost competitiveness. Conventional chemical weeding runs between €35 and €85 per hectare depending on pass complexity, according to both partners. They have set cost parity with that range as a target – making the system viable across a broad range of farm operations, not only among early adopters.
Business model: Direct sales, distributor network, and Robot-as-a-Service (RaaS)
Indication of price (Australia): AUD 151,000 – 250,000. Ongoing costs: Approx. AUD 10,000 per year (maintenance, support, software). Estimated ROI: AUD 200,000 after recovery of initial investment. Input cost savings: Approx. AUD 70,000 per year.
Markets: Western and Central Europe, North America, Australia
