articles.title_original: CIMMYT and APSA forge new opportunities for advanced innovations in maize for the Asian region
articles.content:
By Sara Safikhan, Knowledge and Capacity Building Manager, Asia and Pacific Seed Alliance (APSA), Bangkok; Seetharam Ananda, Chief Technology Officer, Nuziveedu Seeds, Hyderabad & Chair of Special Interest Group of Field Crops (SIG-FC), APSA, and P.H. Zaidi, CIMMYT Asia Maize Program, Hyderabad
By Sara Safikhan, Knowledge and Capacity Building Manager, Asia and Pacific Seed Alliance (APSA), Bangkok; Seetharam Ananda, Chief Technology Officer, Nuziveedu Seeds, Hyderabad & Chair of Special Interest Group of Field Crops (SIG-FC), APSA, and P.H. Zaidi, CIMMYT Asia Maize Program, Hyderabad
CIMMYT and the Asia Pacific Seed Association (APSA) convened a high-level meeting in Hyderabad on 21 August 2026 to explore opportunities for closer collaboration between international agricultural research and the Asian seed industry, and to bring together perspectives from across regions and sectors. The meeting brought together representatives from APSA’s Special Interest Group on Field Crops and CIMMYT’s global and regional teams to discuss how global maize science, technology, and industry experience can work together to address emerging challenges in maize and meet the exponentially increasing demands in the Asia region. The discussions were built around earlier conversations between APSA and CIMMYT and focused on how stronger connections between research institutions and seed companies can help translate scientific advances into practical solutions for breeding programs and seed markets across Asia and the wider tropical regions.
The meeting covered a broad range of topics, reflecting the evolving priorities of the maize and broader seed sector. These included emerging and transboundary pests and diseases, disease resistance and screening, germplasm access and characterization, modern breeding approaches, genome editing, speed breeding, hybrid seed production technologies, and opportunities related to specialized end uses of maize.
Participants also discussed the importance of strengthening breeding programs through better use of genetic resources, improved data, and modern breeding tools. The conversation highlighted that while advanced technologies can open new possibilities, their value ultimately depends on how effectively they respond to real breeding and market needs. Rather than attempting to define a broad portfolio of activities immediately, the discussion emphasized the importance of identifying practical areas where collaboration can demonstrate tangible value for seed companies and breeders.
The meeting also included a visit to CIMMYT’s experimental and research fields in Hyderabad, which gave APSA members and industry participants an opportunity to see CIMMYT’s breeding materials, research facilities, and field-based activities first-hand. The field visit complemented the technical discussions by providing a closer look at the environments, materials, and research infrastructure underpinning CIMMYT’s work. For industry participants, it also offered an opportunity to connect scientific discussions with the realities of breeding and product development. The combination of discussion and field exposure helped create a more direct exchange between researchers and industry practitioners, moving the conversation from what is technically possible to what could be practically useful for seed companies.
One major strength of the meeting was its international character. Under the leadership of Dr. Ashish Saxena, Director of the Global Maize Program at CIMMYT, the maize scientists from India, Kenya, Mexico and Zimbabwe brought perspectives and experiences from different regions, including Africa, Asia and Latin America, reflecting the increasingly interconnected nature of crop improvement and seed systems. The exchange highlighted that challenges affecting maize production and breeding are rarely confined to a single geography. Emerging pests and diseases, climate-related pressures, changing production systems and new breeding technologies are creating common questions across tropical regions, while solutions may increasingly benefit from collaboration and knowledge exchange across borders. This global perspective was especially relevant for APSA, which plays a key role in connecting Asia’s seed industry with international research, innovation, and capacity-building networks.
For APSA, the meeting represents an important step towards creating more structured channels through which its members can engage with CIMMYT’s scientific expertise, germplasm resources, technologies, services and training opportunities. The discussions also highlighted potential opportunities for future technical learning and capacity development, including areas related to molecular and modern breeding, genome editing, and other emerging technologies. Such initiatives could help industry professionals strengthen technical capabilities while also building greater understanding between research institutions and commercial breeding programs.
The meeting concluded with agreement to continue developing the areas of mutual interest and to explore concrete opportunities for collaboration. Further discussions will help determine which areas can be developed into practical initiatives involving APSA members. For the Asian seed sector, the value of such engagement extends beyond individual projects. Creating spaces where researchers, breeders, and industry leaders can exchange knowledge, identify common priorities, and understand each other’s capabilities can help strengthen the pathways between research, capacity development, and innovation.
As APSA and CIMMYT move forward, the Hyderabad meeting represents more than a single event. It signals a growing commitment to connect regional seed industry needs with global agricultural research expertise. By working together, both organizations can help strengthen innovation pathways, support stronger breeding programs, and contribute to a more resilient and competitive seed sector across Asia.
Raghavendra Singh and K.M. Singh, ANDUAT, Ayodhya, and P.H. Zaidi, CIMMYT
South Asia’s smallholder farmers are no strangers to climate stress, but erratic rainfall and rising temperatures are pushing rainfed agriculture to its limits. Five new maize hybrids from CIMMYT’s South Asia breeding program, validated across up to 106 trial locations in India, Bangladesh, Nepal, and Pakistan, offer a science-based response
CIMMYT’s systematic and targeted breeding strategy in South Asia helped develop 20 high yielding and heat-stress tolerant maize hybrids. The ongoing efforts strengthens the livelihood of farm families who are highly vulnerable to climate change in the Asian tropics.

articles.title_original: Building Grain and Flour Phenotyping Capacity at Kiboko (Kenya) and Thies (Senegal): A Journey in Progress
articles.content:
CIMMYT is expanding grain quality research in Africa, giving scientists new tools to uncover the nutritional and processing potential hidden inside dryland crops.
The establishment of grain and flour phenotyping platforms for groundnut, sorghum, pearl millet and finger millet represents an important milestone, but it is only one step in a longer journey.
Across CIMMYT and its partners under the Africa Dryland Crops Improvement network (ADCIN), we are expanding the capacity to generate meaningful information on grain quality, nutritional value, processing characteristics, and end-use potential. By establishing these platforms within the regions where these crops are grown and studied, researchers, breeders, students, and partners are gaining access to tools and data to support innovation and decision-making. It’s exciting to see instruments being installed and laboratories becoming operational, but the true impact of these investments will be measured by how effectively the tools are used to create value for research, breeding, education, and agrifood systems.
These platforms bring together high-throughput phenotyping tools that enable rapid assessment of grain and flour quality traits in groundnut, sorghum, pearl millet and finger millet. Beyond physical grain characteristics, they generate information on nutritional and functional attributes, including protein, oil, starch, grain color, and essential minerals including iron (Fe), zinc (Zn), and calcium (Ca). By making quality assessment fast and accessible, these tools can support breeding programs, nutrition research, and product development. And these platforms can also be used for other crops.
While these platforms are in the early stages of operation, there are encouraging signs of growing interest among user groups. Plant breeders are beginning to consider how nutritional and processing quality traits can complement traditional breeding targets such as yield, adaptation, and resilience. Laboratory technicians are building experience and confidence in generating quality-related data, while students and young scientists are exploring opportunities to incorporate grain quality into their research. Collaborators are identifying potential applications, and interest is emerging among professionals and agripreneurs about product development and value-adding opportunities. These early interactions suggest that the foundations for a broader grain quality community are taking shape.
This progress is the result of collaboration across teams and institutions. It builds on the commitment, experience, and support of CIMMYT colleagues in Senegal, Kenya, and our Grain and Food Quality and Nutrition Laboratory in Mexico, and our partners at the Senegalese Institute for Agricultural Research’s (ISRA) Regional Center for the Improvement of Adaptation to Drought (CERAAS). Each contribution, whether technical, scientific, logistical, or operational, has been essential in moving this initiative forward.
Much work remains to be done. Methods must be validated and optimized, and data management systems and analytical workflows must continue to evolve. A recent achievement was overcoming challenges in calibrating software and integrating data by using CropSense , a platform developed by CERAAS’s Bioinformatics and Artificial Intelligence team. This collaboration with CERAAS demonstrated how local expertise, digital innovation, and scientific partnership can accelerate the effective deployment and utilization of phenotyping technologies.
The next phase must go beyond generating more data; it must build a community of practice around grain quality. This community must ask new questions, share experiences, develop applications, and demonstrate the value of phenotyping quality traits for crops that are central to food security, nutrition, and livelihoods across Africa. We are particularly excited about the work that two VACS fellows, Odilon-Parfait Akotchaye and Meron Bogale, will begin next month in Kiboko, Texcoco, and Thiès, contributing to this growing network of collaboration, learning, and innovation.
We have made an important start. Now follows the crucial task of ensuring that knowledge, skills, partnerships, and demand for these new platforms grow, and result in better varieties and products for farmers and consumers.
Africa’s next food revolution is taking shape in a Nairobi lab, led by a new generation of researchers. Over three weeks, more than 40 emerging scientists learned to read the continent’s future in genomic data and crops long overlooked.

articles.title_original: Where Research Journeys Begin: Nurturing the Next Generation of Agricultural Researchers
articles.content:
In India, 30 Kerala Agricultural University students complete five-week research training with CIMMYT and partner scientists in Hyderabad, Telangana.
Where Research Journeys Begin: Nurturing the Next Generation of Agricultural Researchers
Long before Sanjaya Rajaram became one of the world’s most influential wheat breeders, he was a young researcher learning alongside Norman Borlaug in Mexico.
Rajaram credited Borlaug with teaching him the value of hands-on field research over desk-based work. Born on a small farm in Uttar Pradesh, Rajaram went on to build an extraordinary career at CIMMYT, developing wheat varieties that reached farmers around the world and eventually receiving the World Food Prize. His legacy, however, extended beyond his science. Over decades at CIMMYT, he trained and mentored hundreds of young researchers, many of whom went on to lead research programs themselves.
His journey from young researcher to scientist and mentor reflects an idea central to CIMMYT’s approach to capacity building. Scientific progress depends not only on generating knowledge, but also on investing in people who can take that knowledge forward and find solutions to emerging challenges.
Decades later, that tradition continues through opportunities for students to step beyond university classrooms and experience agricultural research first-hand. In India, one such opportunity has brought students —over 30 final-year undergrads— from Kerala Agricultural University (KAU) to CIMMYT for the past three years.
For many KAU students, the intensive internship at CIMMYT India is their first opportunity to experience what working in an international agricultural research organization involves.
The most recent cohort brought together seven final-year undergraduate students from a batch of 55 applicants as part of CIMMYT-IRRI-FAS (Foundation for Agrarian Studies) internship program at CIMMYT in Hyderabad. They were selected based on the statement of purpose submitted and an interview with Vijesh Krishna, Principal Scientist (Socioeconomics) at CIMMYT, who leads the KAU internship program for CIMMYT.
These interns arrived with academic foundations in agricultural science and economics. What awaited them was a different kind of classroom. Over five weeks, the interns followed the research process from start to finish. They began with research methodology and an introduction to CIMMYT and CGIAR’s research areas, then moved to research question identification, descriptive and empirical analysis, and drafting findings. A field visit near Hyderabad connected their learning with real-world agricultural contexts, while engagement with the FAS brought perspectives on rural and agrarian issues. The internship culminated in final presentations, where students brought together their research questions, analysis and findings before researchers and mentors.
Beyond completing modules, the students saw how questions are framed, data examined, evidence interpreted and findings debated. There were unfamiliar concepts and new analytical approaches to navigate. What impressed their mentors was not simply how much they learned, but how they approached the experience.
Alfiya Nizar , who won the Best Intern Award in 2026, describes the process as, “What I learned from this internship is that research does not always go as planned. Emerging contexts in the field, changing questions at times to ensure robust results, and unexpected findings taught me to stay flexible and adapt. By my final presentation, the challenges felt worthwhile. The experience and feedback from my mentors strengthened my interest in applied research and will help guide my future career.”
That transition from studying research to participating in it is where internships can add something distinctive to university education. Academic programs provide theoretical and methodological foundations, while an active research environment allows students to see those concepts questioned, tested and applied. Five weeks cannot teach all the nuances of research. Those come with experience, mistakes, discoveries and many more research questions. But five weeks can begin to teach something fundamental: how to think like a researcher.
For Athul Krishna , one of the seven interns of the 2026 batch, the five weeks gave that experience a larger sense of purpose. “This internship greatly increased my curiosity about empirical research and gave me the confidence to pursue socioeconomic research in my further studies. The experience became even more rewarding when, soon after completing my degree this year, I returned to CIMMYT, this time as a research consultant. I have the opportunity to put everything into practice now as a researcher.”
Often, important lessons happen outside formal training sessions. They emerge when a scientist explains why one methodology was chosen over another, a mentor questions an assumption, or an unexpected result leads to a new discussion.
According to Vijesh Krishna, these interactions are central to the experience. “Such experiences can help demystify research. Students discover that research is not simply about arriving at the correct answer. It starts from asking the right questions, accepting uncertainty, developing critical thinking, perseverance and, importantly, learning to work as a team. This year, we collaborated with IRRI and FAS, and this has helped students get a broad picture of socioeconomic research beyond the institutional boundaries.”
The benefits can extend beyond technical knowledge. “Internships can build confidence, communication and problem-solving skills, while exposing students to interdisciplinary ways of working. For some students, a meaningful career in international agricultural research can begin in learning spaces like those created by CIMMYT’s socioeconomics team in India,” says Stephen Gudz, Director of CIMMYT’s Sustainable Agrifood Systems . “I am glad that I could interact with the interns of the 2026 batch and encourage them for their future research endeavours,” he added.
Hadiya Jaz experienced this first-hand. When she interned at CIMMYT in 2024, research was something she had largely encountered through university studies. The internship gave her a glimpse of what doing research could look like and influenced what she chose to do next.
“I still remember my internship days at CIMMYT in 2024. CIMMYT gave me a different perspective on applying my academic knowledge in a real-world scenario. Our study on women’s Self-Help Groups in Kerala further strengthened my interest in social sciences and prompted me to pursue my Master’s in Agricultural Extension Education.”
Her experience illustrates an impact that cannot necessarily be measured on the final day of an internship. Sometimes, the more meaningful question is what students choose to do afterwards. Supporting this internship program from KAU, Dr Archana Sathyan Assistant Prof. at KAU said, “I have been closely involved with the CIMMYT-KAU internship program since 2023 and I have seen how exposure to and interaction with scientists and researchers strengthen students’ research aptitude, skills, and career aspirations. Its impact goes beyond individual interns, as the program builds networks and inspires other students to explore new research and career opportunities.”
Today’s students will encounter increasingly complex agricultural challenges, from climate change and natural resource pressures to rapidly evolving technologies and changing rural economies. Addressing them will require researchers who can work across disciplines and connect scientific evidence with the realities of farmers and food systems.
Universities will remain central to preparing that generation. Partnerships with research organizations can complement this by exposing students to applied research while they are still shaping their interests, skills and ambitions. For CIMMYT, with more than six decades of collaboration with India, these opportunities are an investment in the people who will carry agricultural research and solutions forward.
That investment can have a multiplier effect. A student mentored today may become a researcher developing innovations tomorrow and, in time, a mentor to another generation.
At the end of five weeks, the interns leave CIMMYT with new skills and a better understanding of socioeconomic research. But some of the more consequential outcomes may take years to become visible.
One may pursue a Master’s, as Hadiya did. Another may discover a question that eventually becomes a PhD. Others may become agricultural economists, scientists, development practitioners or policymakers. In time, some may mentor young researchers themselves.
Sanjaya Rajaram once arrived at CIMMYT as a young researcher. He learned alongside Borlaug, became an extraordinary scientist, and then invested his own knowledge in generations who followed him.
Today’s interns will write their own stories. The value of an internship extends far beyond the time spent in a research environment. For these students, five weeks of learning, mentorship and discovery may be only the beginning, shaping the questions they ask, the paths they pursue and the contributions they make to agricultural research in the years ahead.
Sahad Puliyancheri from the 2026 internship batch shares this optimism. “The five-week internship gave me a strong foundation to understand both the real-world impact and limitations of socioeconomic research. As I move forward, I remain committed to enriching my current capacity to undertake research that informs policy and decision-making, strengthens understanding, and supports farming communities.”

articles.title_original: IRRI and CIMMYT Strengthen Collaboration to Accelerate Delivery of Climate-Resilient Crop Varieties
articles.content:
Los Baños, Philippines / Texcoco, Mexico (10 September 2026) — The International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) and CIMMYT are strengthening their collaboration to advance CGIAR's vision of a more integrated, efficient and data-driven crop breeding system. Through a new collaboration, led by CIM
Los Baños, Philippines / Texcoco, Mexico (10 September 2026) — The International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) and CIMMYT are strengthening their collaboration to advance CGIAR’s vision of a more integrated, efficient and data-driven crop breeding system.
Through a new collaboration, led by CIMMYT with funding support from the Gates Foundation, the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) will provide substantial technical and operational contributions. The investment aims to modernize breeding pipelines across a portfolio of high-priority crop-and-region combinations, sharpening product profiles, improving trial design and data quality, and strengthening ties with national research systems, so that CGIAR and national breeding programs can advance and release new varieties faster and more predictably.
The initiative is part of a broader CGIAR effort to modernize crop breeding systems and strengthen food security in low- and middle-income countries through Breeding for Tomorrow , CGIAR Science Progr am bringing Centers together around a shared vision for modern crop breeding.
The partnership will leverage the complementary expertise of both CGIAR Centers to enhance crop breeding efficiency through shared services, common tools, harmonized processes, regional collaboration, and data-driven decision-making across CGIAR breeding networks in Southeast Asia.
IRRI will play a central role in delivering technical, operational, and coordination support across these breeding networks.
Key areas of collaboration include strengthening shared genotyping services, expanding the adoption of CGIAR’s digital breeding tools, streamlining breeding workflows and logistics, and enhancing analytics and bioinformatics capacity across the network.
Through its Genotyping Services Laboratory and Digital Solutions teams, IRRI will help deliver these priorities by providing CGIAR and partner breeders with access to shared breeding services and supporting the adoption of the Breeding Analytics Pipeline, Bioflow , and the Enterprise Breeding System (EBS). Together, these tools will enable more efficient, data-driven breeding decisions. The collaboration will also promote compliance with global standards for data sharing, intellectual property, and open access, ensuring that research outputs are widely accessible and can be effectively shared and reused.
The project will also support capacity development and business process management to standardize operations across breeding programs and build long-term institutional capability.
These activities will be coordinated and align with the vision of the Breeding Resources Area of Work within CGIAR Breeding for Tomorrow, which provides world-class shared breeding and research services to CGIAR and national partner breeding teams worldwide.
“Our partnership with IRRI has repeatedly shown what’s possible when two of the world’s leading crop research institutions align their expertise and move with urgency”, said Dr Bram Govaerts, CIMMYT Director General. “This project builds on that track record, putting shared breeding infrastructure and technical know-how directly into the hands of CGIAR and national breeding programs, to reach farmers faster. Every improved variety we deliver sooner translates directly into food security and livelihood gains.”
The project is expected to deliver measurable outcomes, including operational genotyping services, improved sample logistics systems, increased uptake of digital breeding tools, and strengthened analytical capabilities across breeding programs.
“This agreement highlights the significance of strong partnerships in achieving widespread impact,” said Dr. Yvonne Pinto, IRRI Director General. “By leveraging our expertise and aligning with CGIAR’s shared vision, we are developing more efficient, collaborative, and responsive breeding systems that meet the evolving needs of farmers and food systems worldwide.”
IRRI and CIMMYT will continue to engage closely with partners across Asia and Africa to support the implementation of the project and lay the groundwork for expanded efforts in future phases.
CIMMYT is a cutting-edge, non-profit, international organization dedicated to solving tomorrow’s problems today. It is entrusted with fostering improved quantity, quality, and dependability of production systems and basic cereals such as maize, wheat, triticale, sorghum, millets, and associated crops through applied agricultural science, particularly in the Global South, through building strong partnerships. This combination enhances the livelihood trajectories and resilience of millions of resource-poor farmers, while working towards a more productive, inclusive, and resilient agrifood system within planetary boundaries.

articles.title_original: New evidence strengthens business case for climate smart mechanization in Zimbabwe’s sorghum sector
articles.content:
Field-tested technologies and financial analysis are helping guide smarter investments in sustainable mechanization for smallholder farmers.
As Zimbabwe continues to expand sorghum production to strengthen resilience to climate variability, investments in mechanization must answer two important questions: Do the technologies work under local conditions? And can they support financially sustainable service businesses?
To help answer these questions, the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) supported Food and Agriculture Resilience Mission Pillar 3 (FARM P3 ) implemented by CIMMYT generated new evidence that is helping the Government of Zimbabwe, financial institutions and private-sector partners make informed mechanization investments. The work combines field-based machinery assessments with financial analysis to provide practical guidance for scaling mechanization in Zimbabwe’s sorghum value chain.
Rather than relying on manufacturer specifications or data generated elsewhere, CIMMYT scientists evaluated basin diggers, two-wheel tractor-mounted rippers, ploughs and trailers under real smallholder farming conditions in Zimbabwe.
The assessments measured field capacity, fuel consumption, labour requirements and operational efficiency to determine how different technologies perform in local production systems.
The results showed that rippers completed land preparation more efficiently than conventional ploughs while disturbing less soil, making them well suited to conservation agriculture practices. Basin diggers also demonstrated strong potential to reduce labour while improving the precise placement of seed, manure and fertilizer. Trailers expanded the value of mechanization by supporting transport of agricultural inputs and harvested grain throughout the season.
These findings provide practical information for farmers, equipment suppliers and development partners seeking technologies that improve productivity while strengthening climate resilience.
Reliable machinery is only part of the equation. Mechanization will only expand if entrepreneurs can build profitable businesses that provide affordable services to farmers.
CIMMYT therefore assessed the financial viability of selected mechanization technologies using investment indicators including Net Present Value, Internal Rate of Return, Benefit-Cost Ratio and Return on Investment.
The analysis showed positive financial potential across the technologies assessed when supported by sound business management and adequate equipment utilization. Basin diggers and trailers demonstrated particularly strong commercial opportunities because they support multiple income-generating services throughout the agricultural season.
The findings also reinforce a shift from machinery ownership to mechanization as a service. By offering ripping, basin preparation and transport services, entrepreneurs can improve equipment utilization while enabling more smallholder farmers to access mechanization without purchasing machinery themselves.
The findings were reviewed by representatives from government, financial institutions, research organizations, development partners, equipment suppliers and farmer organizations, who endorsed the value of the evidence while recommending refinements to strengthen the final reports.
Participants called for continued machinery testing under different seasonal conditions, stronger operator training, improved maintenance systems and financing models that respond to the needs of emerging mechanization businesses.
As Zimbabwe continues to strengthen climate-resilient sorghum production, locally generated evidence is helping reduce uncertainty around mechanization investments. By combining technical performance with financial analysis, FARM P3 provided decision-makers with practical information to guide investments that improve productivity, strengthen conservation agriculture and expand access to mechanization services for smallholder farmers.

In Mérida, Yucatán, we took another step toward strengthening seed systems in southern and southeastern Mexico through our collaboration with the Centro de Investigación Científica de Yucatán (CICY).
As part of this partnership, we are implementing the Applied Training Program on Seed Systems: Seed Production, Conservation and Seed Bank Management, combining scientific knowledge, territorial experience and technical support to build capacities that can be applied and multiplied directly within communities.
The training brings together around 35 technicians from Campeche, Yucatán, Quintana Roo, Oaxaca and Morelos, linked to programs and initiatives that support farmers, as well as 26 community leaders and young students, primarily from Quintana Roo, Yucatán and Campeche.
Through theoretical sessions and practical activities, participants are strengthening their knowledge of seed production, selection, conservation, management and quality, as well as formal and informal seed systems, post-harvest management, certification, commercialization and seed bank management.
The goal goes beyond training. We want this knowledge to reach communities and be multiplied through technicians, farmers, organizations and programs working directly in the field, helping conserve agricultural diversity, increase the availability of seeds adapted to local conditions and strengthen the resilience of production systems.
As Jelle Van Loon, Regional Representative for Latin America, highlighted, strengthening seed systems allows us to connect our science with technical capacities and local networks, bringing practical solutions adapted to the needs of farmers and their communities.
This collaboration is part of our efforts to bring science closer to the communities we work with and build capacities that remain in the territories, helping them better prepare for increasingly changing production and climate conditions.

articles.title_original: Exploring how AI can bring farmer voices closer to breeding
articles.content:
On Wednesday 19th August 2026, we welcomed a delegation of Chinese science communicators and digital influencers to Kenya for an exchange on how artificial intelligence can help agricultural research better understand farmers and bring their priorities closer to breeding decisions. The v
On Wednesday 19th August 2026, we welcomed a delegation of Chinese science communicators and digital influencers to Kenya for an exchange on how artificial intelligence can help agricultural research better understand farmers and bring their priorities closer to breeding decisions.
The visit formed part of a Gates Foundation China initiative exploring how AI can help reduce inequality and deliver impact in real-world settings. For our colleagues, it was also an opportunity to look beyond the technology itself and explore a practical question: can AI help us listen to farmers better?
The delegation began its engagement with our teams in Nairobi, learning about the organization’s market intelligence work and how insights from farmers, consumers and markets can help inform crop improvement priorities.
The conversation then moved to the field at KALRO Katumani in Machakos, where the delegation saw Sikia, an AI-powered tool developed by the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT, being used in conversations with farmers.
Sikia takes a different approach from a conventional survey. Rather than moving through a fixed questionnaire, the tool responds to what a farmer says, asking relevant follow-up questions that can uncover the reasoning, preferences and trade-offs behind an answer. It can also work offline, making it practical for research in areas where connectivity is limited.
That ability to probe deeper is particularly relevant to crop improvement. Farmers make decisions based on much more than yield alone. Understanding which traits they value, why they value them and what trade-offs they are willing to make can provide breeding teams with stronger evidence when determining which traits and products to prioritize.
Seeing the tool at work also opened a wider conversation about how AI can complement, rather than replace, engagement with farmers. Its value lies in helping researchers capture more from those conversations and connect farmer insights more effectively with market intelligence and breeding.
The visit highlighted the value of collaboration across us, KALRO and CGIAR partners in exploring practical applications of emerging technologies and ensuring that innovation remains grounded in farmers’ realities.
As we continue strengthening the connection between market intelligence and crop improvement, tools such as Sikia offer another way to make farmer voices count — turning better listening into better evidence and, ultimately, better-informed breeding.

articles.title_original: Turning research into investment for Zimbabwe’s sorghum farmers
articles.content:
How FARM P3 is helping build the partnerships, business models and confidence needed to expand sustainable mechanization
Research can identify technologies that improve productivity. Demonstration plots can show farmers what is possible. But lasting agricultural transformation depends on something more: investment, partnerships and local businesses that can take proven innovations to scale.
That is the opportunity emerging from the Food and Agriculture Resilience Mission Pillar 3 (FARM P3) , where the CIMMYT, with support from the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD), is helping build the evidence, partnerships and business models needed to strengthen mechanization across Zimbabwe’s sorghum value chain.
With practical evidence now available, the FARM P3 Zimbabwe Results Webinar shifted the focus from generating research to creating the partnerships, financing mechanisms and business opportunities needed to expand sustainable mechanization across Zimbabwe’s sorghum value chain. Bringing together representatives from government, financial institutions, development partners, equipment suppliers and farmer organizations, the discussions highlighted how coordinated action can turn proven innovations into greater investment, wider adoption and lasting benefits for smallholder farmers.
One of the strongest messages emerging from the webinar was that successful investment begins with credible, locally generated evidence. Over the past year, FARM P3 has produced three complementary evidence products that together strengthen decision-making across the mechanization value chain. Field assessments confirmed that technologies such as two-wheel tractor-mounted rippers, basin diggers and multi-crop threshers can improve operational efficiency while supporting conservation agriculture.
Financial analysis demonstrated that mechanization services can operate as commercially viable businesses, particularly when entrepreneurs combine complementary services to maximize equipment utilization throughout the agricultural season. A third assessment identified and profiled prospective mechanization service providers with the technical and business potential to expand services across Zimbabwe’s major sorghum-producing districts.
Opening the webinar, IFAD Country Director Francisco Rispoli reinforced the importance of translating research into practical action. “This project was never just about introducing mechanization technologies. It was about demonstrating practical solutions that strengthen private sector engagement, improve market opportunities and create lasting benefits for smallholder farmers. The evidence generated through FARM P3 now provides a strong foundation for future investment and partnership.” His remarks reflected a shared view among participants that evidence helps reduce uncertainty for investors, financial institutions and development partners while creating greater confidence to support commercially viable mechanization models.
The webinar reinforced that expanding mechanization will depend on more than access to equipment. Participants highlighted the importance of strengthening the wider ecosystem that supports mechanization, from financing and business development to after-sales service, maintenance networks and stronger market linkages.
Innovative financing approaches, including equipment leasing, blended finance and viability-based lending, were identified as practical options for reducing investment risk while improving access to mechanization services for smallholder farmers. Participants also encouraged closer collaboration between financial institutions, equipment suppliers, government agencies and off-takers to strengthen opportunities for emerging mechanization enterprises.
Reflecting on the broader significance of the initiative, Minenhle Ngwenya, Programme Officer at IFAD, noted that FARM P3 has helped create an important platform for collaboration. “One of the project’s greatest strengths has been its ability to bring together government, the private sector, financial institutions and development partners around shared evidence and shared objectives,” he said. “That collaboration creates opportunities to continue expanding mechanization through partnerships that respond to farmers’ needs,” Minenhle added.
Discussions throughout the webinar highlighted that mechanization is as much about people and businesses as it is about technology. Through FARM P3, prospective mechanization service providers have been profiled and linked with financial institutions, equipment suppliers, extension services and Agricultural Producer Groups. These connections help create new opportunities for entrepreneurs while improving farmers’ access to reliable and affordable mechanization services.
This integrated approach is particularly important for Zimbabwe’s sorghum value chain, where timely land preparation, harvesting and post-harvest handling can significantly improve productivity, reduce labour demands and strengthen farmers’ participation in reliable markets. Participants agreed that building sustainable mechanization systems will require continued investment in entrepreneurship, technical skills, market development and partnerships that enable local businesses to thrive.
Delivering the closing remarks on behalf of the Chief Director of Agricultural Engineering, Mechanization and Farm Infrastructure Development, Engineer Nhlanhla Magama called on partners to build on the momentum created through FARM P3. “The evidence generated through FARM P3 demonstrates that sustainable mechanization is achievable through strong collaboration. Continued investment, innovation and partnerships will be essential to expand access to mechanization services, strengthen the sorghum value chain and support Zimbabwe’s broader agricultural transformation.”
As Zimbabwe continues to strengthen climate-resilient agriculture, FARM P3 is demonstrating how evidence can do more than inform decisions. By connecting research with finance, entrepreneurship and strategic partnerships, the initiative is helping create practical investment pathways that can expand sustainable mechanization, strengthen the sorghum value chain and improve opportunities for the smallholder farmers at its center.

articles.title_original: Growing Zimbabwe’s next generation of mechanization entrepreneurs
articles.content:
A new pipeline of business-ready service providers is creating opportunities to expand mechanization beyond the life of FARM P3.
For many smallholder farmers, owning agricultural machinery remains beyond reach. The future of mechanization, however, does not depend on every farmer owning a tractor. It depends on whether reliable mechanization services are available when farmers need them most.
Recognizing this, CIMMYT, through the Food and Agriculture Resilience Mission Pillar 3 (FARM P3) – an initiative under the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) and funded by the French Government – has invested in identifying and strengthening the entrepreneurs who will drive mechanization long after the project ends.
A structured assessment screened approximately 400 prospective mechanization entrepreneurs across districts supported under the Smallholder Agriculture Cluster Project (SACP). From this process, 73 entrepreneurs and Agricultural Producer Groups were identified as investment-ready candidates with the technical and business potential to establish sustainable mechanization enterprises.
Mechanization succeeds when farmers can access reliable, affordable services close to home. That requires entrepreneurs who can manage equipment, build viable businesses and respond to local demand throughout the agricultural season.
The assessment looked beyond machinery ownership to evaluate business readiness, operational capacity, access to markets and the ability to grow sustainable enterprises. It also highlighted the importance of partnerships among financial institutions, equipment suppliers, government agencies and development partners in creating an enabling environment for mechanization businesses.
The entrepreneur pipeline builds on momentum already created through FARM P3. Machinery demonstrations, awareness meetings and stronger engagement with private-sector partners have increased interest in mechanization among farmers, creating new opportunities for service providers to expand their businesses.
The results indicate that the pipeline consists of middle-aged farmers, with an average age of 48 years. The majority (85%) of the pipeline SPs completed secondary education level, and 78% are linked to off takers showing strong market integration. However, participation by women and youth remains limited, with women accounting for only 17% of the interviewed prospective and youth representing just 9%. This demographic composition suggests that the pipeline is largely dominated by older male farmers, highlighting the need for targeted strategies to enhance the inclusion of women and young farmers. Most pipeline SPs operate mixed crop-livestock systems, own relatively large landholdings compared to typical smallholder farmers, and derive most of their income from crop and livestock sales
As demand grows, these entrepreneurs will play a critical role in ensuring that farmers can access timely land preparation, planting and transport services that improve productivity and strengthen climate resilience.
The assessment also recognized the importance of expanding opportunities for women and young entrepreneurs, whose participation can increase employment while strengthening the sustainability of mechanization services in rural communities.
While FARM P3 has laid the groundwork, the mechanization service provider pipeline represents one of the project’s most enduring legacies.
The entrepreneurs identified through the assessment provide a foundation for scaling mechanization well beyond the project’s lifetime. Supported by continued partnerships with financial institutions, equipment suppliers, government agencies as well as linkages with the IFAD funded loan, SACP, they have the potential to expand access to mechanization services across Zimbabwe’s sorghum-growing districts.
By investing in local businesses as well as technologies, CIMMYT and its partners are helping build a mechanization system that can continue growing, creating opportunities for rural entrepreneurs while improving livelihoods for smallholder farmers.

articles.title_original: Piden comunidades mayas de Hopelchén cumplimiento al fallo de la Corte vs pesticidas
articles.content:
El fallo de la Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nación (SCJN) a favor de 17 comunidades mayas de Hopelchén, que pedían la protección de la justicia frente a la grave contaminación del agua por pesticidas que prevalece en sus comunidades, es una buena noticia que debe ser acompañada de forma urgente por acciones articuladas …
El fallo de la Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nación (SCJN) a favor de 17 comunidades mayas de Hopelchén, que pedían la protección de la justicia frente a la grave contaminación del agua por pesticidas que prevalece en sus comunidades, es una buena noticia que debe ser acompañada de forma urgente por acciones articuladas que garanticen la efectividad de la sentencia y el monitoreo de la calidad del agua en la región.
En conferencia, el Colectivo de Comunidades Mayas de los Chenes, acompañados de especialistas científicos y del equipo legal, hablaron sobre los elementos relevantes de la sentencia y el importante precedente que ésta sienta a favor de la naturaleza y los derechos humanos de las comunidades mayas de la Península de Yucatán.
Instaron a las autoridades implicadas en la resolución a trabajar de forma conjunta para hacer efectivo el acceso a la justicia para las comunidades y sus medios de vida.
Resaltaron que la resolución de la SCJN llega luego de seis años, dado que en el 2020 las 17 comunidades de Hopelchén iniciaron un proceso de amparo por el aumento en el uso de sustancias altamente peligrosas en la agricultura industrializada, las cuales por su naturaleza, terminan depositadas en el agua de los pozos profundos del territorio donde habitan las personas, que la beben de forma cotidiana.
En el año 2024, tras una resolución del Juzgado Primero de Distrito del estado de Campeche que negó el amparo a las comunidades, éstas solicitaron a la SCJN la atracción del caso, buscando una sentencia integral que proteja de forma efectiva el agua de las comunidades de la región.
El pasado 26 de agosto, el pleno de la Suprema Corte votó de forma unánime a favor del proyecto de sentencia de la ministra María Estela Ríos, el cual otorgaba el amparo y la protección de la justicia a las comunidades de Hopelchén, reconociendo, además, las pruebas en el amparo donde se establece que en el agua de la región maya de los Chenes hay presencia de plaguicidas altamente peligrosos para el medio ambiente y la salud de las personas.
Durante esta rueda de prensa las comunidades expresaron la importancia de que esta sentencia no se quede en el papel, sino que, a partir de ella, se configure un nuevo modelo de desarrollo que involucre y tome en cuenta a las comunidades y su forma de vida. Para ello, dijeron, se requiere una visión integral del tema del agua, cuya implementación en políticas públicas involucre a las autoridades en los distintos niveles de gobierno.
destacaron la urgencia de generar acciones articuladas para garantizar la efectividad de la sentencia y el monitoreo del agua que se consume en sus comunidades”.
El equipo legal explicó las dos cuestiones puntuales que exigen las comunidades en relación con el resolutivo de la Corte: * Que las autoridades responsables, entre ellas la Secretaría del Medio Ambiente y Recursos Naturales (Semarnat), la Comisión Nacional del Agua (Conagua) y la Comisión Federal para la Protección contra Riesgos Sanitarios (Cofepris), entre otras, cumplan de forma íntegra y en un plazo razonable lo que establece la sentencia. * Que se realice un monitoreo sistemático y constante del agua en la región a fin de garantizar agua limpia, libre de plaguicidas y de sustancias altamente peligrosas para las comunidades mayas de Hopelchén.

articles.content:

El incentivo para la producción y comercialización de maíz blanco de Sinaloa para el ciclo otoño-invierno 2025-26 tendrá un avance, al cierre de esta semana, del 80.5 por ciento, al entregar más de 19 mil millones de pesos (mdp) a productores de la entidad, quienes reciben 800 pesos de apoyo por tonelada del grano.
La Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader) recordó que el monto total del incentivo suma 2 mil 800 mdp y beneficiará a más de 24 mil agricultores sinaloenses, con el propósito de fortalecer su economía.
La dependencia precisó que, en el último corte, se han sumado 24 mil 972 productoras y productores al registro, de los cuales 23 mil 701, es decir, 94.91 por ciento, ya cuentan con su número de folio activo en el Sistema de Ordenamiento de la Producción y la Comercialización del Maíz Blanco y dispondrán de su tarjeta del Banco del Bienestar para la recepción directa de los apoyos.
A través de un comunicado, la Sader refirió que 14 mil 869 agricultores han recibido el pago adicional de apoyo al financiamiento agrícola, equivalente a 500 pesos por tonelada de maíz blanco, el cual será totalmente cubierto en el transcurso de la siguiente semana, al tiempo que se avanza en la integración de la documentación de las y los beneficiarios restantes.
Hizo hincapié en que los productores beneficiarios del apoyo de 800 pesos, “han completado satisfactoriamente su expediente en la Oficina de Representación de Sader, los Centros de Apoyo al Desarrollo Rural (CADER) y los Distritos de Desarrollo Rural (DDR) en Sinaloa; el proceso de atención continuará para el resto de las y los productores”.
La Sader —a cargo de Columba Jazmín López Gutiérrez— indicó que la ventanilla de atención y registro se encontrará abierta hasta el próximo 20 de septiembre del año en curso y que personal de la Oficina de Representación, CADER y DDR mantendrá un servicio y acompañamiento permanente en apoyo a productores que realizaron —en tiempo y forma— su registro, pero aún tienen documentación pendiente.
La dependencia precisó que el depósito del incentivo se realiza una vez concluido el trámite y después de la entrega y activación de la tarjeta del Banco del Bienestar, cuyo proceso tarda entre tres y cinco días. Hizo un llamado a los beneficiarios a acudir por su tarjeta y así asegurar el cobro oportuno de los apoyos.

articles.content:
La Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader) anunció que el próximo 24 de septiembre se reanudarán las exportaciones de ganado en pie mexicano, desde la estación cuarentenaria de San Jerónimo, Chihuahua, hacia Santa Teresa, Nuevo México, Estados Unidos. Durante la primera semana, la dependencia prevé que se enviarán, en promedio, 800 cabezas, cuyo número …
La Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader) anunció que el próximo 24 de septiembre se reanudarán las exportaciones de ganado en pie mexicano, desde la estación cuarentenaria de San Jerónimo, Chihuahua, hacia Santa Teresa, Nuevo México, Estados Unidos.
Durante la primera semana, la dependencia prevé que se enviarán, en promedio, 800 cabezas, cuyo número se incrementará, en forma gradual, hasta alcanzar mil 500 cabezas diarias, a partir de la cuarta semana de exportación-
En un comunicado, la Sader puntualizó que con el fin de cumplir la solicitud del Departamento de Agricultura de los Estados Unidos (USDA, por sus siglas en inglés) de reducir el riesgo de propagación del gusano barrenador del ganado (GBG) se realizaron modificaciones a las instalaciones del puerto ganadero,
Entre las adecuaciones realizadas por el Servicio Nacional de Sanidad, Inocuidad y Calidad Agroalimentaria (Senasica), productores pecuarios y el gobierno del estado de Chihuahua están las correspondientes a las líneas de preinspección para proporcionar las condiciones necesarias a los binomios caninos detectores de GBG, se construyeron dos áreas de resguardo, un espacio adecuado para la estancia y descanso de los perros.
Estas mismas modificaciones se replicaron en las áreas de inspección utilizadas por el personal del Servicio de Inspección de Sanidad Animal y Vegetal (APHIS, por sus siglas en inglés).
Para la transición hacia el uso de aretes electrónicos del Sistema Nacional de Identificación Individual del Ganado (SINIIGA) para la identificación del ganado se instalaron lectores de radiofrecuencia en las dos líneas de inspección de APHIS de la cuarentenaria de San Jerónimo.
Esta infraestructura permitirá realizar la lectura electrónica de los identificadores durante el proceso de inspección y fortalecer la trazabilidad de los animales destinados a exportación”.
También se instalaron ventiladores en puntos estratégicos de las áreas de inspección de APHIS, con el fin de facilitar la identificación de olores a los caninos detectores.
La Sader puntualizó que las modificaciones se realizaron también en la estación cuarentenaria de Puerto Palomas, Chihuahua, “ante la pronta reapertura a la exportación”.
interview_ideas: Voz local: productor(a) u organización de Chihuahua sobre cómo les afecta este tema.

articles.title_original: Reporta Sader avance del 99.4% en ejercicio presupuestal de Bienpesca
articles.content:
El componente Bienpesca reporta un avance financiero del 99.4%, con relación al presupuesto anual modificado de mil 683.8 millones de pesos (mdp), lo que representa un incremento real de 5.3% con relación al presupuesto modificado de 2025, informó la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader). En su Segundo Informe de Labores 2025-2026, la dependencia …
El componente Bienpesca reporta un avance financiero del 99.4%, con relación al presupuesto anual modificado de mil 683.8 millones de pesos (mdp), lo que representa un incremento real de 5.3% con relación al presupuesto modificado de 2025, informó la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader).
En su Segundo Informe de Labores 2025-2026, la dependencia indicó que al 30 de junio de 2026, el presupuesto modificado para subsidio de este componente es de mil 664.8 mdp, que se han destinado para el pago de 8 mil pesos a 182,961 personas derechohabientes.
En el documento se precisa que del presupuesto anual autorizado en 2026 para este componente, mil 564.3 mdp corresponden a subsidios y 119.6 mdp para gastos de operación.
La Sader expuso que Bienpesca tiene como objetivo “contribuir a fortalecer las actividades acuícola y pesquera, mediante el otorgamiento de apoyos económicos directos y capacitación básica a los productores de pequeña y mediana escala, para generar condiciones de igualdad para un desarrollo sustentable; su cobertura es nacional”.
El informe también refirió que al 1 de abril de 2026, a través del Proyecto Emergente de Apoyo al sector pesquero de los estados afectados por el derrame de hidrocarburos en el Golfo de México 2026, se apoyó a mil 584 mujeres que recibieron un apoyo adicional de 15,000 pesos (1,154 de Tabasco y 430 de Veracruz), con una inversión federal de 23.8 mdp, que representa 46.9% de los 50.7 mdp pagados a 3,379 personas beneficiarias.
De igual forma, recalcó, fue posible apoyar a 61 personas ubicadas en comunidades indígenas y/o afromexicanas en el estado de Veracruz, para quienes se destinó un monto de 915 mil pesos, lo que representó 1.8% del total de los recursos ejercidos.
Al referirse al Segundo Informe de Labores 2025-2026, la titular de la Sader, Columba López Gutiérrez, manifestó que Bienpesca impulsa el bienestar en las costas mexicanas y subrayó que en 2026, se canalizaron mil 664 mdp en beneficio de 182,961 personas derechohabientes”.
La secretaria de Estado hizo hincapié en que este programa “respalda a quienes viven de la pesca y fortalecen la seguridad alimentaria de México”.
interview_ideas: Voz local: productor(a) u organización de Veracruz sobre cómo les afecta este tema.

articles.title_original: Países árabes, oportunidad real para diversificar y ampliar exportación agroalimentaria de Mëxico
articles.content:
Los países árabes representan una oportunidad real para que México pueda diversificar sus exportaciones agroalimentarias y ampliar su presencia internacional, afirmó la presidenta de la Cámara Árabe Mexicana de Industria y Comercio (CAMIC), Mariana Tuma. Sugirió que con una estrategia adecuada y una visión de largo plazo, las empresas mexicanas tienen el potencial de consolidarse …
Los países árabes representan una oportunidad real para que México pueda diversificar sus exportaciones agroalimentarias y ampliar su presencia internacional, afirmó la presidenta de la Cámara Árabe Mexicana de Industria y Comercio (CAMIC), Mariana Tuma.
Sugirió que con una estrategia adecuada y una visión de largo plazo, las empresas mexicanas tienen el potencial de consolidarse en mercados con una demanda creciente y perspectivas favorables para el comercio de alimentos.
En la actualidad, entre los productos más exportados por México a esa región se encuentran: aguacate, berries, limón y snacks saludables; sin embargo, existen categorías con posibilidades de ampliar su presencia en distintos mercados árabes, como las frutas y hortalizas frescas, garbanzo y determinados alimentos procesados.
La creciente demanda de opciones saludables, productos premium e ingredientes naturales también favorece la entrada de alimentos con mayor valor agregado.
“La región representa una oportunidad estratégica para impulsar la diversificación de las exportaciones mexicanas. Se trata de mercados con una creciente demanda de alimentos y una alta dependencia de importaciones donde México puede aportar calidad, capacidad productiva y experiencia exportadora”, subrayó Mariana Tuma.
Los países árabes –expuso- han incrementado sus importaciones de alimentos como resultado del crecimiento de su población, el aumento del turismo, la urbanización y la limitada disponibilidad de tierras agrícolas en gran parte de la región.
El reto ahora es acercar la oferta agroalimentaria mexicana a las necesidades de estos mercados y construir relaciones comerciales de largo plazo”, agregó Tuma.
A través de un comunicado, la CAMIC planteó que el primer paso para exportar a estos mercados es identificar las oportunidades de manera específica en cada país. Entre los aspectos que las empresas mexicanas deben considerar destacan las condiciones de acceso, el marco regulatorio, los canales de distribución y los hábitos de consumo, ya que estos factores varían entre mercados y pueden determinar la viabilidad comercial de un producto.
El éxito en estos mercados –aseveró– depende de una estrategia bien informada y adaptada a cada país. Identificar las oportunidades con mayor potencial, comprender las condiciones comerciales y establecer relaciones con socios confiables son factores clave para construir una presencia sólida y sostenible en el largo plazo.
De acuerdo con los datos más recientes disponibles de la Organización Mundial de Comercio (OMC),
México ocupaba en 2024 la quinta posición entre los mayores exportadores de productos del campo a nivel mundial”.

articles.title_original: Aumenta 151% inversión social para acopio de maíz y frijol, alcanza 10.7 mil mdp: Sader
articles.content:
La inversión social erogada por el gobierno federal para el acopio de dos de los principales granos básicos que se cultivan en México, maíz y frijol, registró un crecimiento del 151.3%, al pasar de 4 mil 260 millones de pesos (mdp) a 10 mil 706 mdp, entre el 1 septiembre de 2025 al 30 de …
La inversión social erogada por el gobierno federal para el acopio de dos de los principales granos básicos que se cultivan en México, maíz y frijol, registró un crecimiento del 151.3%, al pasar de 4 mil 260 millones de pesos (mdp) a 10 mil 706 mdp, entre el 1 septiembre de 2025 al 30 de junio de 2026, respecto al mismo periodo de 2024-2025
De acuerdo al Segundo Informe de Labores 2025-2026 de la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader), los recursos se operaron a través del Programa Acopio para el Bienestar, que observó un aumentó del 167.5% en el volumen de maíz y frijol acopiado, al pasar de 354 mil 423 a 948 mil 141 toneladas (t).
En dicho periodo de referencia, detalla el informe de la Sader, el número de productores beneficiados se incrementó 134%, al pasar de 28 mil 150 a 65 mil 885, de las cuales 33% fueron mujeres y 67% hombres.
En el desglose del acopio alcanzado, el maíz absorbió 749 mil 876 t, en beneficio de 39 mil 214 personas y una inversión social de 5 mil 399 mdp; para el maíz nativo o criollo pigmentado se registraron 2 mil 406 t, 268 beneficiarios y una inversión de 19.7 mdp
En el caso del frijol las toneladas acopiadas sumaron 195 mil 858.1, con 26 mil 403 beneficiarios y 5 mil 287 mdp de inversión social.
En el marco de este Informe , la titular de la Sader, Columba López Gutiérrez, destacó “el acopio histórico de maíz y frijol de 948 mil toneladas, mientras que más de 6.2 millones de toneladas de maíz han sido comercializadas de manera anticipada”.
estos resultados reflejan el trabajo que desde el Gobierno de México estamos haciendo para fortalecer la producción nacional y avanzar hacia la soberanía alimentaria”.
El Segundo Informe de Labores 2025-2026 explica que el Programa Acopio para el Bienestar, anteriormente denominado Precios de Garantía a Productos Alimentarios Básicos, “se orienta al apoyo de las personas productoras de pequeña escala de maíz y frijol, mediante un esquema de precios de acopio con lo que se contribuye a fortalecer la comercialización de sus cosechas, mejorar sus ingresos y avanzar hacia la soberanía alimentaria”.
Por ello, indica, del 1 de septiembre de 2025 al 30 de junio de 2026, el programa operó con precios de acopio de 7 mil pesos por tonelada para maíz y 8 mil pesos por tonelada para maíz nativo o criollo pigmentado, ambos con un apoyo adicional de 200 pesos por tonelada para flete.
Puntualiza que en el caso del frijol se mantuvo un precio de acopio de 27 mil pesos por tonelada y expone que “derivado de las condiciones observadas en el mercado nacional del frijol y con el propósito de focalizar la atención en las principales regiones productoras, a partir del 1 de mayo de 2026 se implementó un esquema temporal de acopio con un apoyo equivalente a 16 mil pesos por tonelada”.
Adicionalmente, señala, durante 2026 se amplió la adquisición de frijol en los principales estados productores, particularmente en Zacatecas, lo que permitió incrementar progresivamente la meta de acopio de 60 mil a 106 mil toneladas, en beneficio de las personas productoras de pequeña escala.
La dependencia precisa que en maíz se alcanzó una cobertura territorial de 384 localidades, ubicadas en 240 municipios de 23 entidades. En maíz nativo o criollo pigmentado la cobertura comprendió 11 localidades, distribuidas en 10 municipios de tres entidades federativas.
Por otra parte, el acopio de frijol incidió en 120 localidades, pertenecientes a 61 municipios de 14 entidades, lo que permitió ampliar la presencia territorial del programa en las principales regiones productoras del país.
El Segundo Informe de Labores 2025-2026 de la Sader se refiere que como parte del fortalecimiento del Plan Frijol, el 28 de marzo de 2026 fue inaugurada la Planta Embolsadora Beatriz González Ortega, ubicada en Zacatecas, con capacidad para procesar hasta mil 400 toneladas mensuales de frijol.

articles.title_original: Regionalización de Conapesca atenderá, desde el territorio, a más de 333 mil productores acuícolas y pesqueros
articles.content:
La pesca y la acuacultura son actividades productivas relevantes para México por su contribución a las economías locales y nacional, dado que en 2025 generaron empleos e ingresos para 333 mil 630 productores en beneficio, directo e indirecto, de 1.6 millones de personas, por lo que la Comisión Nacional de Acuacultura y Pesca (Conapesca) anunció …
La pesca y la acuacultura son actividades productivas relevantes para México por su contribución a las economías locales y nacional, dado que en 2025 generaron empleos e ingresos para 333 mil 630 productores en beneficio, directo e indirecto, de 1.6 millones de personas, por lo que la Comisión Nacional de Acuacultura y Pesca (Conapesca) anunció la regionalización de sus oficinas, con el objetivo de fortalecer la coordinación y su capacidad operativa territorial.
La Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader) detalló que la regionalización de las Oficinas de Representación Estatal y Local (ORES) de la Conapesca será de la siguiente manera: 1) Baja California, Baja California Sur, Nayarit, Sinaloa y Sonora; 2) Chihuahua, Coahuila, Durango y Zacatecas; 3) Nuevo León, San Luis Potosí, Tamaulipas y Veracruz; 4) Campeche, Chiapas, Quintana Roo, Tabasco y Yucatán; 5) Ciudad de México, Estado de México, Guerrero, Hidalgo, Morelos, Oaxaca, Puebla y Tlaxcala; y 6) Aguascalientes, Colima, Guanajuato, Jalisco, Michoacán y Querétaro.
La pesca y la acuacultura, consideradas un asunto de seguridad nacional, contribuyen a la soberanía alimentaria, por lo que la titular de la Sader, Columba López Gutiérrez, detalló que cada coordinación regional tendrá la función de enlace territorial, de apoyo en la ejecución y seguimiento de la información.
Lo anterior, explicó la servidora pública, “impulsará el acercamiento de la toma de decisiones al sector pesquero y acuícola, agilizará la atención para asuntos con enfoque regional, incrementará la capacidad operativa y mejorará los mecanismos de seguimiento”.
El Programa Nacional de Pesca y Acuacultura 2026–2030 destaca que la gestión de la pesca y la acuacultura “es impostergable, ya que México cuenta con 629,925 hectáreas de cuerpos de agua de las lagunas costeras en el litoral del Océano Pacífico y 647,979 hectáreas en el Golfo de México y el Mar Caribe, con una Zona Económica Exclusiva de 200 millas marinas con potencial pesquero y ostenta una gran variedad de sistemas costeros y marinos dentro de sus aguas territoriales: 12,500 km² de superficie de lagunas costeras y esteros, además de 6,500 km² de aguas interiores como lagos, lagunas, represas y ríos donde también se desarrolla la acuacultura, a la cual se destinan 250,860 hectáreas” .
Este universo, agrega el documento, ha hecho posible “mantener un nivel de captura y producción superior a los 2.1 millones de toneladas anuales de peso vivo, con más de 50 especies pesqueras comercializadas”. Estima que
“en México 1.6 millones de toneladas de productos pesqueros y acuícolas se destinan al consumo humano directo con lo que el consumo per cápita en México se registra en casi los 15 kilogramos”
El anuncio de la regionalización de las ORES se hizo durante el Encuentro Nacional de Comisionadas y Comisionados Estatales 2026, la Conapesca, donde el titular de la Conapesca, Rigoberto Salgado Vázquez, pidió a los comisionados estatales asumir con responsabilidad su encomienda de representar a la dependencia en sus estados para servir y fortalecer al sector pesquero y acuícola.
Para ello, en las oficinas centrales de Conapesca se capacitaron a 32 comisionados estatales, a través de 10 mesas de trabajo, donde se abordaron temas como procesos administrativos, inspección y vigilancia, ejecución de programas sociales, trazabilidad, normatividad, diseño de artes de pesca, programa de fomento para el consumo de pescados y mariscos mexicanos, monitoreo satelital, talleres sobre documentación gráfica y proceso de notificaciones.

articles.title_original: Alta temperatura pone en riesgo un millón de especies, al 2100
articles.content:
Para el año 2100 se puede extinguir un millón de especies de plantas y animales, lo cual es parte de los efectos por el aumento de la temperatura planetaria, alertó la doctora honoris causa por la UNAM e integrante de El Colegio Nacional, Julia Carabias Lillo. Además del alto riesgo de desaparición de varios grupos …
Para el año 2100 se puede extinguir un millón de especies de plantas y animales, lo cual es parte de los efectos por el aumento de la temperatura planetaria, alertó la doctora honoris causa por la UNAM e integrante de El Colegio Nacional, Julia Carabias Lillo.
Además del alto riesgo de desaparición de varios grupos taxonómicos de animales, está el desplazamiento de las plantas hasta 10 kilómetros por año.
Hasta ahora está en peligro de extinción 41 por ciento de los anfibios, 26 por ciento de mamíferos y 34 por ciento de plantas coníferas. Con el aumento de temperatura de 1.5 grados Celsius, que ya se obtuvo en 2024, 90 por ciento de las especies endémicas del orbe experimentarán una reducción y 95 por ciento de las marinas estarán en riesgo, añadió.
De acuerdo con la universitaria, la degradación ambiental amenaza el alcance de los 17 Objetivos de Desarrollo de la Agenda 2030 para el Desarrollo Sustentable.
Los relativos al cambio climático, ecosistemas marinos y terrestres son la base para lograr los demás, pero para que sus soluciones sean efectivas se requiere entender las interacciones entre ellos, atenderlas de manera simultánea (con metas alineadas, financiamiento y estableciendo tiempos), así como considerar las condiciones naturales, sociales y económicas, afirmó.
La bióloga y profesora de la Facultad de Ciencias de la UNAM también dijo que se han rebasado umbrales planetarios -marco científico que define los márgenes de seguridad para la estabilidad y habitabilidad de la Tierra frente a la actividad humana- necesarios para la vida de las personas y de las demás especies: integridad de la biósfera, calentamiento global, modificaciones en el sistema de tierras, acidificación del océano, cambio de agua dulce y flujos biogeoquímicos.
Al participar en el seminario Emergencia Climática. Análisis de las Opiniones Consultivas de Cortes Internacionales, organizado por el Instituto de Investigaciones Jurídicas de la Universidad Nacional, indicó que las metas a las que deberíamos aspirar son: llegar a cero en deforestación, sobreexplotación de especies, emisiones netas de gases de efecto invernadero, residuos y contaminación, además de restaurar y recuperar los ecosistemas.
La conservacionista ambiental consideró que para lograrlo es necesario implementar estrategias con un sistema alimentario sostenible, que tenga prácticas agrícolas sustentables, planeación ecológica y productiva, preservación de la diversidad genética, reducción de carne y productos lácteos, ordenación pesquera y disminución del desperdicio de alimentos y agua.
También conservación y uso de la biodiversidad, fortalecimiento de las áreas naturales protegidas, cadenas de mercados verdes, opciones de empleos e ingresos para quienes no tienen tierra y fomento de sistemas productivos sostenibles (manejo de suelo, ecoturismo, pesca responsable y manejo forestal sostenible).
Otras acciones son la aplicación de energías limpias y renovables, con rápida transición a sistemas con bajas emisiones de carbono en producción y consumo, inversiones que deben sextuplicarse al 2050; así como fomento de la economía circular, que debe minimizar la extracción de recursos naturales mediante el reúso, reparación, restauración y reciclado, promover el consumo sustentable y aumentar el financiamiento.
Asimismo, rediseñar ciudades resilientes, reordenar la economía local y generar fuentes de trabajo, reducir la movilidad y el congestionamiento, crear espacios de convivencia en calles iluminadas, incrementar las áreas verdes y los mercados locales. Es importante planificar, ordenar y tener políticas para cada una en distintas regiones del país o de otras naciones, propuso Carabias Lillo.

articles.title_original: Logra México incremento de captura del 4.6% para atún aleta azul del Pacífico
articles.content:
Al amparo de reglas sustentadas en información científica y con prácticas que buscan la estabilidad de las pesquerías, México logró un incremento de 4.6 por ciento en su límite comercial de captura de atún aleta azul del Pacífico, al pasar de 10 mil 763 a 11 mil 256 toneladas para el bienio 2027–2028. Durante la …
Al amparo de reglas sustentadas en información científica y con prácticas que buscan la estabilidad de las pesquerías, México logró un incremento de 4.6 por ciento en su límite comercial de captura de atún aleta azul del Pacífico, al pasar de 10 mil 763 a 11 mil 256 toneladas para el bienio 2027–2028.
Durante la 104.ª Reunión de la Comisión Interamericana del Atún Tropical (CIAT), celebrada del 31 de agosto al 4 de septiembre en Lisboa, Portugal, también se informó que el máximo para dicha especie, en un solo año, se eleva de 6 mil 296 a 7 mil 35 toneladas.
En un comunicado, la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader) informó que en en el encuentro México obtuvo resultados favorables para la conservación y el aprovechamiento sustentable de los recursos pesqueros, donde destaca precisamente la adopción de nuevas medidas para la ordenación del atún aleta azul del Pacífico, una pesquería de alto valor económico y estratégico para nuestro país.
Dicho logro forma parte de un nuevo esquema de manejo del atún aleta azul —impulsado entre México, Japón y Estados Unidos—, “que establece reglas sustentadas en la mejor información científica disponible y busca dar mayor estabilidad y previsibilidad a la pesquería”.
México también presentó una iniciativa para fortalecer la coordinación y cooperación entre la CIAT y los procesos derivados del Acuerdo sobre la Conservación y el Uso Sostenible de la Diversidad Biológica Marina de las Zonas Situadas Fuera de la Jurisdicción Nacional (BBNJ, por sus siglas en inglés).
“La propuesta mexicana –recalca la Sader– busca que la aplicación de este nuevo instrumento internacional sea complementaria con las responsabilidades y capacidades de las organizaciones regionales de ordenación pesquera, además de contribuir efectivamente a la conservación de los ecosistemas marinos”.
La iniciativa –añade– plantea fortalecer el intercambio de información y la coordinación científica y técnica, identificar mecanismos de cooperación en materia de medidas de conservación basadas en áreas, documentar las contribuciones que realiza la CIAT a la protección de la biodiversidad marina y generar un espacio de diálogo sobre la implementación del Acuerdo BBNJ.
La Sader subrayó que México reafirma una política pesquera que concilia la conservación de los recursos marinos con su aprovechamiento responsable, promueve decisiones sustentadas en la ciencia y defiende una participación justa y equilibrada de los países del Pacífico oriental en la gestión de los recursos que comparten.

articles.title_original: Senasica implementará un plan de tres meses para eliminar olores en la planta de mosca estéril, en Chiapas
articles.content:
Representantes de la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural, del Gobierno del Estado de Chiapas, del ayuntamiento de Metapa de Domínguez y pobladores locales alcanzaron un acuerdo para reanudar la operación de la Planta de Producción de Moscas Estériles del Gusano Barrenador del Ganado (GBG). Las autoridades instalaron una mesa de diálogo para atender las …
Representantes de la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural, del Gobierno del Estado de Chiapas, del ayuntamiento de Metapa de Domínguez y pobladores locales alcanzaron un acuerdo para reanudar la operación de la Planta de Producción de Moscas Estériles del Gusano Barrenador del Ganado (GBG).
Las autoridades instalaron una mesa de diálogo para atender las demandas de la población ante los olores derivados de la operación del complejo. Al respecto, se aclaró que estas emanaciones obedecen a la formulación natural —a base de huevo, leche, celulosa y otros componentes— empleada en la alimentación de las larvas, por lo que no representan riesgo toxicológico alguno para la salud ni para el medio ambiente.
Entre los acuerdos destaca que el Servicio Nacional de Sanidad, Inocuidad y Calidad Agroalimentaria (Senasica) —organismo adscrito a AGRICULTURA— implementará las medidas técnicas necesarias para reducir los olores a un nivel imperceptible en un plazo de tres meses. Asimismo, presentará un cronograma de actividades ante la mesa de diálogo con el fin de agilizar los trabajos y acortar dicho periodo al máximo.
La mesa de diálogo se mantendrá activa para dar seguimiento y cumplimiento a los planteamientos formulados entre autoridades federales, estatales, municipales y representantes de la comunidad de Metapa de Domínguez.
Por otra parte, el Senasica analizará la posibilidad de incrementar la contratación de personal originario de Metapa de Domínguez, Chiapas, de acuerdo con las necesidades operativas de la planta.
Este viernes 11 de septiembre se llevará a cabo una reunión de trabajo con la titular de la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural, Columba Jazmín López Gutiérrez. Posteriormente, el sábado 12 de septiembre, el gobernador del estado, Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar, recibirá a una comisión de la comunidad para dar atención a sus planteamientos y revisar las acciones correspondientes.
Durante la mesa de trabajo, los funcionarios manifestaron su disposición para mantener el diálogo institucional y atender las peticiones locales, con pleno respeto a las competencias de cada dependencia y priorizando la búsqueda de soluciones. Como parte del seguimiento, el subsecretario de Gobierno de Chiapas, Jorge Enrique Hernández Bielma, visitará el municipio cada quince días para supervisar el cumplimiento de los acuerdos.
Tras la firma del compromiso y en muestra de buena voluntad, los habitantes de Metapa de Domínguez retiraron el bloqueo que mantenían en las instalaciones.
