articles.title_original: Sound Agriculture launches seed-applied biological to preserve yields on high ammonium corn acres
articles.content:
The new product added an average of 6 bushels per acre and increased yield at 11 of 12 test sites in 2025 field trials.
Ammonia and manure are two of the most effective ways to give corn the nitrogen it needs, but they come with a cost to the soil, says Jeff Divan, VP of agronomy at US-based Sound Agriculture .
Ammonia makes the soil more acidic and kills off some helpful microbes where it’s applied. Manure can hold its nitrogen in a form the plant can’t use until after the corn needs it most.
“High ammonium creates a harsh environment for soil biology — it reduces microbial diversity, which leads to inconsistent root development and lower yields,” notes Divan.
To help farms combat this, Sound Agriculture just released its latest product, INFLECT, a seed coating made of “helpful” microbes and designed specifically for corn fields fertilized with anhydrous ammonia or heavy amounts of manure.
The product launches at a time when most US corn growers are “ more or equally concerned ” about their farm costs compared to one year ago, and as many look for ways to reduce dependence on synthetic fertilizers. More and more, farms are turning to nature—or as Divan puts it, “making something from what’s already there” in the soil.
INFLECT is a planter box seed treatment applied as a powder to seeds at planting time.
Once seeds are in the ground, two species of bacteria ( Bacillus simplex and Bacillus subtilis ) and one fungus ( Coniochaeta nivea ) go to work, says Divan. The company selected these strains based on their ability to tolerate the high-salt, high-stress conditions high ammonium fertility creates.
When an anhydrous substance is present in the soil, it often causes an imbalance of pH in a plant’s root zone, making nutrients less available to the plant.
The two strains of bacteria in INFLECT create a buffer between roots and the anhydrous substance, which stabilizes pH and promotes root growth. The fungal strain, meanwhile, breaks down manure and other complex compounds, so that organic nitrogen and other nutrients can reach the plant.
Divan says the product has been several years in development, including a year’s worth of field trials across the corn belt in the Midwestern US. He did not disclose total acreage of those trials, but noted they are “commercial scale” and taking place at 12 different sites across lllinois, Kansas, and Missouri.
The company says it has so far raised corn yields by about six bushels per acre on average and improved yield at 92% of the sites.
For now, corn is Sound Agriculture’s main focus for INFLECT. Divan says the company is “exploring other crops” for potential application in the future.
INFLECT is Sound Agriculture’s third product , joining its signaling chemistry SOURCE, which helps crops get more out of the nitrogen and phosphorus in the soil, and BLUEPRINT, an arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) solution that enhances nutrient and water uptake.
Divan says there may be an opportunity in future to pair SOURCE’s signaling technology with INFLECT to also increase phosphorus efficiency in corn. This is similar to the way SOURCE “ supercharges ” BLUEPRINT currently, he says.
“We’re combining our products in ways to support biology’s ability to create organic acids and enzymes, and pull phosphorus from the soil and reduce synthetic dependency.”
Equally important is helping growers understand that they can build their overall fertility plans around these beneficial microbes, versus simply adding biology on top of existing plans.
“It’s important to not just add [biologicals] on top of existing programs but create space for them,” says Divan. “Let biology and products like [those from Sound Agriculture] be your first 25 pounds of fertility. When folks take that approach and peel out expensive applications, we see really good results.
“Far and away, as time goes on, our best wins are when somebody reduces or replaces a portion of dry fertilizer with an active soil microbiome.”

articles.title_original: 🎥Agrifood VC needs a different playbook, says Pymwymic: “Corporate venture capital needs to step in earlier”
articles.content:
In agrifood investing, says Pymwymic, it is time to stop shooting for the stars and instead aim for the moon — and consistently land there.
In agrifoodtech investing, says Pymwymic managing partner Rogier Pieterse, it might be time to stop shooting for the stars and instead aim for the moon — and consistently land there.
“We don’t believe in what we call the US VC model, where you invest in one or two winners, which are then supposedly going to return your fund.”
Meanwhile, corporates will need to provide more support to the sector, he says. “I believe corporate ventures will need to take that innovation risk a bit more, and then private equity growth capital will come in later to accelerate that growth.”
AgFunderNews ( AFN ) caught up with Pieterse (RP) at the World Agri-Tech innovation summit in London to discuss why Pymwymic is targeting more modest but consistent returns, the funding gap facing agrifood startups, and where he sees opportunities in areas from precision agriculture and biologicals to robotics and AI.
AFN : You’ve challenged the Silicon Valley model of VC investing for agrifoodtech?
RP : We don’t believe in what we call the US VC model, where you invest in one or two winners, which are then supposedly going to return your fund. We believe in investing in not per se just one winner, but in what we say the middle layer, and trying to avoid losers.
We are not looking for 10x, 100x return expectations when we do an investment, but like on average, just having a reasonable margin, so 10% or so. That’s what we promised to our investors.
AFN : If returns of 10% are acceptable and we need to reset our expectations, with that kind of proposition, can you attract enough institutional capital from LPs?
RP : It is a challenge, especially nowadays, where institutional investors say, well, we want to have at least 15%. I always challenge them: so in all the other investments that they have done, how many of those funds actually delivered on that promise?
So far, which makes us quite unique, we have been able to create a proper DPI, so funds returned to our LPs in this apparently tough market, and also we are still on the trajectory to meet our 10% which we have promised.
Obviously, it also helps that we have quite a strong private investor base, which supports all our funds as a cornerstone investor [ the Pymwymic Coöperatief an investment coop made up of private investors: families, family foundations and selected individuals]. But still, 11 years down the track, we feel that we have a certain credibility and certainly the new LPs that come feel like Pymwymic provides them a safe haven.
AFN : When you’re thinking about who’s going to fund the next round for your portfolio companies, are you encouraged by what you see or worried?
RP : Let’s start with the fact that there’s less capital available for these types of innovations now. The environment we are in nowadays is way more short-term versus long-term focused. The fact that there are fewer investors in this space, and especially in the early or still loss-making phase, provides us the opportunity to invest at a better entry point, so there is the economic reasoning of buy low, sell high.
But obviously, there are concerns for follow-up rounds. So what we have done to mitigate that is we’ve just added an evergreen growth fund to our platform, which is more focused on profitable businesses [the Pymwymic Healthy Food Systems Growth Impact Fund III, which Pymwymic launched in 2026 by taking over the Triodos Food Transition Europe Fund]. So what we hope is that the ventures that are successful in our early-stage funds can roll over to the growth portfolio. And that fund is evergreen, so it allows us to stay in longer because what we see in this market is that it simply takes more time for companies to flourish [the fund doesn’t have a fixed end date in the way a typical VC fund does].
AFN : Five years from now, will there be fewer dedicated agri-food tech VCs? More corporate capital? Different funding models?
RP : I think there is no way around it. Yesterday in a panel I was in on stage, I mentioned that more corporate venture [funds] will need to step in earlier, which currently is not happening. In fact, it’s now the other way around, where venture has been taking this initial development risk and then later on tried to access corporate venture money.
I believe corporate ventures will need to take that innovation risk a bit more, and then private equity growth capital will come in later to accelerate that growth. That’s what we’re now trying to solve with this platform play that we are implementing within Pymwymic. For all our venture plays, we want to have strategics on the cap table.
AFN : Are there certain areas that you would have invested in three, four years ago that you wouldn’t touch today?
RP : Our thesis hasn’t changed. We have always had the approach of under promising and over delivering and we haven’t luckily been dragged into many rat races on vertical farming or alternative proteins, and always stuck to the idea that we need to enter into portfolio companies at a low valuation point.
We never felt the urge around this total addressable market promise [startups pitching on the size of a theoretical market opportunity]. We’ve always looked at true farmer adoption or unit economics, that is still the same.
Yes, there have been markets where probably four years ago, I thought they were amazing, and now I’m thinking that’s scary. But everything goes in cycles, right? Things change and things evolve. So last year we actually made our first alternative protein investment against the cycle, which four years ago I never would have done. But we have learned many lessons [in that market segment] over the past few years.
AFN : Are there any agrifoodtech areas you’re particularly excited about, or that you feel are currently underfunded relative to the potential opportunity?
RP : I don’t believe that this input-driven system as it is right now, will last forever. You’re putting in $100 million of inputs in the ground and getting $80 million out of it, which is economically not sensible.
If you look at precision farming, precision spraying, but also nutrient management, the soil contains the signals that farmers need to make the right decisions. So that is the bet that we are currently placing. On top of that, if you think about underfunded areas, I’d say regenerative practices, and that is something we are trying to support.
But we also realize that we are in a transition period. So things will take time, like renewables did, and the trend towards biologicals also will come.
RP : It’s becoming more driven by off-the-shelf components, so unit prices are going down. Data usage and artificial intelligence also help. Still, the brutal fact for robotics is that when you speak to a farmer, he or she will still say that the actual reality of, for example, autonomous driving is a bit more brutal, whether there’s irrigation lines still laying on the field, which prevents a robot from passing, or the robot doesn’t recognize that an implement is heating up because there’s a rock stuck [in the field].
So it’s getting there, it’s getting more investable, but I think the fact that there’s still human intervention needed can still hold true scaling back.
AFN : How is AI changing the space in your view? And how, as an investor, do you think about what is a moat versus what anyone can now do in-house with the available AI tools?
RP : Our portfolio is 75-80% hardware-software, data driven. So the quality of the data and the uniqueness of the data is often the defensibility of a business.
What a company can do with a data set and how it has been historically annotating data, recognizing one specific pest versus the other, makes it unique, and especially when it can translate it to a specific actionable insight for a farmer.

articles.title_original: New CIMMYT maize hybrid available from South Asia Breeding Program
articles.content:
CIMMYT is happy to announce a new, improved tropical maize hybrid that is now available for uptake by public and private sector partners, especially those interested in marketing or disseminating hybrid maize seed across the lowland tropics of South Asia and similar agro-ecologies in other regions.
CIMMYT is happy to announce a new, improved tropical maize hybrid that is now available for uptake by public and private sector partners, especially those interested in marketing or disseminating hybrid maize seed across the lowland tropics of South Asia and similar agro-ecologies in other regions. NARES and seed companies are hereby invited to apply for licenses to pursue national release, scale-up seed production, and deliver these maize hybrids to farming communities.
The newly available CIMMYT maize hybrids were identified through rigorous, years-long trialing and a stage-gate advancement process which culminated in the 2025 ADTY On-Farm Trials. The products were found to meet the stringent performance and farmer acceptance criteria for CIMMYT’s breeding pipelines that are designed to generate products tailored in particular for smallholder farmers in stress-prone agroecologies of South Asia.
Applications must be accompanied by a proposed commercialization plan for each product being requested. Applications may be submitted online via the CIMMYT Maize Licensing Portal and will be reviewed in accordance with CIMMYT’s Principles and Procedures for Acquisition and use of CIMMYT maize hybrids and OPVs for commercialization . Specific questions or issues faced with regard to the application process may be addressed to GMP-CIMMYT@cgiar.org with attention to Nicholas Davis , Program Manager, Global Maize Program, CIMMYT.
South Asia’s smallholder farmers are no strangers to climate stress, but erratic rainfall and rising temperatures are pushing rainfed agriculture to its limits. Five new maize hybrids from CIMMYT’s South Asia breeding program, validated across up to 106 trial locations in India, Bangladesh, Nepal, and Pakistan, offer a science-based response
CIMMYT’s systematic and targeted breeding strategy in South Asia helped develop 20 high yielding and heat-stress tolerant maize hybrids. The ongoing efforts strengthens the livelihood of farm families who are highly vulnerable to climate change in the Asian tropics.
CIMMYT unveils eight new tropical maize hybrids for uptake by partners targeting Eastern Africa and similar regions.

articles.title_original: Avance del mar amenaza viviendas, tierras agrícolas e infraestructura, alerta ONU
articles.content:
¿Puede seguir existiendo un país si parte de su territorio desaparece bajo el agua? ¿Y qué ocurre con las comunidades que ya no pueden permanecer donde han vivido durante generaciones? ¿O las ciudades y zonas rurales costeras? El nivel del mar no solo está subiendo, sino que lo está haciendo cada vez más rápido. En …
El nivel del mar no solo está subiendo, sino que lo está haciendo cada vez más rápido. En 2024 alcanzó un máximo histórico y su ritmo de aumento se ha más que duplicado, de unos 2,1 milímetros anuales entre 1993 y 2002 a 4,7 milímetros entre 2015 y 2024.
Alrededor de 900 millones de personas, aproximadamente una de cada diez en el mundo, viven en zonas costeras de baja elevación. Para los pequeños Estados insulares y otros países costeros especialmente expuestos, el avance del mar amenaza viviendas, fuentes de agua, tierras agrícolas e infraestructura, pero plantea además preguntas que van mucho más allá de la adaptación física.
Ante ese escenario, los Estados adoptaron en la Asamblea General este jueves la Declaración de la ONU sobre el aumento del nivel del mar, que busca mejorar la información sobre los riesgos, reforzar la adaptación y la financiación y proteger a las comunidades más expuestas. El texto también aborda algunas de las preguntas más complejas que abre la subida del mar, entre ellas qué ocurre con un país, sus derechos y sus fronteras marítimas si pierde parte de su territorio.
Saber con mayor precisión qué zonas quedarán expuestas y con qué rapidez es una parte central de la respuesta.
Los países acordaron reforzar la observación científica, la recopilación de datos y los modelos, además de mejorar las alertas tempranas y las evaluaciones de riesgo”.
En la práctica, esa información puede servir para decidir dónde y cómo construir infraestructuras, qué zonas necesitan mayor protección y qué servicios deben reforzarse antes de que aumenten las inundaciones.
Puertos, hospitales, sistemas de agua y energía, transportes y telecomunicaciones tendrán que planificarse teniendo en cuenta cómo puede cambiar el nivel del mar durante las próximas décadas.
La respuesta no pasa únicamente por obras de infraestructura. Manglares, arrecifes de coral, humedales y otros ecosistemas costeros también pueden reforzar la resiliencia frente a inundaciones y tormentas, por lo que su protección y restauración forman parte de las medidas señaladas.
Todas estas medidas cuestan dinero, y algunos de los países con mayor riesgo cuentan con menos recursos para protegerse. Por eso la declaración pide aumentar la financiación pública y privada para los países en desarrollo, especialmente los pequeños Estados insulares y los países menos adelantados. También se reclama que los recursos lleguen de manera más rápida y previsible y que acceder a los fondos internacionales sea menos complicado.
Esa financiación puede marcar la diferencia entre poder reforzar infraestructuras, ampliar sistemas de alerta o proteger comunidades con antelación, o tener que responder una vez que el daño ya se ha producido.
¿Puede seguir existiendo un país si pierde territorio? Se trata de una de las cuestiones más delicadas de la declaración, acordada tras varios meses de negociaciones intergubernamentales desde finales de 2025.
Los Estados afirman que la pérdida de territorio por la subida del nivel del mar no significa necesariamente que un país deje de existir”.
El texto respalda una presunción a favor de la continuidad de esos Estados, incluidos su soberanía, sus derechos y responsabilidades y su pertenencia a Naciones Unidas. Esto busca dar mayor certeza a países, como las pequeñas islas del Pacífico, que podrían perder parte de su territorio físico sin que ello implique automáticamente perder su condición de Estado.
Algo parecido ocurre con las zonas marítimas. Aunque una costa cambie físicamente, aquellas que ya hayan sido establecidas conforme a la Convención de las Naciones Unidas sobre el Derecho del Mar pueden mantenerse, afirma la declaración.
Eso importa porque esas zonas están directamente vinculadas a los derechos que los Estados ejercen sobre el océano y sus recursos.
Las consecuencias de la subida del nivel del mar no se limitan a la pérdida física de tierra, sino que también pueden salinizar tierras agrícolas y fuentes de agua dulce, aumentar las inundaciones y la erosión y afectar actividades como la pesca, el turismo y el transporte. La declaración pide que estos riesgos se incorporen a la planificación del desarrollo y a las políticas de protección social.
Para algunas comunidades, permanecer en el mismo lugar puede llegar a ser cada vez más difícil. El texto señala que, en esos casos, deben apoyarse las decisiones voluntarias de las personas afectadas y que cualquier traslado debe hacerse con dignidad. Si implica cruzar una frontera, tendrá que acordarse con los Estados correspondientes y respetar el derecho internacional.
Asimismo, el aumento del nivel del mar puede dejar inaccesibles o destruir tierras tradicionales, cementerios, lugares sagrados, sitios arqueológicos y paisajes costeros de importancia cultural. Por eso, el texto pide proteger, preservar y documentar ese patrimonio.
No. No se trata de un tratado y, por sí sola, la declaración no crea nuevas obligaciones jurídicas comparables a las de un acuerdo internacional vinculante. Sin embargo, sus dimensiones jurídicas se apoyan en normas ya existentes del derecho internacional, incluida la Convención de las Naciones Unidas sobre el Derecho del Mar.
El documento también toma nota de la opinión consultiva de la Corte Internacional de Justicia sobre las obligaciones de los Estados frente al cambio climático y del trabajo de la Comisión de Derecho Internacional sobre el aumento del nivel del mar.
Su importancia está, por tanto, en que los países han fijado una posición común sobre problemas que para algunos Estados costeros e insulares son cada vez menos hipotéticos.
El secretario general, António Guterres, celebró la adopción del documento y destacó su importancia, aunque dejó claro que el siguiente paso será llevarlo a la práctica.
“El aumento del nivel del mar se mide en milímetros. Pero su costo se mide en millones de vidas destrozadas, comunidades desarraigadas y futuros robados”.

articles.title_original: México reanuda la exportación de ganado bovino en pie hacia EU, desde Chihuahua
articles.content:
Con un primer envío de 430 cabezas de ganado, este jueves México reanudó las exportaciones de ganado bovino en pie, desde la estación cuarentenaria de San Jerónimo, Chihuahua, hacia Estados Unidos, por el cruce fronterizo de Santa Teresa, Nuevo México, informó la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader). La dependencia detalló, a través de …
Con un primer envío de 430 cabezas de ganado, este jueves México reanudó las exportaciones de ganado bovino en pie, desde la estación cuarentenaria de San Jerónimo, Chihuahua, hacia Estados Unidos, por el cruce fronterizo de Santa Teresa, Nuevo México, informó la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader).
La dependencia detalló, a través de un comunicado, que dicha cifra se incrementará de manera paulatina hasta alcanzar mil 500 animales diarios en la cuarta semana.
Por su parte, el Consejo Nacional Agropecuario (CNA) consideró que esta noticia, “es un avance relevante en la recuperación gradual de las exportaciones ganaderas mexicanas, resultado del trabajo coordinado entre productores, organizaciones ganaderas y autoridades sanitarias de México y Estados Unidos para fortalecer las medidas de prevención,inspección, trazabilidad y control sanitario frente al gusano barrenador del ganado”.
También celebró el anuncio de la Sader de que la estación cuarentenaria de Puerto Palomas, Chihuahua, será el tercer punto fronterizo en reanudar las exportaciones de ganado en pie hacia el país vecino, lo que permitirá continuar avanzando hacia la recuperación comercial.
Mediante una comunicación, el CNA reconoció el trabajo del Servicio Nacional de Sanidad, Inocuidad y Calidad Agroalimentaria (Senasica), del Servicio de Inspección de Sanidad Animal y Vegetal del Departamento de Agricultura de Estados Unidos (APHIS- USDA), “por el trabajo técnico, el diálogo y la coordinación bilateral que han permitido avanzar en la generación de las condiciones necesarias para esta reapertura”.
esta reapertura es resultado de una serie de estrictas medidas zoosanitarias implementadas por el Senasica, organismo dependiente de la Sader, para combatir al gusano barrenador del ganado (GBG)”.
Recordó que el Departamento de Agricultura de los Estados Unidos (USDA, por sus siglas en inglés) solicitó extremar las medidas para evitar la dispersión del GBG, lo que llevó a modificar la infraestructura de la estación cuarentenaria e incorporar binomios caninos (perro y manejador) en los procesos de preinspección e inspección.
El CNA anotó que “es indispensable mantener y fortalecer las acciones para la prevención, vigilancia y contención del gusano barrenador, así como dotar al Senasica “de los recursos humanos, técnicos, presupuestales y de infraestructura necesarios para cumplir con esta responsabilidad estratégica”.
El organismo cúpula del sector empresarial indicó que “ante esta clase de desafíos es fundamental que las decisiones sanitarias y comerciales continúen sustentándose en evidencia científica y criterios técnicos, por encima de consideraciones políticas. La cooperación técnica y la confianza entre ambos países son indispensables para proteger la sanidad animal y mantener un comercio seguro y ordenado”.
interview_ideas: Voz local: productor(a) u organización de Chihuahua sobre cómo les afecta este tema.

articles.title_original: Diseñar un plan integral para la ganadería sinaloense, a cuatro años, propone titular de la Sader
articles.content:
Ante representantes del sector ganadero sinaloenses, la titular de la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader), Columba Jazmín López Gutiérrez, planteó acabar con los programas temporales y las soluciones de escritorio y los exhortó a trabajar, en forma conjunta, para impulsar un plan integral, en un horizonte de cuatro años, que garantice la rentabilidad, …
Ante representantes del sector ganadero sinaloenses, la titular de la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader), Columba Jazmín López Gutiérrez, planteó acabar con los programas temporales y las soluciones de escritorio y los exhortó a trabajar, en forma conjunta, para impulsar un plan integral, en un horizonte de cuatro años, que garantice la rentabilidad, la certeza y el crecimiento de esta industria local.
Dicho plan deberá considerar el fortalecimiento del estatus sanitario, la trazabilidad, la genética del ganado, el acceso al agua y contemplar financiamiento accesible, a través del crédito con Cosechando Soberanía.
Al presidir una reunión de trabajo con líderes de organismos ganaderos, encabezados por el presidente de la Unión Ganadera Regional de Sinaloa, José Alfredo Sáinz Aispuro, la funcionaria federal propuso trabajar en un programa para fortalecer la ganadería estatal, a cuatro años, que permita a este sector tener la visión de hacia dónde quieren llegar en ese tiempo.
La responsable de la Sader expresó: “venimos a transformar el campo, no a administrarlo. Se acabaron los programas temporales y las soluciones de escritorio; hoy construimos trajes a la medida para que las instituciones se adapten a las necesidades de las y los productores, garantizando rentabilidad, certidumbre y bienestar para sus familias”.
López Gutiérrez expuso que la soberanía alimentaria requiere impulsar el consumo de forrajes locales para la engorda de ganado en lugar de insumos importados, el acompañamiento técnico y la promoción de campañas intensivas contra la brucelosis, la tuberculosis y el aprovechamiento de la temporada invernal para acelerar la dispersión de moscas estériles contra el gusano barrenador del ganado (GBG).
La funcionaria federal, quien realiza una gira de trabajo por la entidad, convocó a los presentes a volverse a reunir en 15 días para revisar los avances de las propuestas.
En tanto, la gobernadora de Sinaloa, Graciela Domínguez Nava, quien acompañó a la titular de la Sader, refrendó el compromiso de su administración a aportar los recursos presupuestales y técnicos necesarios dentro de este plan estratégico.
Consideró que la recuperación del estatus zoosanitario representa una oportunidad histórica y prioritaria para la entidad, por lo que sumarán esfuerzos de manera coordinada con la Sader para consolidar los proyectos en beneficio de los ganaderos sinaloenses.
El director general del Servicio Nacional de Sanidad, Inocuidad y Calidad Agroalimentaria (Senasica), Javier Calderón Elizalde, informó que el gobierno de México fortalece la estrategia contra el GBG mediante el control de la movilización ganadera, la capacitación a más de 10 mil productores y una producción récord de hasta 50 millones de moscas estériles —provenientes de la planta de Metapa de Domínguez, Chiapas— para contener el avance de la plaga.
En su oportunidad, el titular de Leche para el Bienestar, Antonio Talamantes Geraldo, informó que en los municipios de Ahome y Mazatlán se destinará una inversión de 50 millones de pesos para construir dos nuevos centros de acopio, los cuales tendrán capacidad de 15 mil litros de recepción. En una primera etapa se comprará el 10 por ciento de la producción del estado, a 11.5 pesos por litro.
El director general de Producción Ganadera de Sader, David Palos, detalló que se trabaja en un esquema a la medida de Sinaloa para agilizar el financiamiento con la banca de desarrollo, fortalecer los programas de mejoramiento genético y modernizar la infraestructura de los rastros TIF (Tipo Inspección Federal) en coordinación con las uniones ganaderas.
Por su parte, el director general de Fideicomisos Instituidos en Relación con la Agricultura (FIRA), Jesús Alán Elizondo Flores, recordó que con el programa Cosechando Soberanía se tiene acceso a esquemas de financiamiento de hasta 1.3 millones de pesos con una tasa anual del 8.5 por ciento, con un tope de 17 por ciento, y créditos grupales de hasta 8 millones de pesos para solicitudes asociativas.

articles.title_original: There’s a market for saline agriculture. It just needs a boost
articles.content:
Saline agriculture is no longer just a series of crop, soil and water management practices. It’s also a business ecosystem.
Rich Bellis completed an MSc. in environment and resource management at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam in June 2026, focusing on food system transformation. His 15-year business journalism experience includes staff editor roles at NBC News, the Wall Street Journal and Fast Company in New York.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of AgFunderNews.
Years of research and field trials have demonstrated many ways to grow crops sustainably in saline conditions. But even as punishing droughts, saltwater intrusion and intensive irrigation threaten to drive up salinity, commercial recognition of the problem remains weak, and so does the nascent market for solutions to it.
The FAO estimates that elevated soil salinity already affects nearly 1.4 billion hectares worldwide, or at least 10% of global land . Salinization is forecast to keep chipping away at the productivity of key agricultural regions and scrambling farm economics . It doesn’t help that “saline agriculture” is mainly thought of as series of steps producers can take to adapt to salinity, overlooking the constellation of businesses purpose-built to grow food on salt-affected land. Nor that these diverse enterprises currently lack a collective vision for their role in the next-generation food system they’re striving to build.
This is the picture that arose from interviews with 15 such businesses in eight countries across North America, Europe, Asia and Australia. Some grow salt-loving “halophyte” plants, like salicornia and saltbush, in settings from coastal deltas to arid interiors. Others are biotech and agrochemical firms improving salt-tolerance in rice or potatoes, irrigation consultancies and desalination technology providers. Yet in research the IVM Institute for Environmental Studies in Amsterdam recently published in a report I coauthored with Dr. Kate Negacz, ties across this ecosystem proved uneven: While halophyte farmers form a tight-knit niche, some operators focusing on conventional crops are scarcely aware of each other.
Nonetheless, one common thread emerged: Most of these actors said market development challenges were holding back their ambitions to scale.
“It all comes down to demand,” a small salicornia grower said. (All were granted anonymity to discuss their businesses for research purposes.) “We’re investing into marketing and spreading awareness about how efficient and good of a plant this is.” But these costly efforts would make “better sense in terms of numbers and farming when we have better demand,” he said, “rather than simply burning money.”
Among climate-adaptive agriculture’s top targets, from extreme heat to freshwater scarcity, salinization is something of an ugly duckling.
The problem has been rigorously studied but rarely makes headlines, and entrepreneurs routinely described how hard it’s been to put salinity-focused interventions on the map. One biotech addressing multiple abiotic stressors said that salinity was currently the “least priority.” Even at gatherings like the annual UN conference on desertification that wrapped up in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, recently, salinization hasn’t seemed to feature prominently in discussions of land degradation.
Some of this may reflect what’s easy to notice on the ground. “When the blight is killing your field, [farmers] see it,” one seed treatment expert said in the study. “The heat, they feel when it’s very warm and they see that the crop needs water.” Salt buildup is stealthier. It can require special instruments to diagnose and tends to progress gradually, unlike a heat wave, disease outbreak or storm surge.
That doesn’t mean the responses offered by saline agriculture ventures are a lost cause. Many providers of these solutions said demand was rising, albeit more slowly than hoped. Most said their ability to innovate and experiment, find collaborators and valuable resources was relatively strong. In fact, the chronic funding shortfalls and bankability constraints that have long plagued agrifood ( including in saline agriculture ) weren’t described as a primary obstacle.
Instead, weak awareness, steep customer acquisition costs and the chicken-and-egg dilemma of how and whether to invest in the large operational buildouts needed to secure major supplier contracts were core challenges. Even so, many saline agriculture entrepreneurs insisted they were ready to scale up, if only they could generate sufficient revenue growth and sustained adoption. Most were admirably committed to sticking it out even if they couldn’t.
Research and policy around saline agriculture has been well-attuned to the idiosyncrasies of dealing with salinity, and for good reason: The problem has multiple causes; what works in one crop or region—or even on a single plot—may fail in another; and contextual factors like local production methods and market dynamics vary just as widely. Yet much less attention has been paid to the shared barriers operators face to commercializing their interventions.
This gap matters. Indeed, many of the same market-development challenges were identified repeatedly among vastly different businesses in the study, and these resembled some of the most common obstacles faced by maturing startups and scale-ups across the agrifood industry. ( They map almost identically , for instance, onto the demand issues seen in the adjacent category of seaweed aquaculture.) What’s more, saline agriculture operators frequently viewed business models that could crack these traction problems as the most scalable. They placed comparatively less emphasis on sales growth, cash flow and other more conventional metrics.
Some entrepreneurs voiced deep frustration, bordering on disbelief, that market development has proved so difficult. Many see their paths to scale as running through, rather than around, incumbent firms and believe corporate partnerships should be easier to come by.
“How do we get into the boardrooms of these companies? How do we do it?” one experienced halophyte grower asked rhetorically. “I thought it would all happen organically…but it hasn’t.”
This disappointment reflects operators’ firm conviction in the value—commercial, social and ecological—of their products and services. A developer of desalination and greenhouse infrastructure for arid environments described his approach as a simple, clearly superior alternative to drilling ever deeper irrigation wells in the desert. But the market kept saying otherwise. “I’m a slightly lonely voice bleating in the wind,” he said, “and nobody’s listening.”
One halophyte grower operating in an abandoned salt flat described herself as pioneering a form of farming that ticked multiple boxes—sustainably cultivating undervalued, nutrient-rich crops with multiple uses, all while restoring an ecosystem and valorizing land that’s otherwise worthless. “We are preparing the future, that’s why we started this,” she said. “And because they are super-plants.”
For this and other entrepreneurs, sustainability was a core motivator. In fact, none of the 15 operators said they were in it primarily to make money. Even those who saw their businesses as moonshot bets with significant potential returns were driven by the chance to make societal and environmental impacts, too.
However, sustainable outcomes were defined and prioritized very differently from one operator to the next—a misalignment that threatens their upscaling. With few agreed-upon sustainability metrics, actors across the sector may struggle to develop a coherent narrative with which to engage investors, business partners, policymakers, institutions and the public. This also risks putting a ‘green ceiling’ on their environmental impacts; few saw themselves as having to make business-vs.-sustainability tradeoffs. But scale, should it come, might change that—as the widespread preference for compatibility with incumbents may put pro-environmental decisions in the crosshairs.
Future policy, research and institutional support should address this risk head on, ideally by spurring greater coordination among saline agriculture operators on environmental goal-setting and measurement. External stakeholders and organizations should also redouble support for advancing growth and commercialization among the actors already running salinity-focused companies. Help establishing trade groups, developing market research, exploring partnerships and fine-tuning brand strategies are just as essential for the emerging space today as further agronomic innovation.
Indeed, if this study underscored anything, it’s that saline agriculture is no longer only a series of crop, soil and water management practices for farmers to implement. It’s also a business ecosystem of purpose-driven entrepreneurs whose diverse portfolio of interventions are tailored to different customers and contexts around the world. It just needs to be cultivated to grow.

articles.title_original: Multifunctional landscapes begin with behavior change
articles.content:
Through participatory landscape visioning, communities and institutions in Zimbabwe’s Mbire District identified the behavior changes, existing assets and partnerships needed to build a climate-resilient, multifunctional landscape.
Visioning is a participatory process through which communities and other landscape actors define the future they want and the changes needed to reach it. For community development, it creates a shared direction for coordinating land use, livelihoods, and institutions. During the first Landscape Vision to Action (LV2A) session in 2025, stakeholders envisioned a well-governed, multifunctional, and climate-resilient Zambezi Valley.
The second session shifted from defining the destination to identifying how to get there: which actors need to behave differently, what enables or constrains those changes, and which existing assets can support them. Within CGIAR’s Science Program on Multifunctional Landscapes (MFL), LV2A helps unpack community priorities and challenges and translate them into actor-specific behaviour changes. This evidence helps align research and implementation activities with the shared vision and shows how existing knowledge, skills, institutions and relationships can be leveraged. Participants developed and consolidated these findings through women’s, men’s and institutional stakeholder groups, a World Café and plenary discussion.
Participants working in a facilitated group to identify actor-specific behavior changes, barriers, enablers and assets needed to achieve the shared landscape vision Photo: CIMMYT
At village and ward levels, proposed changes centered on land-management practices, change in mindset, and local accountability. Participants called for safer management of pesticide containers and residues, soil-erosion control, retention of crop residues, afforestation, regulated tree cutting, regulated gold panning, and community-led gully rehabilitation. Suggested measures included conservation agriculture, intercropping, vegetative barriers, sandbagging, legislation, and tree planting. Traditional leaders and local committees were assigned roles in communicating rules and monitoring compliance.
At district and national levels, the emphasis shifted from individual practice to institutional delivery. Participants identified stronger enforcement against streambank cultivation and illegal alluvial mining; irrigation development; alternative household energy; improved waste management; management of invasive species; stronger human–wildlife conflict mitigation; restoration after mining; and improved health, water and road services. Several proposals also required research, including wildlife-conflict mitigation, crop traits less attractive to wildlife and control of invasive species.
The results show that barriers were not uniform across the landscape. Lack of knowledge and communication breakdown were prominent in proposals directed at farmers, the public and traditional leadership. For government agencies and development actors, funding, staffing, equipment, research capacity and policy constraints dominated. Human–wildlife conflict, for example, was linked not only to community practices but also to patrol resources, compensation arrangements, legislation and coordination among ZimParks, local government, CAMPFIRE and safari operators.
Participants also identified enablers at different scales. At village and ward levels, these included locally available plant materials/natural resources, by-laws and legislation, knowledge, and institutional support. At district and national levels, enablers included policies and penalties, human and financial resources, irrigation and solar-energy infrastructure, trained farmers, research capacity and development partners. Funding and policy appeared as both enablers and barriers depending on their availability and implementation.
Participants identified knowledge, skills, motivations and relationships that could support the desired behavior changes. Available assets included knowledge about crop and livestock farming, forests, rivers, wildlife, environmental management, and indigenous knowledge. Practical skills included farming, carpentry, sewing, baking, beekeeping, gardening, aquaculture, livestock production, tree planting, and gully rehabilitation. Participants also identified shared commitments to food security, education, cultural practices, environmental protection, faith, community gatherings and youth wellbeing. Participants also identified relationships with government departments, traditional leaders, churches, schools, development partners, farmer groups, and other local institutions as important landscape assets. These networks can support information exchange, resource mobilization, coordination, and the uptake of new practices.
Together, these assets provide a foundation for achieving the shared vision of a well-governed, climate-resilient and multifunctional landscape. Livelihood skills and enterprises support income generation and food security, while environmental knowledge and restoration practices contribute to healthier ecosystems. Social and institutional relationships enable coordination, knowledge exchange and collective action. By linking these assets, the landscape can support multiple functions including agricultural production, biodiversity conservation, resilient livelihoods and community wellbeing.
Four practical lessons emerge. First, a landscape vision must be translated into changes assigned to named actors. Second, barriers and enablers must be diagnosed at the scale where they operate. Third, transition pathways should build on existing capabilities rather than begin only with external inputs. Fourth, relationships determine whether knowledge, finance, authority and services can be mobilised across scales.
The workshop outputs now provide inputs for the next LV2A stage. Behaviour-change statements can be linked to specific assets and constraints; weak or missing institutional relationships can become coordination priorities; and bilateral discussions with key agencies can test assumptions about mandate, capacity and political economy. Combined with natural and physical resource mapping, these findings will support the co-design of transition pathways that specify actions, responsibilities and enabling conditions. The next step is to prioritize the proposals, verify their feasibility, assign responsibilities and define indicators of progress towards the ten-year vision.
From policy ambition to coordinated action, a perspective which unpacks the value of using multifunctional landscapes to operationalise Zimbabwe’s climate-resilient agrifood transformation.

articles.title_original: Right seed, right soil, right management: Rethinking zinc biofortification in wheat
articles.content:
A wheat variety called Melka is helping researchers rethink biofortification in Ethiopia, showing how the right genetics and management can improve both harvests and nutrition.
A recent multi-year experiment, covering more than 600 locations across three major wheat belts in Ethiopia demonstrates that the combination of a zinc-efficient wheat genotype with specific/targeted fertilizer management practices can enhance both grain productivity and zinc concentration. This offers a promising pathway to tackle hidden hunger. For hundreds of millions of people who rely so heavily on cereals as their staple foods, having enough food does not necessarily mean getting enough nutrition. Micronutrient deficiencies, often referred to as hidden hunger, remain a major nutrition challenge, particularly where access to diverse, nutrient-rich foods is limited.
Among the nutrients linked to hidden hunger, zinc remains a major concern. Wheat provides a substantial share of daily calories for millions of people, yet conventional wheat varieties often contain relatively low levels of zinc in the grain to meet nutritional needs. Biofortification can help close this gap by increasing grain zinc concentration. In wheat, this can be achieved through breeding varieties that accumulate more zinc in the grain and through agronomic practices such as applying zinc fertilizer. Recent research under the CGIAR Sustainable Farming Program, conducted by CIMMYT and partners across multiple locations in three major wheat-growing areas (Arsi Zone, East Shewa, and North Shewa in Amhara), shows why these approaches are most powerful when considered together through the interaction of genotype, environment, and management (G×E×M).
Understanding the genotype-environment-management interactions
The study examined three interconnected factors: the genetic characteristics of the wheat variety, the zinc status of the soil, and the way zinc fertilizer is applied. Using Bayesian modeling, researchers estimated the probability of achieving specific grain-yield and grain-zinc targets under different combinations of these factors. This approach moves beyond average treatment effects and helps identify which combinations are most likely to succeed under particular production conditions. The results show that no single biofortification strategy works equally well everywhere. The effectiveness of an intervention depends on how the variety, soil conditions and fertilizer management interact.
According to Dr. Tesfaye Shiferaw Sida, Systems Agronomist at CIMMYT, the key question is not simply whether zinc fertilizer works, but where it works, with which variety and under what management conditions. Understanding those differences provides a stronger basis for recommendations that respond to farmers’ actual production environments.
This shift, from asking whether an intervention works on average to identifying where and under which conditions it is most effective, is central to developing more precise and practical biofortification strategies.
A key finding came from Melka, a zinc-efficient wheat variety evaluated against a conventional variety. Even without additional zinc fertilizer, Melka showed a genetic advantage in both grain yield and zinc accumulation.
In zinc-deficient soils, the probability of simultaneously reaching high-yield and high-zinc targets increased from near zero for conventional wheat to more than 27% for Melka under baseline conditions. The result underscores the importance of genetics as a foundation for biofortification: varieties that acquire and accumulate zinc efficiently can improve the likelihood of achieving nutritional gains, particularly where soils are deficient in the micronutrient.
“What we see with Melka is that genetics gives us a strong starting point. A zinc-efficient variety can already improve our chances of achieving both yield and nutritional targets before additional fertilizer is considered. Management can then build on that genetic advantage,” Sida explained.
The research also showed that soil conditions strongly influence the effectiveness of zinc fertilizer. Where soil zinc was already sufficient, additional zinc applications produced limited yield benefits. In zinc-deficient soils, however, fertilizer management became much more important, regardless of the Zn-efficiency level of the genotypes.
The study identified complementary roles for different application methods. Basal zinc application, applying fertilizer to the soil at planting, was particularly effective in supporting grain yield. Foliar applications, spraying a zinc solution directly onto the crop, were more effective in increasing zinc concentration in the grain.
These findings suggest that soil zinc status should be considered when developing fertilizer recommendations for farmers. Instead of applying the same treatment everywhere, understanding the zinc status of the soil can help target fertilizers to locations where it is most likely to deliver meaningful agronomic and nutritional benefits. It can also guide the choice of application method depending on the intended objective, whether to improve yield, increase grain zinc concentration, or achieve both.
One concern surrounding crop biofortification is a possible trade-off between yield and nutrient concentration. As plants produce more grain, nutrient concentrations can sometimes become diluted. The Ethiopian study, however, provides evidence that higher productivity and improved grain nutrition can be achieved together when genetics, soil conditions and management are appropriately combined.
In zinc-deficient soils, combining the Melka variety with a higher zinc fertilizer rate increased the probability of achieving both a grain yield of at least 4.5 tonnes per hectare and a grain zinc concentration of 40 mg/kg to approximately 75–80%.
The result is important because it shows that biofortification does not necessarily require a choice between productivity and nutritional quality. With the right variety and management for the local soil conditions, both objectives can be pursued at the same time.
The study points to a broader way of thinking about wheat biofortification.
Breeding zinc-rich or zinc-efficient varieties remains essential, but genetics alone cannot address the diversity of conditions farmers face. Likewise, fertilizer application without considering soil zinc status or varietal characteristics may not deliver consistent results. Biofortification is therefore most effective when genetics, soil conditions and crop management are considered together rather than as separate interventions. Matching the right variety with the right production environment and management practices provides a stronger pathway to improving productivity and nutritional quality at the same time.
“Farmers cannot be expected to sacrifice productivity for nutrition. What is encouraging about these results is that the two objectives do not have to compete. With the right seed, right soil conditions and right management, we can substantially increase the probability of producing more wheat while also improving its nutritional quality,” Sida said.
This principle extends beyond zinc. Rather than relying on one-size-fits-all solutions, agricultural recommendations need to recognize the diversity of farmers’ production environments. Integrating genetics, soil information and agronomic management can help make interventions more targeted, efficient and relevant to local conditions.
Ultimately, tackling hidden hunger through agriculture requires more than increasing the amount of food produced; it also means improving the nutritional quality of the foods people already grow and consume. By combining better genetics, a clearer understanding of soil conditions and targeted crop management, wheat biofortification can help build food systems that deliver both higher productivity and better nutrition.
“Our goal is not simply to produce more grain. It is to help build farming systems that produce enough nutritious food for people while remaining practical and profitable for farmers. Bringing the right seed, right soil and right management together takes us closer to that goal,” Sida concluded.

articles.title_original: Fertilizer, Fiscal Risk, and Food Security: Rationalizing Bangladesh’s Subsidy System in an Era of External Shocks
articles.content:
Bangladesh imports 75–80% of its fertilizer, and it fixes retail prices before each season. As a result, every global price shock lands directly on the public budget. The 2026 Strait of Hormuz disruption pushed urea prices up by 70–80%, and five of the country's six urea factories closed because of
Bangladesh imports 75–80% of its fertilizer, and it fixes retail prices before each season. As a result, every global price shock lands directly on the public budget. The 2026 Strait of Hormuz disruption pushed urea prices up by 70–80%, and five of the country’s six urea factories closed because of gas shortages. It is the latest reminder that the fertilizer subsidy bill is driven by external shocks rather than domestic policy choices.
In this policy note, CIMMYT’s Dr. Ravi Nandi and Dr. Wais Kabir, former Executive Chairman of the Bangladesh Agricultural Research Council (BARC), argue that the current system is fiscally risky and inequitable. Fertilizer subsidies absorb nearly 80% of the agriculture ministry’s budget, yet the largest 20% of farms receive about half the benefits. Only 5% of farmers apply a balanced mix of nutrients. The authors recommend gradual reform, not removal. That means moving from blanket subsidies toward targeted support, balanced nutrient management, stronger extension services and crop diversification, while protecting food security and farmers’ livelihoods.
On 9 September 2026, co-author Dr. Wais Kabir discussed the fertilizer situation on Channel 24’s talk show Muktobak (“Agriculture, Farmers and Fertilizer”). Watch here .

articles.title_original: México y Corea fortalecerán intercambio científico y tecnológico, incluyendo la IA
articles.content:
México y Corea fortalecerán el intercambio científico, tecnológico y de innovación, y trazarán una ruta de trabajo para dar prioridad al uso de inteligencia artificial (IA), el desarrollo de biofertilizantes y la mecanización agrícola. Por ello, representantes de ambos países, a través de la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader) y la Administración de …
México y Corea fortalecerán el intercambio científico, tecnológico y de innovación, y trazarán una ruta de trabajo para dar prioridad al uso de inteligencia artificial (IA), el desarrollo de biofertilizantes y la mecanización agrícola.
Por ello, representantes de ambos países, a través de la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader) y la Administración de Desarrollo Rural de Corea (RDA, por sus siglas en inglés) suscribieron dos memorándums de entendimiento que buscan fortalecer la cooperación agroalimentaria.
En un comunicado, la Sader detalló que el primer instrumento —firmado entre el Instituto Nacional de Investigaciones Forestales, Agrícolas y Pecuarias (INIFAP) y la RDA— establece las bases para desarrollar proyectos de investigación científica, particularmente en materia de agricultura sostenible.
El segundo —suscrito entre el Ministerio de Seguridad en Alimentos y Medicamentos de Corea (MFDS, por sus siglas en inglés) y el Servicio Nacional de Sanidad, Inocuidad y Calidad Agroalimentaria (Senasica)— promoverá la certificación electrónica de productos agropecuarios para contribuir a modernizar y agilizar los procesos de comercio entre ambos países.
Al respecto, el director general Interino del INIFAP, Alejandro Espinosa Calderón, calificó como positivas estas iniciativas porque consolidan una alianza que trasciende fronteras geográficas, al unir el conocimiento científico y el compromiso tecnológico en favor del desarrollo sustentable de ambos pueblos.
Particularmente, indicó que el documento formaliza una ruta de trabajo para dar prioridad al uso de inteligencia artificial, el desarrollo de biofertilizantes y otros insumos necesarios en el campo. “Confiamos en que estos encuentros clave, como el de la Asociación Mexicana de Distribuidores de Maquinaria, abran nuevas opciones para avanzar en la mecanización del campo mexicano”.
En su intervención, el administrador de la RDA, Lee Seungdon, refirió que el acuerdo conducirá a reforzar los resultados obtenidos en otras colaboraciones, como con la Cooperación Económica Asia-Pacífico (APEC), y subrayó que
Corea es un ejemplo mundial en la mecanización del proceso de cultivo de arroz y el uso de la inteligencia artificial”.
“Trabajando juntos podremos alcanzar resultados aún mayores y ofrecer un apoyo más sustancial”, expresó el representante de la delegación coreana, al reafirmar el compromiso de su país para fortalecer la seguridad alimentaria de México.
En representación de la titular de Sader, Columba Jazmín López Gutiérrez, el coordinador de Asuntos Internacionales, Santiago Ruy Sánchez de Orellana, agradeció la suscripción del memorándum y los trabajos conjuntos entre México y Corea que permitirán fortalecer la relación bilateral y remarcó: “México quiere acercarse más a Corea, queremos cooperar más”
La firma de ambos acuerdos se realiza en el marco de la Cumbre Corea-México, que sostendrán la Presidenta de México, Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo, y su homólogo de la República de Corea, Lee Jae-myung.

articles.title_original: Recolectan 70 toneladas de envases vacíos de plaguicidas en Mexicali, Baja California
articles.content:
La Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader) informó que al término de la Segunda Jornada Gratuita de Recolección de Envases Vacíos de Agroquímicos, realizada en Mexicali, Baja California, se logró recolectar 70 toneladas de envases vacíos de plaguicidas, La dependencia informó que está acción se enmarca en el Plan de Justicia para los Trabajadores …
La Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader) informó que al término de la Segunda Jornada Gratuita de Recolección de Envases Vacíos de Agroquímicos, realizada en Mexicali, Baja California, se logró recolectar 70 toneladas de envases vacíos de plaguicidas,
La dependencia informó que está acción se enmarca en el Plan de Justicia para los Trabajadores Agrícolas, bajo el lema El destino de tu envase es responsabilidad compartida, con la cual se registró un acopio de 60 toneladas de estos plásticos en San Quintín, a las que se sumaron 10 toneladas adicionales del Centro de Acopio Temporal (CAT) de Mexicali.
La Sader engatizó que la jornada también forma parte de la Estrategia Nacional para el Manejo de Envases Vacíos de Plaguicidas, que impulsa el gobierno de México para promover el manejo responsable de los residuos agrícolas, prevenir la contaminación del suelo y del agua, y fortalecer la seguridad de toda la cadena agroalimentaria.
Hizo hincapié en que un envase de plaguicida puede conservar hasta 1.5 por ciento del producto original, por lo que su disposición inadecuada genera riesgos de contaminación en suelo y agua, además de posibles afectaciones a la salud de las personas y a los ecosistemas.
Para reducir este riesgo, la Sader impulsa el protocolo “Lava, perfora y entrega”, el cual permite disminuir hasta en un 99 por ciento los residuos químicos que permanecen en los recipientes y facilitar su manejo seguro.
Además de la Sader, en la jornada participaron las secretarías de Medio Ambiente y la de Salud, junto con el Senasica y la Comisión Federal para la Protección contra Riesgos Sanitarios (Cofepris)—, así como las autoridades estatales y municipales, productoras y productores agrícolas, distribuidores, empresas de plaguicidas, la industria nacional de protección de cultivos y la asociación Amocali.
En el marco de este evento, el Senasica entregó a la empresa Agroquímicos Peninsulares el Certificado de Cumplimiento de la Norma Oficial Mexicana NOM-033-FITO-1995, en reconocimiento a la correcta aplicación de las especificaciones fitosanitarias.

articles.title_original: 🎥 Eclipse Ingredients scales human lactoferrin platform: ‘We’re executing at a speed that is unheard of in this space’
articles.content:
"We've got two platform technologies and we’re executing at a speed that is unheard of in this space," says CEO Siobhan Coster.
[Disclosure: AgFunderNews’ parent company AgFunder is an investor in Eclipse Ingredients]
Australian precision fermentation startup Eclipse Ingredients is gearing up for commercial launch of its human lactoferrin next year, starting in cosmetics before moving into adult nutrition and, longer term, infant formula.
The company has already signed memorandums of understanding (MOUs) with five distributors and begun tech transfer to pilot scale, says cofounder and CEO Siobhan Coster.
“We’ve got two platform technologies and we’re executing at a speed that is unheard of in this space.”
AgFunderNews ( AFN ) caught up with Coster (SC) at the Future Food-Tech summit in London to discuss the case for human versus bovine lactoferrin and Eclipse’s asset-light approach to scale-up.
SC : Human and bovine lactoferrin are essentially different proteins, so there’s a 30% difference in amino acid structure between the cow version and the human version. The cow version is designed for calves, and the human version is designed for humans. And we can see that from our own testing, where we have superior results of the human version on human cells, which makes sense.
AFN : Lactoferrin is in breast milk, which is consumed by infants, but most startups are initially targeting adult nutrition. Is there any evidence that lactoferrin actually benefits adults?
SC : Lactoferrin is naturally produced by the human body, and it’s found throughout the human body. So it’s in immune cells, in tears, and saliva. The highest concentrations are in breast milk, as you say, but its benefits are really diverse.
There is a lot of clinical data to support its efficacy in a number of different applications from helping to support iron regulation, to reducing inflammation, and supporting longevity. So there are a lot of different applications that make human lactoferrin really interesting across women’s health, sports nutrition, and healthy aging. We can really help to increase our health span alongside our lifespan.
AFN : Human lactoferrin isn’t currently on the market, whereas bovine lactoferrin is. How do you know there’s a market for it, or is it a case of build it and they will come?
SC : For us it was the opposite. We spent years validating the market opportunity and making sure that there were customers that wanted this first and foremost. And that’s been fundamental to everything that we do at Eclipse Ingredients: making sure that it’s about the consumer and that there is demand.
It’s definitely not build it and they will come! We know that there’s demand. Our first market is in the cosmetics space. We’ve got really strong demand there and we’re really excited about what we’re building there.
AFN : Many precision fermentation startups have struggled to get over the valley of death. How are you navigating manufacturing and scale-up?
SC: We’re leveraging four partnerships with research organizations that gives us access to infrastructure, equipment, and skills that go from micro-liter plate scale all the way up to 2,000-liter pilot scale. We’re leveraging existing infrastructure rather than building our own.
Beyond that, we’re also scaling up really smart. We’re starting with a market that has a smaller volume requirement, which means that we can scale up in stages, and we can prove everything that we’re doing in those stages towards our end goal of getting into infant formula, where we’ll be generating tons and tons of material.
AFN: Can you talk about advances you’ve made over the last year or two to improve the efficiency of your bioprocess, optimize your strains or improve your downstream process?
SC : We’ve achieved a lot in the last 18 months. We’ve built our first proprietary technology platform and we’ve got a second in development. We are using applied AI across everything that we are doing, and that’s been built in from day one. We’ve started our tech transfer to pilot scale, and we’re gearing up for tech transfer to our commercial manufacturer.
SC : We’re a B2B ingredients provider; that’s our core strategy. Bur we’re open to partnerships and exploring different models. At the moment, we’re building towards distribution partnerships. We’ve already signed MOUs with five distributors, and we’ve got a few more in development. We’ve got a global launch in our plans next year.
AFN : There are a few players now in the lactoferrin space. How do you see companies differentiating themselves?
SC : First and foremost, these are massive markets, and we need multiple suppliers of human lactoferrin to support a healthy industry. For Eclipse, we are built to lead in this space. We’ve got two platform technologies and we’re executing at a speed that is unheard of in this space. We have gone from our first raise to [approaching] commercial launch in two years.
AFN : Which geographical markets are you targeting, and what’s the regulatory pathway for those markets?
SC : We have a global regulatory strategy, and we are targeting all of our key jurisdictions at once across all of our markets. APAC and the US will be our first markets, followed by the EU, where we know it takes a bit longer to get regulatory approval.
SC : For our first market, which is cosmetics, we have local [regulatory] compliance already, and we have really strong customer traction, so we’re super excited about that market.
The next market is in the adult nutrition space. That’s a growing and emerging market where we’re seeing an increased interest in the nutrition, precision nutrition, and food-as-medicine areas.
And then finally we’re targeting infant formula. Here, different regulations will require a more precise or a more focused dossier and it [regulatory approval] will take a little bit longer.

articles.title_original: Autonomous spraying cuts chemical use by 85% at Coggan Farms
articles.content:
Labour shortages and rising machinery costs prompted Australian mixed farmer Tom Coggan to invest in autonomous spraying.
Labour shortages and rising machinery costs prompted Australian mixed farmer Tom Coggan to invest in autonomous spraying. Coggan Farms now operates 2 SwarmFarm Robotics SwarmBots equipped with Weed-It spot-spraying cameras and AutoFill technology. During fallow spraying, the farm typically saves around 85% on chemical use.
Coggan Farms has been operating 2 autonomous SwarmBots since 2021 and 2022 respectively. The machines are mainly used for weed control on fallow land, where targeted spraying has significantly reduced chemical use. The business later added SwarmFarm Robotics’ AutoFill technology, allowing the machines to refill their spray tanks automatically and further reducing the amount of labour required.
Spread across more than 65,000 acres near Meandarra in Queensland, Australia, Coggan Farms combines crop production with livestock farming. The business is run by Phillip and Cindy Coggan together with their children Emily, Tom and Sarah. Tom Coggan is the fifth generation of the family to farm there and has been closely involved in introducing robotic technology to the business. “Our business includes cattle and lamb feedlots, irrigated and dryland farming, extensive grazing country and a Meatmaster Stud operation,” he says. “The properties have been family-owned and operated since 1937, with multiple generations involved in the business. Around 32,000 acres is used for our cropping programme, growing barley, wheat, chickpeas, canola, sorghum and forage sorghum. Our crop rotations are designed and changed to suit seasonal conditions. Yield averages vary significantly depending on rainfall and those conditions.”
The decision to go for robots was driven by ongoing staff shortages, increasing equipment and operational costs
Operating such a large area requires considerable labour. As recruiting staff became increasingly difficult, the family started looking for ways to automate some of its fieldwork. “The decision to go for robots was driven by ongoing staff shortages, increasing equipment and operational costs, and the need to consistently repeat weed-control operations with high accuracy and efficiency,” Coggan says.
Before the autonomous machines arrived, weed control was carried out using operator-driven tractors fitted with camera-based spraying systems. “The first robot, the SB032 called Delta 2, arrived in December 2021 and the second, the SB036 called Hotel 2, came in 2022. We later invested in the AutoFill technology in 2025.”
The 2 robots are predominantly used in the cropping operation, particularly during fallow periods when repeated and targeted weed control is required. Their ability to work for extended periods also reduces the need for additional operators. “Our robots are SB032 and SB036 from the SwarmBot 5 platform. Each machine is fitted with an 18-metre Hayes boom and Weed-It optical spot-spray cameras, along with a 3,000-litre spray tank,” Coggan says. “The machines are powered by approximately 75hp diesel engines and generally require refuelling every 24 to 30 hours of operation, depending on conditions and workload.”
Targeted spraying has produced some of the largest savings. “The biggest advantage for us has been chemical savings through targeted spot spraying. In some situations, we have achieved reductions of up to 95% in chemical usage, although typical savings average around 85%.”
Introducing autonomous machinery required changes to existing working practices, particularly during the initial implementation period. “There was definitely a learning curve initially, particularly around integrating the technology into daily farm operations and adapting existing workflows,” Coggan says.
“However, once the systems were established and staff became familiar with the platform, the setup and day-to-day operation became straightforward. The support from SwarmFarm during implementation and training was also very valuable in helping with the transition.”
Coggan Farms added SwarmFarm Robotics’ AutoFill system in 2025. The autonomous docking and chemical-handling system allows a SwarmBot to return to a filling station, refill its spray tank and resume work without an operator carrying out the process manually. The system can store, measure and mix multiple chemicals, flush valves and record each fill. “The AutoFill system has been a major advantage from both a labour and efficiency perspective,” Coggan says. “It allows the robots to refill and return to work with minimal operator involvement, which reduces downtime and keeps the machines operating for longer periods. “From a logistics standpoint, it has simplified chemical handling and improved workflow around spray operations. Instead of constantly moving people and machinery around paddocks, the robots can operate more independently while staff focus on other jobs around the farm. “It also improves consistency and accuracy in chemical mixing and loading.”
Coggan sees consistency as another important benefit of autonomous spraying, particularly across large areas. “One of the biggest benefits that is sometimes overlooked is consistency,” he says. “The robots are able to repeatedly carry out operations with the same level of accuracy regardless of time of day or operator fatigue. That consistency becomes extremely valuable during large-scale fallow spraying programmes. Another major factor is scalability. Autonomous systems allow operations to expand spraying capacity without needing to proportionally increase labour, which is becoming increasingly important in agriculture.”
The biggest advantage for us has been chemical savings through targeted spot spraying
The initial investment in autonomous machinery is substantial, Coggan acknowledged. However, he said the combination of lower chemical use, labour savings, reduced machinery wear and the ability to make better use of spraying windows has produced positive results for the business. “The payback can vary depending on the season, spray area and chemical prices, but the robots have definitely saved us a lot through reduced chemical use, lower labour needs and better overall efficiency,” he says. “We generally see around 85% chemical savings during fallow spraying, which makes a huge difference to input costs. Being able to keep the machines running for long hours with very little supervision has also helped us get across more country and stay on top of operations when timing matters.”
According to SwarmFarm Robotics, a SwarmBot costs about AUD$360,000 (€220,000). Implements such as sprayers, mowers and slashers represent a further investment, while the AutoFill system costs around AUD$80,000 (€50,000). The company says some customers achieve a payback period of 12 to 18 months through savings on chemicals, fuel and labour. Actual payback depends on factors including machine utilisation, input costs and the type of work performed.
SwarmFarm Robotics has also developed an online calculator that allows farmers to compare autonomous machinery with conventional self-propelled sprayers or tractor-based systems. Users enter information including farm area and chemical, fuel and labour costs. The tool then calculates annual costs such as capital expenditure, depreciation, repairs, fuel, labour and chemicals for 3 different machinery setups.
The comparison is intended to give farmers an indication of the potential operating-cost differences between conventional and autonomous spraying systems.
Family: Phillip and Cindy Coggan with children Emily, Tom and Sarah
Crops: Barley, wheat, chickpeas, canola, sorghum and forage sorghum
