articles.title_original: Future Farming Five: what autonomous weeding taught Kilter
articles.content:
Kilter’s AX-1 robots apply herbicide in precise micro-droplets directly onto weeds, and have helped growers avoid spraying.
Kilter’s AX-1 robots apply herbicide in precise micro-droplets directly onto weeds, and have helped growers avoid spraying more than 1 million litres of herbicide mixture compared to what conventional broadcast spraying would have used. Future Farming asks the Norwegian company how this number was calculated, which growers benefit most from the AX-1, and what buyers should consider before investing.
“The figure comes from telemetry data: AX-1 logs the number of droplets it applies, each 1 µL, giving the actual volume of herbicide mix used. That’s compared with what a conventional broadcast spray would have used on the same area, at a standard rate of 250 L/ha. Row crop growers with high-value vegetables benefit most, especially root vegetables and leafy greens. These are crops where weeds hit yield hard, herbicide options are limited, and manual weeding is expensive and hard to staff. Root vegetables have a long growth cycle, and keeping weeds under control all the way through it pays off at harvest: higher yield and a more even crop with fewer defects. Leafy greens are the opposite case but just as strong a fit. Fast growth and short cycles mean several crops per season and a narrow window for weed control, so precise, repeatable treatment pays off quickly. Kilter has both small and large farms as customers, and the technology scales well with the size of the operation. AX-1 is used on both flat fields and bed-formed fields.”
“The biggest one is yield. With up to 99% drift reduction, AX-1 can treat weeds right next to the crop plant, which is exactly where weeds compete hardest. And because the crop itself is not targeted, it avoids the herbicide stress that broadcast spraying causes. In our trials we have measured yield increases of 30 to 40%, along with more uniform growth and a higher share of marketable produce. Labour is the other major gain. AX-1 runs autonomously, freeing up hours that went into spraying or hand weeding in a sector where seasonal labour is scarce. We haven’t measured soil health effects yet, but reducing herbicide use by an average of 97% is naturally a step in the right direction.”
“That the robot makes the decisions. AX-1 takes over the repetitive, precise work in the field, but the agronomic judgement stays with the grower: which product to use, when to treat, and how to plan the season around it. Good planning matters just as much as before. What changes is that the plan gets executed with more precision. We believe no manual or broadcast method can match it. Timing is another thing growers sometimes get wrong. AX-1 works best on small weeds, so treatment should start earlier than with broadcast spraying. Treating early makes it possible to reduce volumes drastically. In slower-growing crops, new germination means the application has to be repeated, but the benefits clearly outweigh the extra passes.”
“How does it perform in my crop, my soil and my conditions, and can I see it running on a farm like mine? Who supports it locally when something goes wrong in the middle of the season? How does it fit my existing workflow, equipment and field layout? For AX-1, we have strong reference farms running it in large-scale operations, and our fleet has logged approximately 20,000 hours of autonomous operation so far in 2026, with the most heavily used machines passing 1,700 hours each. Local support is important, and comes through our distributors, Kubota in Europe and Croplands in Australia, so growers deal with a dealer network they already know.”
“That’s a question we prefer to answer with results rather than predictions. Development at Kilter is continuous, and AX-1 gets better through software updates and the experience we gain in the field. Our priorities are shaped by what growers need. What matters is what works reliably in their fields. When new capabilities are proven and ready, we’ll be happy to share them.””
Main markets: Norway, Sweden, Germany, the Netherlands and Australia. AX-1 is distributed by Kubota in Europe and Croplands in Australia, and Kilter is now planning to enter France and the UK together with Kubota.
Product category: Detecting and eliminating weeds in row crops
Number of machines in operation: 54 AX-1 robots were in operation in 2026, across Norway, Sweden, Germany, the Netherlands and Australia, together treating 4,265 hectares between 1 January and 16 August. More robots are scheduled for delivery both this year and next.

articles.title_original: México importa cada año un millón de t de maíz blanco transgénico para consumo humano: Víctor Suárez
articles.content:
A pesar de que la reforma al artículo cuarto constitucional prohíbe la siembra de maíz genéticamente modificado y que se destinen maíces transgénicos para otros usos que no sea consumo pecuario, sin que haya una evaluación de riesgos, “hoy se están importando un millón de toneladas cada año de maíz blanco transgénico para consumo humano”, …
A pesar de que la reforma al artículo cuarto constitucional prohíbe la siembra de maíz genéticamente modificado y que se destinen maíces transgénicos para otros usos que no sea consumo pecuario, sin que haya una evaluación de riesgos, “hoy se están importando un millón de toneladas cada año de maíz blanco transgénico para consumo humano”, expresó el procurador agrario, Víctor Suárez Carrera .
Durante la 16.ª conferencia del ciclo Rescate, defensa y revalorización de los ejidos y comunidades agrarias , realizada en conmemoración del Día Nacional del Maíz , el ex miembro de la Campaña nacional sin maíz no hay país y de la Acción Colectiva –organismos de la sociedad civil que detuvieron la siembra de maíces transgénicos en México–, expuso que lo anterior sucede sin que haya trazabilidad y sin que nadie diga nada.
Ante organizaciones de la sociedad civil, productores y funcionarios federales, Suárez Carrera subrayó que existen desafíos porque, “decimos no al maíz genéticamente modificado en la palabra, pero los hechos estamos consumiendo tortillas con maíz genéticamente modificado, importado de Estados Unidos, un millón de toneladas cada año”.
Expuso que si es que queremos seguir en la lucha en defensa del maíz y de todo lo que éste significa hay hay temas pendientes que deben ser abordados, como el hecho de que el mercado mexicano de maíz blanco no genéticamente modificado para consumo humano esté desvinculado “absoluta y totalmente de la bolsa de Chicago” y que “se determine en función de costo de producción más utilidad razonable y ese es el precio justo que debe recibir un productor de maíz, pero en general todos los productores del campo”.
México, recordó, es el primer país productor de maíz blanco para el consumo humano, no genéticamente modificado, pero se preguntó por qué Chicago, que es una bolsa de especulación, está determinando un precio ficticio, por los subsidios estadounidenses, y la agricultura en el mundo está determinada por otros factores, como los mercados de energía y financieros.
esto es una tarea difícil, pero no hay otro camino si es que queremos resguardar la autonomía y la independencia y la autosuficiencia en maíz blanco para consumo humano no genéticamente modificado”.
No sé si esto lo tiene en cuenta o no la Campaña nacional sin maíz no hay país; pero todos somos responsables, también el gobierno.
Otro desafío, consideró, Víctor Suárez es la publicación de la Ley general de la alimentación adecuada y sostenible, que aunque tiene más de dos años que se aprobó la ley reglamentaria del derecho constitucional a la alimentación, no se ha publicado, “porque no le gusta a los gringos, no le gusta a los empresarios y no se quiere incomodar a no sé quién”.
Refirió que dicha la promueve la agroecología, la alimentación saludable, las compras gubernamentales, el etiquetado de alimentos que contengan organismos genéticamente modificados y que plantea un sistema de coordinación institucional para vincular los temas de agricultura, alimentación, salud y medio ambiente,
En su exposición cuestionó que las condiciones del neoliberalismo, de los tratados comerciales y de los gobiernos neoliberales, “se ve como natural que los productores acepten vender su cosecha por debajo de sus costos de producción, a pérdida. Nadie produce para perder, sólo los campesinos, sólo los productores, para beneficio de los grandes monopolios que comercializan los productos y que los procesan y que los distribuyen”.
Por estos factores, explicó, el campo está empobrecido permanentemente y cada vez menos campesinos se quedan en la tierra, tienen que venderla, alquilarla o generar desórdenes en el manejo de los usos comunes y de sus recursos.
Añadió que este tema es difícil, pero “pues no le gusta a Trump, no le gusta a los que dominan la industria agroalimentaria en el mundo y puede afectar las negociaciones del T-MEC, sí; pero pues tomemos decisiones, difíciles..”.
En su exposición el titular de la Procuraduría Agrario también manifestó que “los ejidos y comunidades agrarias sostienen esta causa al resguardar las semillas, el territorio y los conocimientos que permiten alimentar al país y conservar la capacidad de decidir qué producir, cómo hacerlo y en beneficio de quiénes”.
Esta lucha –enfatizó– busca proteger la diversidad de nuestros cultivos frente a los organismos genéticamente modificados y fortalecer a las familias campesinas ante la concentración del mercado de semillas y la dependencia alimentaria.
La integrante de la Campaña nacional sin maíz no hay país, Dulce Espinosa de la Mora, señaló que proteger el maíz implica también preservar los territorios, el agua y las formas comunitarias de producción.
Advirtió que está en juego la capacidad de decidir colectivamente qué alimentos producir y bajo qué criterios, así como el reconocimiento de las generaciones de familias campesinas e indígenas que han conservado esta riqueza biológica y cultural.

articles.title_original: Prioritario acelerar la investigación científica para atender retos del campo: Sader
articles.content:
Frente al cambio climático, la sequía, plagas o enfermedades que inciden en los cultivos agrícolas, es prioritario acelerar la investigación científica para desarrollar variedades de semillas más resistentes e impulsar proyectos relacionados con granos básicos, como maíz y arroz, consideró la titular de la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader), Columba Jazmín López Gutiérrez. …
Frente al cambio climático, la sequía, plagas o enfermedades que inciden en los cultivos agrícolas, es prioritario acelerar la investigación científica para desarrollar variedades de semillas más resistentes e impulsar proyectos relacionados con granos básicos, como maíz y arroz, consideró la titular de la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader), Columba Jazmín López Gutiérrez.
Al inaugurar, en Tlaltizapán, Morelos, el Centro de Capacitación Internacional en Tecnologías Agrícolas Sustentables (CIMCITI) —perteneciente al Centro Internacional de Mejoramiento de Maíz y Trigo (CIMMYT)—, la funcionaria federal hizo un llamado a transitar decididamente hacia la agroecología, la recuperación del suelo, mediante consorcios microbianos, y la gestión eficiente del agua para asegurar la sostenibilidad del ecosistema agrícola en el largo plazo.
En esta nueva etapa de gestión en la Sader, López Gutiérrez resaltó que la prioridad es eliminar la fragmentación institucional y construir un plan articulado en beneficio del sector primario. El compromiso del gobierno de la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo es, ”trabajar en coordinación con las instituciones del sector y orientar la ciencia y la tecnología a atender oportunamente los retos de las y los productores del país”.
La titular de la Sader también propuso reducir los costos de producción, mediante esquemas de financiamiento, compras consolidadas y una mayor articulación entre productores. En este sentido habló de la implementación del programa Cosechando Soberanía y la compra organizada de insumos para generar ahorros clave en la producción agrícola..
Acompañada de la gobernadora de Morelos, Margarita González Saravia, Columba López se congratuló por colocar la tecnología e innovación agrícola como un pilar estratégico en el estado de Morelos
La gobernadora de la entidad reconoció al CIMMYT como aliado estratégico “para colocar a Morelos como el primer estado agroecológico del país”, de ahí que anunció el respaldo de su gobierno para impulsar un nuevo centro en el surponiente de la entidad.
En su oportunidad, la oficial de Asuntos Económicos de la Embajada de Estados Unidos en México, Cat Haseman, resaltó que su país mantiene el compromiso con esta alianza mediante una inversión de 40 millones de dólares para apoyar al CIMMYT, institución que calificó como “un socio valioso” por su experiencia en investigación, mejoramiento de cultivos y vinculación directa con productores y el sector privado.
Finalmente, el representante regional del CIMMYT para América Latina, Jelle Van Loon, resaltó que transformar los sistemas agroalimentarios es llevar el conocimiento al territorio para probarlo, adaptarlo y convertirlo en resultados que dejen un doble beneficio: en el bolsillo de quien produce y en la salud de los suelos, agua y ecosistemas.
Resaltó que el CIMCITI cuenta con 20 hectáreas activas con cultivos, tratamientos y experimentos que integran maíces nativos, arroz, manejo de agua, tecnologías digitales y mecanización adaptada a distintos contextos. Esta base permitirá ampliar las actividades de demostración, capacitación e intercambio de conocimiento.

articles.title_original: Antobot scales UV-C robotics push with 300 deployments targeted in 2027
articles.content:
“We're getting great results, big reductions in chemical spraying and also quite good increases in yield as well," says Antobot VP Marc Jones
UK-based startup Antobot is aiming to deploy 300 autonomous robots in strawberry crops next year as more growers become comfortable with using UV-C light to tackle powdery mildew and other fungal pathogens.
Rather than spraying fungicides on crops, the ‘bots apply UV-C light to damage the pathogens’ DNA so they can’t replicate. The tech—also utilized by firms including Saga Robotics , TRIC Robotics and CleanLight —can reduce labor and input costs and help firms adopt a chemical-free positioning, according to VP commercial Marc Jones.
“We’re getting great results, big reductions in chemical spraying and also, interestingly, quite good increases in yield. Some of that is obviously from having less disease, but also we’re seeing that the canopy in general is healthier,” added Jones, who was speaking to AgFunderNews on the sidelines of the World Agri-Tech Innovation Summit in London .
Antobot, which was founded by Howard Wu, PhD, in 2019, is now operating in the UK, Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Canada and parts of Asia. It has historically engaged directly with customers including Driscoll’s and Tiptree but is now building out a distributor network, said Jones.
“We’ve signed distributor agreements in the UK and Spain. We’re looking at Canada and we’ve set up a joint venture in Asia.”
As deployment numbers increase, Antobot is also changing its business model.
Until last year, it operated exclusively through robots-as-a-service, lowering the upfront barrier for growers but leaving Antobot responsible for servicing and day-to-day operations, said Jones. “But as you grow, this model gets more challenging, so next year we’re going to move most of our customers over [to acquiring the machines and operating them themselves].”
Capital equipment grants in markets including the UK and Spain can make upfront purchasing more attractive, he noted.
In the UK, concerns from retailers and consumers about pesticide residues are an important driver for “chemical-free” UV-C light treatment, whereas in Asia, growers are interested primarily because existing approaches are struggling to control disease, said Jones.
Spain combines both dynamics, with exporters serving the UK market while also facing pressure to shift growers toward more sustainable production methods.
Canada presents another use case, with many strawberry growers operating on just two or three hectares and unable to justify the kind of spraying equipment used by large UK growers, he said.
In some cases, improved disease control is also giving growers greater confidence to expand production because it reduces the risk of having to shut down part-way through the season.
While using UV-C light to zap fungal threats is its primary focus, Antobot has also developed scouting modules that enable growers to monitor fruit count, size, and maturity, forecast yields, improve supply chain planning, and optimize sales and marketing strategies, said Jones.
“The 300 targeted are primarily going to be UV-C platforms next year, however a portion of these will be other applications [scouting, spraying, logistics], which will increase over the next few years.”
The key lesson from early deployments has been that introducing autonomous machines onto farms requires changes in day-to-day operations as well as reliable hardware, said Jones.
Operational headaches can be mundane, from tractors blocking routes to locked gates or changed access codes, he observed.
Antobot has also modified its machines in response to experience in the field, including moving to swappable batteries and simplifying aspects of the suspension.
Some growers are already operating more than 10 machines, he said, allowing one person to supervise several units at once.
Antobot—which has to date funded itself through grants, a small seed round led by Intron Technology Holdings , and revenues—is now looking for growth capital to support the next stage of expansion, said Jones.
“We’re looking for growth capital now we’ve got traction. I think we’ve got a good story, a good customer base and a good platform for scaling.

articles.title_original: Austrian alt meat startup Revo Foods targets profitability by Q3 2027 as 3D-printing scales up
articles.content:
With six printers operating at its production facility, Revo Foods can now turn out a product every three seconds, says CEO David Petuzzi.
Austrian alt meat startup Revo Foods is targeting profitability by the third quarter of 2027 as it scales up its patented 3D-printing tech to make whole-cut alternatives to fish and chicken.
The Vienna-based firm expects sales to grow 80-90% this year after triple digit growth in 2025 supplying mostly branded products to the retail market, CEO David Petuzzi told AgFunderNews at the Future Food-Tech summit in London.
“We closed H1 with 70% growth compared to last year, so this year we’ll probably make around €1.5 million ($1.7 million) in sales,” said Petuzzi, who moved from CFO to CEO around a year ago. “Our goal is to become profitable by Q3 of next year.”
Revo is currently raising €2 million ($2.26 million), of which €1 million ($1.13 million) has already been secured, he said.
Founded in 2021, Revo has previously raised money from business angels, crowdfunding campaigns and Austrian public grants.
But Petuzzi said the investment proposition for companies such as Revo Foods has shifted as venture investors have become more focused on businesses capable of generating very large outcomes.
“I think we see in the industry that maybe plant based is not really a VC case anymore. They’re all looking for unicorns, and I don’t think that in our industry there will be a lot of unicorns.”
Instead, he said, family offices and business angels may be comfortable backing companies where potential exit values are “somewhere between €50 and €300 million, which I think is possible.”
Revo’s recent growth has come from a mixture of new listings and velocity gains from existing retail accounts, with Germany and Austria currently accounting for around 80% of revenues, said Petuzzi.
Performance varies significantly depending on where products are stocked, he said. “We have to be in the right supermarkets. In some we have really high velocity whereas in some in the countryside you will barely be purchased.”
He added: “You need to be differentiated in the market, and you have to deliver on all aspects. The taste must be at least as good as the conventional one. You must deliver on the nutrition, especially the protein. You must deliver on texture, and you must deliver on price. If you combine all those, you will be successful.”
Revo initially focused on recreating the texture and flakiness of salmon, turning to 3D printing as a way to integrate protein and fat into layered structures.
It has since expanded into other seafood products and this summer launched a chicken alternative called El Pollo using mycoprotein sourced from a third party.
A key challenge from the outset was turning 3D food printing from a batch process into a continuous one, Petuzzi said. “We were the very first ones to crack this and start a continuous production process with food material.”
Revo subsequently developed a multi-nozzle system with 16 nozzles per printer, enabling each machine to make eight fillets simultaneously. With six printers operating at its production facility north of Vienna, Revo can now turn out product every three seconds.
Scaling, argued Petuzzi, does not therefore require ever-larger machines. “You multiply the nozzles; you multiply the amount of printers.”
The modular setup also enables Revo to take individual machines offline without shutting the whole line and easily switch between products, he said.
“The printers are capable of printing a range of viscous materials, so on one day we can do the white fish filet, the next day the salmon filet, and the other day the chicken.”
Petuzzi claimed the components for each machine currently cost around €25,000 ($28,300), giving Revo an ROI of less than two months on additional printers.
While developing the technology was R&D intensive, “the printers themselves are not expensive,” he said.
Revo is also moving beyond products manufactured using its 3D-printing platform.
Its newest launch, Cottage Protein+, is a fermented cottage cheese alternative made from apricot kernels, salt water and fermentation cultures, said Petuzzi.
“This product has same protein content [as conventional cottage cheese] and it’s higher in fiber. With the current cottage cheese shortage, I think we very much go into the zeitgeist.”
The product has already secured listings with Rewe and Edeka in Germany, he said, with Revo now looking to increase production in response to demand.
Revo Foods is accessing the US market through a partnership with Slovenian whole-cut specialist Juicy Marbles [disclosure: AgFunderNews ‘ parent company AgFunder is an investor in Juicy Marbles], which sells Revo’s salmon and whitefish products under its own brand.
“We all want the industry to succeed, and that’s why we’re trying to do collaborations with others,” said Petuzzi. “They have a fantastic brand.”
For Revo, the immediate priority, however, is reaching the point where continued expansion no longer depends on external capital, he said.
At that point, Revo will have the option of raising additional growth capital or expanding more organically, he said. “We just need another million, and with this, we can achieve break even.”

articles.title_original: Cultivo de aguacate en macrotúnel gestará un sistema agroecológico más productivo, rentable y sin deforestación
articles.content:
En México se cultivan más de 272 mil hectáreas de aguacate, que han tenido un proceso de expansión acelerada en la última década, principalmente en los estados de Michoacán y Jalisco, por el alto valor que alcanza el fruto en los mercados nacional e internacional. Sin embargo, esto ha dejado una huella de deforestación y …
En México se cultivan más de 272 mil hectáreas de aguacate, que han tenido un proceso de expansión acelerada en la última década, principalmente en los estados de Michoacán y Jalisco, por el alto valor que alcanza el fruto en los mercados nacional e internacional. Sin embargo, esto ha dejado una huella de deforestación y contaminación, por el uso intensivo de agroquímicos para su producción, que dañan los ecosistemas, la flora y la fauna.
Frente a este problema, investigadores de la Universidad Autónoma Chapingo (UACh) trabajan en alternativa que revolucionará la forma en que se cultiva hoy en día este alimento, al pasar de un sistema a cielo abierto, a costa de los bosques, a uno en agricultura protegida, con el empleo de macrotúneles, que hace posible cultivar en otros ambientes y latitudes y reducir al mínimo el impacto ecológico. Además, el sistema se convierte en una opción ante el cambio climático.
La diferencia entre un sistema a cielo abierto y el de agricultura protegida es muy grande. El detalle es el manejo basado en podas, pero en un macrotúnel de alta densidad, con 3 mil plantas por hectárea, se pueden cosechar de 40 a 60 toneladas (t) de aguacate en comparación en una huerta al aire libre que anda alrededor de las 12 toneladas.
En la búsqueda de opciones para los productores de pequeña y mediana escala de Texcoco, Estado de México, y para aprovechar los invernaderos subutilizados, los investigadores Enrique Vázquez Robles, Evelyn Vanessa Pérez Álvarez, coordinados por la doctora Rita Schwentesius Rindermann, desarrollaron un proyecto para producir aguacate de manera intensiva bajo el sistema en macrotúneles, con insumos ecológicos.
Para ello instalaron un microtúnel de 500 metros cuadrados, en los campos experimentales de la UACh, en Texcoco, Estado de México, donde contemplan introducir hasta 180 árboles, que cinco años, entre sistemas convencionales y orgánicos, producirán 20 kilos cada árbol, “lo cual nos da un rendimiento excepcional”. En cinco años la meta es obtener de 200 a 300 kilos bajo este sistema, explica Enrique Vázquez.
Detalla que en Michoacán –principal productor de aguacate del país–, bajo un sistema abierto, los árboles son muy grandes y en su edad adulta, de 15 a 18 años, uno solo puede dar 300 kilos, pero con una densidad más baja, de unos 90 árboles por hectárea.
Para tener un comparativo, Evelyn Vanessa Pérez explica que se trabaja con los sistemas orgánico –bajo la norma Estados Unidos–, racional y convencional, los cuales están en evaluación.Constantemente se recogen datos sobre nutrición, altura de la planta, el grosor de tallo, largo y ancho de las hojas y yemas.
Vázquez Robles refiere que es nuestro primer año con esta evaluación. Llevamos cinco meses y esperamos empezar a producir aguacate en un año y medio, y en dos años un árbol ya estén produciendo, al menos, alrededor de cinco kilos.
En aguacate existen experiencias internacionales y nacionales que permiten orientar la investigación. En el ámbito internacional los frutales los ha desarrollado España, principalmente en naranja, mandarinas y empezó con aguacate. “Son los pioneros en ese tipo de producción”. No obstante, en México ya existen experiencias muy buenas en Jalisco, con producciones en maceta y en producción en suelo con macrotúneles.
En la zona de Valles Altos, Estado de México, existen árboles criollos de aguacate y la variedad Hass la han plantado arriba de los 3,000 metros sobre el nivel del mar. Nuestro macrotúnel está a 2,400 metros de altura, comentan los investigadores integrados en Asore, sostenibilidad y resiliencia.
Los árboles de Hass se adaptan a diferentes climas. En la zona de Texcoco ya existe plantaciones de aguacate, pero tienen riesgos de heladas, por eso se decidió utilizar macrotúneles para protegerlos de este fenómeno, principalmente por la cobertura plástica, entonces el frío no asienta la hoja directamente. La planta se puede mantener sin ningún problema.
La ventana de la tecnología de macrotúneles de alta densidad es que protege de heladas y podemos producir e inducir floraciones y entrar en épocas donde el aguacate puede valer más, con podas e inducciones florales en momentos óptimos”, destaca Enrique Vázquez.
También comenta que los suelos de Texcoco son de tepetate, son muy someros, con alrededor de 25-30 centímetros de profundidad. Por eso los árboles se mantendrán siempre pequeños para que no necesiten tanta humedad y el sistema de riego es por goteo localizado, por lo que se tiene un alto aprovechamiento del agua.
En cuanto a la altura de los árboles será de porte pequeño,alrededor de 3 metros, para que el manejo sea rápido, al igual que la aplicación de insumos, el corte y que la cosecha que la realice una persona a pie sin necesidad de utilizar escaleras.
Las plantas de aguacate proceden de un invernadero certificado de Uruapan, Michoacán, están libres de enfermedades. Una planta injertada en una huerta al aire libre tarda de tres a cuatro años en empezar a producir, en este sistema de macrotúneles tienen comportamiento diferente, en dos años tendrá una producción con entre dos a tres kilos por árbol.

articles.title_original: México y Francia dialogan para ampliar y diversificar intercambio agroalimentario
articles.content:
Representantes de los gobiernos de México y Francia sostuvieron una reunión con el objetivo de abordar las oportunidades que ofrece el Acuerdo Global Modernizado México–Unión Europea, así como para ampliar y diversificar el intercambio agroalimentario entre ambas naciones. Durante este encuentro, la titular de la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader), Columba López Gutiérrez, …
Representantes de los gobiernos de México y Francia sostuvieron una reunión con el objetivo de abordar las oportunidades que ofrece el Acuerdo Global Modernizado México–Unión Europea, así como para ampliar y diversificar el intercambio agroalimentario entre ambas naciones.
Durante este encuentro, la titular de la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader), Columba López Gutiérrez, y el ministro de Comercio Exterior de Francia, Nicolas Forissier, coincidieron en la importancia de avanzar hacia un comercio agroalimentario más equilibrado y mutuamente benéfico, diseñado para aprovechar con eficacia las nuevas condiciones de acceso a mercados y generar oportunidades concretas para productores de pequeña y mediana escala.
López Gutiérrez destacó el potencial exportador que el Acuerdo representa para productos mexicanos como café, aguacate, berries, mango, papaya, limón, plátano y miel, al tiempo que subrayó la necesidad de respaldar las preferencias comerciales con avances recíprocos en materia sanitaria y regulatoria.
el interés de México en dar seguimiento al diálogo con la Unión Europea sobre productos orgánicos, con el propósito de ampliar las oportunidades para las y los agricultores”.
En este marco, informó la Sader en un comunicado, la embajadora de Francia en México, Delphine Borione, suscribieron una Carta de Intención para fortalecer la colaboración entre las autoridades agroalimentarias de ambos países.
Este instrumento permitirá profundizar el intercambio de conocimientos en innovación, agricultura sostenible, pesca y acuacultura, además de impulsar la investigación, la transferencia tecnológica y la formación de capacidades.
Como parte de la conmemoración de los 200 años de relaciones bilaterales entre México y Francia, ambas partes acordaron definir una hoja de ruta con proyectos concretos, aprovechando la cooperación actual en agroecología, producción sostenible, el desarrollo rural y la pesca.

articles.title_original: Gobierno federal y exportadores de aguacate firman acuerdos en materia de seguridad laboral, sanidad y deforestación
articles.content:
El gobierno federal firmó dos acuerdos con exportadores de aguacate en materia de seguridad laboral, sanidad y para garantizar que no haya deforestación en la producción de este fruto de exportación, que genera divisas al país por tres mil 500 millones de dólares, además de miles de empleos. “Es un día muy importante para la …
El gobierno federal firmó dos acuerdos con exportadores de aguacate en materia de seguridad laboral, sanidad y para garantizar que no haya deforestación en la producción de este fruto de exportación, que genera divisas al país por tres mil 500 millones de dólares, además de miles de empleos.
“Es un día muy importante para la exportación; les agradecemos mucho la confianza en el gobierno y este trabajo que vamos a seguir desarrollando juntas y juntos para el bienestar de los habitantes; principalmente, de Michoacán”, expresó la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo.
En Palacio Nacional, la jefa del Ejecutivo federal indicó que “a partir de ahora empieza un proceso de difusión de los acuerdos firmados, con el propósito de que todas y todos los productores del aguacate de exportación de Michoacán y todo el país conozcan las nuevas normas”.
A través de redes sociales, agradeció el compromiso del equipo del gobierno federal y de las y los productores, principalmente de Michoacán y Jalisco. Explicó que
estos acuerdos incluyen consolidar seguridad laboral y sanidad. También garantizan que no haya deforestación en la producción de aguacate”.
También en su red social, la secretaria de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader), Columba Jazmín López Gutiérrez, quien estuvo presente en la dicho acto, escribió: “Hoy acompañamos a nuestra Presidenta en la firma de dos acuerdos para garantizar y fortalecer la producción de aguacate de exportación, un producto que representa miles de empleos y genera ingresos por cerca de 3 mil 500 millones de dólares”.
En la firma de los convenios también estuvieron presentes el jefe del Servicio de Administración Tributaria (SAT), Antonio Martínez Dagnino; el director en jefe del Servicio Nacional de Sanidad, Inocuidad y Calidad Agroalimentaria (Senasica), Francisco Javier Calderón Elizalde; y el presidente de la Asociación de Productores y Empacadores Exportadores de Aguacate de México (Apeam), Raúl Ernesto Martínez Pulido.

articles.title_original: En ANP hay más de 680 mil hectáreas ocupadas por concesiones mineras; la ley lo prohíbe
articles.content:
La titular de la Secretaría de Medio Ambiente y Recursos Naturales (Semarnat), Alicia Bárcena, destacó en la conferencia matutina de la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum la recuperación de 272 mil hectáreas de Áreas Naturales Protegidas (ANP) que habían sido concesionadas para la explotación minera; sin embargo, persisten más de mil 300 concesiones mineras vigentes en ANP, …
La titular de la Secretaría de Medio Ambiente y Recursos Naturales (Semarnat), Alicia Bárcena, destacó en la conferencia matutina de la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum la recuperación de 272 mil hectáreas de Áreas Naturales Protegidas (ANP) que habían sido concesionadas para la explotación minera; sin embargo, persisten más de mil 300 concesiones mineras vigentes en ANP, que representan una superficie acumulada de más de 680 mil 270 hectáreas.
Así lo señaló la Colectiva Cambiémosla en un comunicado, donde señala que la Ley de Minería vigente prohíbe cualquier actividad de exploración, explotación o beneficio minero en ANP, por lo que esas concesiones –aún vigentes– deberían ser canceladas de inmediato, porque representan un enorme riesgo para el patrimonio natural del país.
Expresa su preocupación, sobre todo porque el Proyecto de Presupuesto de Egresos de la Federación para 2027 “pretende asignar alrededor de 16.2 pesos por hectárea para la protección y manejo de las ANP”.
La titular de la Semarnat también afirmó que en esta administración federal ya se dio el cambio de paradigma del “extractivismo neoliberal hacia el ambientalismo humanista”. Para la Colectiva Cambiémosla Ya, integrada por comunidades, movimientos, organizaciones de la sociedad civil y personas académicas y defensoras, para que eso suceda, un primer paso debería ser que esta dependencia y la Secretaría de Economía (SE) cumplan con la reforma en materia de minería y agua de 2023 y publiquen los reglamentos, cuyos avances son fundamentales para la protección de los ecosistemas y de los derechos de las comunidades frente a una de las industrias extractivas más voraces y nocivas para las poblaciones y el medio ambiente en México.
Puntualiza que a más de tres años de la reforma a la Ley de Minería, que incorporó regulaciones muy importantes para evitar la vulneración sistemática de derechos y la destrucción impune de los ecosistemas por esta industria, ni la SE ni la Secretaría de Medio Ambiente y Recursos Naturales (Semarnat) han publicado los reglamentos de la Ley de Minería ni de la LGEEPA, la Ley General para la Prevención y Gestión Integral de los Residuos (LGPGIR) ni de la Ley General de Aguas en materia de minería.
Esta omisión, añade la organización, reconocida incluso por la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum, obstaculiza la aplicación a cabalidad de la nueva legislación minera, deja espacios para la interpretación en temas centrales como la restricción de cualquier actividad minera en ANP; la obligación que tienen las empresas de presentar y ejecutar un programa de cierre y post-cierre de minas, además de los medios para sufragar los gastos derivados de las actividades de remediación, por citar solo unos ejemplos.
“Con ello, las autoridades mantienen la puerta abierta para que la industria minera siga causando afectaciones ambientales, muchas de ellas irreparables, como los reiterados derrames de jales mineros de Grupo México que han contaminado terrenos de cultivos, ríos y otros cuerpos de agua”.
Para la Colectiva Cambiémosla Ya, “no hay abandono del modelo “extractivista neoliberal” cuando se siguen construyendo acuerdos con las empresas que más han incumplido sus obligaciones y firman acuerdos para intensificar el extractivismo minero, como el Plan de Acción sobre Minerales Críticos entre México y Estados Unidos, cuyo objetivo prioritario es abastecer de minerales al país vecino y del que no hay información pública sobre los compromisos contraídos”.
Considera la falta de un marco regulatorio robusto y claro para la industria minera allana el camino para afianzar el modelo extractivo que desplaza y enferma a las comunidades, saquea los bienes comunes naturales del país y devasta los ecosistemas.
La Colectiva también expresa que “para las comunidades y las organizaciones resulta muy preocupante que el gobierno federal haya comenzado el proceso de construcción de una Estrategia Nacional de Minerales Prioritarios y Estratégicos, de la que no hay información pública ni se han abierto espacios de participación ciudadana”.

articles.title_original: EU looks to speed agricultural research to market despite budget pressures
articles.content:
Policy chiefs, farmers and researchers debate what’s needed to propel innovations into markets and onto farms faster and at scale.
Scientists, policy experts, NGOs and farmers gathered in Brussels Thursday and Friday to tackle a tough question: How can the European Union’s agricultural research be turned into scalable businesses when public funding is tight?
The EU AgRI 2040 conference, hosted by the European Commission, sought input on the strategic framework adopted September 8 for “future-proofing” agriculture, forestry and rural areas. The roadmap aims to complement a separate but “interlinked” one, called Food 2040 , dealing with food processing, aquaculture, healthy diets and more.
“We’re as good at innovation as any other continent in the world, but then it doesn’t actually find its way to deployment,” said Elisabeth Werner, the EC’s director-general for agriculture and rural development.
To close that gap, AgRI 2040 addresses eight “action areas” from soil health and animal welfare to rural demographics and AI. The commission says these are starting points and can be adapted based on stakeholder input about where R&I can make the biggest impact.
The approach comes as policymakers face “a lot of pressure on the farming budget,” said Christophe Hansen, the European commissioner for agriculture and food. He called to “strengthen the link” between the Horizon Europe R&I program and the Common Agricultural Policy budget, whose dimensions for 2028-2034 are now being haggled over . In addition, authorities hope to attract more private capital with a proposed €234 billion ($264 billion) European Competitiveness Fund that, when combined with Horizon’s proposed €175 billion ($197 billion) pot, would unlock €409 billion ($461 billion) for multisector innovation, including in agriculture.
Whatever the final funding mix, jumpstarting commercialization requires not just “moving faster from lab to farm,” said Ekaterina Zaharieva, the European commissioner for startups, research and innovation, but “better focusing our efforts” amid limited resources.
A few themes emerged as agrifood stakeholders discussed ways to strike that balance.
There was a broad agreement that Europe “must fast-track promising innovation with commercial potential,” as Zaharieva put it.
“There’s a global race going on,” Werner said. “If you want to have an idea about speed, look to China,” she added. “We have to step up.”
Bureaucracy and regulation were repeatedly flagged as hindrances. During a Q&A, one attendee raised concerns about the Horizon program’s administrative burdens. He joked about having to conduct 45-question surveys with farmers, who after the third question typically say, “I have to go, my cow is calling.”
A Finnish farmer described an EU certification process requiring interactions with three or four entities, versus one in the U.S.—where the only hiccup was one of the government’s recent shutdowns.
EU authorities acknowledged these issues and said responses to some were in the pipeline. Hansen said he’d also heard entrepreneurs tell him, “We did the research here, but now we are going to move to the United States” since getting to market there takes a year or two, whereas in Europe “it takes around 10 years and we are bankrupt by the time we get there.”
Farmers said the financial and climate shocks they’re facing require speedier outcomes from R&I.
“Everything that comes to our farm is just coming too late and too expensive,” said Iulia Blagu, who manages a 920-hectare family farm in Romania and leads ANFA, which represents women in the country’s agricultural sector.
“I don’t even know how we survived,” she said of prolonged droughts. “There are solutions out there…in the past six years that were not accessible to my farm, and that is very frustrating.”
Tight public financing raises the importance of striking partnerships and making agrifood innovations more investable. But when the moderator asked a packed plenary session if big businesses were risk-averse, at least half the room’s hands shot up.
Zaharieva said the public sector should “lead by example.” “European governments and public institutions should procure more from our innovators,” she said. If promising startups and scale-ups can clinch a crucial first contract with a public entity, corporations may feel more confident about investing or partnering.
“We have to have an appetite for risk because not everything will succeed,” said Bill Callanan, chief inspector at Ireland’s Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine. He urged policymakers to look at “the nonfinancial elements” that may be keeping industry on the sidelines. Demonstration facilities were one area where “government can help,” he said, by expanding opportunities for companies to validate their processes and test for issues that may arise in production.
Stakeholders repeatedly described a need to stoke demand for novel products and services.
Richard Zaltzman, CEO of EIT Food, pointed out that the agrifood system’s complexity poses a challenge. “You need to have concurrent innovation through the value chain” for adoption to occur, he said, but added that there’s room to shift more attention from projects to end products.
While it came in for a drubbing in other ways, regulation was also positioned as a tool for generating demand. “If you’re a startup, you need money and you need to know that there’s a demand. The two things are linked,” said James Morrison, who leads the “Healthy Planet” Directorate in the EC’s directorate-general for R&I. “Regulation creates markets…as much as being a menace.”
He said expanded regulatory sandboxes could help, while the proposed Competitiveness Fund, as a “twin” of the Horizon program, would propel more startups past the “second valley of death” to scale.
Callanan said better communication “is critical for researchers” to get their innovations out of labs and technical reports and into markets where farmers can take them up. While scientists are constantly urged to publish, volume “isn’t the right metric,” he said. “Effort and impact are not the same thing. Who’s listening?”
The point came up frequently, but there were few concrete ideas about how to transmit information more effectively and speedily. Aside from some approving remarks about farmers using WhatsApp and AI for timely advice, discussions around communication largely centered on the need to build stronger relationships between the R&I ecosystem and external stakeholders. (At the same time, it was hard to overlook how many deeply knowledgeable experts took the main stage for panel discussions only to read prepared remarks from tablets. One farmer in the audience groused that this should be a fireable offense for EU officials.)
Blagu, for her part, communicated the next test clearly: “We need to translate your research and your innovation and your policies” into scalable solutions, without spending too long deliberating over which ones to test in the market.
“If something works in your labs but fails in 10 farms, then we have the answer,” she said. “As a farmer, we are failing 10,000 times a year. Every year, it’s a battle for the right decision…You don’t know, but you try your best.”

articles.title_original: 🎥 Atmonia scales green ammonia with single-step electrochemical process
articles.content:
Atmonia has developed catalysts for a single-step electrochemical process that eliminates the need to first produce and store hydrogen.
Ammonia is essential to modern agriculture, but making it via the traditional Haber-Bosch process is carbon-intensive and typically requires enormous industrial plants. So, what’s the alternative?
Iceland-based Atmonia has spent the past decade developing patented catalysts for a single-step electrochemical process that eliminates the need to first produce and store hydrogen.
The company is now focused on cutting energy demand and scaling its technology toward a 40-foot containerized system producing around 150 tons of ammonia a year.
AgFunderNews (AFN) caught up with cofounder and CEO Helga Dögg Flosadóttir (HDF) at the World Agri-Tech innovation summit in London to discuss the technical hurdles to scale-up, the economics of decentralized ammonia production, and how Atmonia has funded its tech.
HDF : We founded Atmonia in 2016, so we’ve been around for a decade. For a great part of that time, we’ve been engineering and working on developing a catalyst that can produce ammonia in an aqueous electrochemical cell [at ambient temperature and pressure].
This is single-step ammonia production from nitrogen and water so we do not need to produce or store any hydrogen. We also do not need two different systems and have an equilibrium between them. We just have a simple system for ammonia production, rather than hydrogen first and then ammonia.
HDF : This is our nitrogen electrolyzer. It’s a commercially available electrolyzer that we have amended for our purpose. It works like an AEM [anion exchange membrane] aqueous electrolyzer with a membrane electrode assembly, and this way we can bring the nitrogen gas in through a gas stream, and it will have direct access to the catalyst on gas diffusion electrode.
The nice thing about electrolyzers is that they scale up. When we scale up, we scale up in two dimensions. We don’t scale up in three dimensions. Now we’re working with an electrode that is 10 square centimeters. Then we will scale up to 400 square centimeters, but following that, we will start stacking the cells into an electrolyzer stack, similar to the AEM systems.
And this we want to do in collaboration with AEM electrolyzer manufacturers who have already optimized and perfected [producing] AEM electrolyzers at large scale.
AFN : Does this scale in a predictable way? If you know that it works at a small scale, do you know that it will work at a large scale?
HDF : To a certain degree, yes. So we can demonstrate it on a small scale. Then we can use computational fluid dynamics to simulate the way that it will react and operate on a large scale and use the optimized versions there.
There will be, of course, some unknown parameters that we will have to work with and optimize on the way. The nitrogen reduction reaction hasn’t been done on that scale yet in an AEM electrolyzer.
AFN : Why is your approach potentially more efficient than that of other companies making green ammonia?
HDF : First of all, I want to say how extremely important it is, and great that we have competition. It shows how important green ammonia development is, and how we need to find solutions.
Some are going to industrial ammonia production, others are going small scale, and we will be competing in a small scale market where we’re bringing nitrogen fertilizer production directly to the farmer.
There, what we think are the most important factors are energy demand, flexibility, and size. And in all of those areas, we have an advantage over the other systems.
HDF : The catalysts have been developed using density functional theory or quantum chemical simulations. [The key is] understanding the chemical composition of the catalyst and which reaction sites can efficiently activate and attract nitrogen rather than water or hydrogen, and produce ammonia, and selectively produce ammonia rather than hydrogen.
This is extremely important because most other catalysts favor hydrogen production over nitrogen reduction and ammonia synthesis.
We will be focusing on the catalyst in our business model, on the catalyst synthesis and the electrode manufacturing, and we want to collaborate with others on the manufacturing of the hardware and the scale up. The catalysts themselves have a specific reaction site that selectively reduces nitrogen, and in addition to that, they’re also made of abundant raw materials.
AFN : What is the biggest technical bottleneck right now? Is there something particular you need to optimize to get to viable unit economics?
HDF : We’ve demonstrated the chemistry, which took us 10 years of research. And now we’re optimizing the energy demand, and we’ll do that both via optimization of the catalyst itself and an optimization of the environment around the chemical reaction inside the electrolyzer.
We have a very clear and structured approach to that, and we anticipate to reach that milestone before the end of next year.
AFN : What size plants would be needed at a commercial scale for this to be viable?
HDF : Our goal is to scale up to a 40-foot containerized production process, and this process will be producing about 150 tons of ammonia per year. This should create viable economics, even at electricity prices that we are seeing today.
HDF : We aim to be a catalyst and electrode producer and partner up with hardware manufacturers closer to end user markets. Atmonia is located in Iceland, and we could saturate the market in Iceland with 80 containers, so the market in Iceland is limited.
We will go global and bring the manufacturing closer to the end user. With the business model in general, what we’re looking at is a leasing model to the farmer to remove the barrier of capex for the farmer.
HDF : We’ve been extremely successful in receiving grant funding, which has provided most of the runway that the company has needed over the past decade, from Icelandic research bodies, the European Innovation Council, and Horizon Europe.
AFN : What about equity? Have you got any institutional investors, and what kind of money are you looking for going forward?
HDF : We have Icelandic venture capitalists that have joined the company throughout the past years, and Canadian agriculture angels that joined us a couple of years ago. We have just kicked off our seed investment round, where we’re looking for agritech investors, deep tech investors, and other investors that have a slightly longer horizon than conventional venture capitalists.
Our next milestone is to optimize the energy demand and then start scaling up. This funding should get us to TRL-6, so we can demonstrate a prototype operating on-farm.

articles.title_original: International Training Strengthens Global Response to Maize and Wheat Diseases to Protect Food Security
articles.content:
Specialists from 11 countries strengthened their capacity to identify, monitor and manage maize and wheat diseases, combining molecular diagnostics, field assessment, resistance breeding, surveillance and early warning to address emerging crop health risks.
Texcoco, Mexico. Wheat and maize diseases can threaten food security by reducing yields, affecting grain quality and, in some cases, contaminating grain with harmful mycotoxins. Strengthening the ability of scientists and plant health specialists to identify, monitor and manage these threats is increasingly important as crop pathogens evolve and move across regions.
Mexico, CIMMYT and its partners are helping consolidate and strengthen these capabilities through research, surveillance and specialized training to detect threats, anticipate risks and respond in a timely manner to diseases that can affect maize and wheat production. From August 3 to 14, 2026, CIMMYT brought together 22 specialists from Bangladesh, Bolivia, Brazil, China, Colombia, El Salvador, Guatemala, Kenya, Mexico, Pakistan and Uruguay at its headquarters in El Batán, Mexico, for the Workshop on Surveillance, Identification, and Management of Maize and Wheat Diseases . The training was organized by the Global Surveillance and Advisory System (GSAS) and the Global Wheat Health Alliance (GWHA).
The training addressed disease identification and field monitoring, integrated disease management, seed health and resistance breeding, with a focus on diseases including Fusarium head blight, wheat blast and wheat rusts, as well as tar spot and maize lethal necrosis. The program combined theoretical sessions with hands-on work in laboratories, greenhouses and the field. Participants gained experience in DNA isolation, molecular marker diagnostics and mycotoxin quantification, as well as pathogen manipulation, disease screening and phenotypic assessment. They also visited CIMMYT facilities connected to this work, including the Genebank, BioScience and Biosafety facilities, and the Seed Health Laboratory.
The learning continued at CIMMYT’s experimental stations. At Agua Fría, participants examined pre-breeding and breeding plots focused on lowland maize diseases, while in Toluca they learned from active disease field trials. A visit to SENASICA’s National Phytosanitary Reference Centre introduced participants to multispectral drone surveillance for crop anomaly detection and risk prioritization, surveillance of quarantine-important pathogens, and biological pest control technologies in Mexican maize production. The program also dedicated two days to disease surveillance, forecasting and advisory activities supported by GSAS.
GSAS builds on more than two decades of wheat and maize disease surveillance led by CIMMYT, Cornell University and partners. It strengthens and expands these capabilities through a system that brings together near-real-time field monitoring, advanced diagnostics, predictive modelling, data integration and advisory systems. The approach also connects field intelligence with breeding and seed systems, while incorporating capacity development and knowledge networks to strengthen preparedness for crop disease threats.
Among the recent initiatives that have contributed to this experience is the Disease Early Warning and Advisory System (DEWAS), which strengthened networks for disease surveillance, diagnostics, forecasting and capacity development. Through DEWAS, more than 500 national partners from 25 countries were trained in areas including wheat rusts, wheat blast, Fusarium head blight, diagnostics and the interpretation of disease forecasting models. Cornell University led the project’s capacity development component, working with CIMMYT and other participating institutions.
During the opening session, Flavio Breseghello, Director of CIMMYT’s Global Wheat Program, emphasized CIMMYT’s commitment to addressing food security and food safety challenges through scientific innovation, collaborative and inclusive partnerships, and global capacity building. At the closing session, Laurajean Lewis, Director of CIMMYT’s Genetic Resources Program, and course coordinator Pawan Singh highlighted the importance of developing a skilled global network of crop health specialists capable of strengthening surveillance and breeding strategies.
This collaboration connects national research and plant health institutions with scientific partners including USDA-ARS Cereal Disease Lab, Cornell University, the University of Minnesota, NASA Harvest, Aarhus University, the Global Rust Reference Centre, the University of Cambridge, the UK Met Office, the John Innes Centre and The Sainsbury Laboratory, alongside institutions across the Americas, Africa and South Asia. In Latin America, the GSAS network includes INIFAP in Mexico, INIA in Uruguay, INIAF in Bolivia, ICTA in Guatemala, DICTA in Honduras, AGROSAVIA in Colombia and CENTA in El Salvador.
The training acknowledges support from the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR), India’s Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, One CGIAR Initiatives B4T, the Gates Foundation, the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office, and the Government of the United States of America.
By connecting hands-on training with a broader international scientific and surveillance network, the workshop strengthens the capacity to identify emerging disease threats, share information across regions and translate that knowledge into earlier, better-informed responses. Strengthening these capabilities is particularly important when diseases affecting staple crops can disrupt production and food supply, creating risks that extend beyond agriculture to food security and, in some circumstances, national security.
CIMMYT and the World Food Prize Foundation co-organized DialogueNEXT—Seeds of strength: Nurturing farmer resilience, held at CIMMYT headquarters in Mexico from 10 to 11 July 2024. The event brought together scientists, agribusiness leaders, farmers, and policymakers from over 200 organizations and 55 nations, to help shape global collaboration and strategies for sustainably producing nutritious food for all, within planetary boundaries.
At lectures at Cornell University, CIMMYT director general calls for quick united action to avert the unfolding food security crisis.
Legacy websites and photo exhibition mark the closing of the CGIAR Research Programs on Maize and Wheat, and their impact on sustainable agricultural development.

En …
Para el ciclo cafetalero 2026/2027, la producción de café en México tendrá un ligero repunte, al ubicarse en 4.1 millones de sacos, mientras que el consumo también observa crecimiento al pasar de 2.1 del ciclo anterior a 2.3 millones de sacos para el actual, de acuerdo con datos de organismos internacionales y organizaciones nacional es.
En el marco del Día Internacional del Café, nuestro país reporta que para este año sus exportaciones sumarán 3.41 millones de sacos, cuyo principal destino serán los Estados Unidos.
La Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader) destacó el trabajo que realizan los productores primarios para que el aromático llegue hasta el consumidor final, tras recorrer “una larga cadena en la que participan familias productoras, comunidades, jornaleras y jornaleros, quienes trabajan para conservar y aprovechar la riqueza agrícola y cafetalera de México”.
La titular de la Sader, Columba López Gutiérrez, destacó –en un videomensaje– la apertura de la “La Camfetería”, en las instalaciones de la dependencia en la Ciudad de México, que es “un espacio único”, donde se busca “que estén conectados directamente productores y consumidores finales para que ese dinero que antes se llevaban los intermediarios hoy quede en manos de las y los productores”.
Invitó a los consumidores a que “si van a comprar un café que sea de un productor mexicano” y refirió que en este espacio se comercializan diversos productos del campo, chocolate, canela molida, té, botana de nopal con chile, harina de plátano, frutas en almíbar, miel, amaranto, maíz azul, pinole, jaleas y leche, entre otros alimentos, que llegan directamente de comunidades rurales y de iniciativas impulsadas por programas como Sembrando Vida, Escuelas del Campo y los Programas para el Bienestar.
La dependencia puntualizó en su sitio web, que “uno de los principales objetivos de este espacio es acercar esas historias a los paladares de las y los consumidores, así como a reducir la distancia entre quien produce y quien compra. La idea es sencilla: que quien toma una taza de café pueda conocer de dónde viene, quién lo produjo y cómo establecer una relación comercial directa con las comunidades rurales”.
La Camfetería –señala– también busca convertirse en un punto de encuentro para restaurantes, cafeterías, tiendas y otros negocios interesados en adquirir directamente productos del campo mexicano.
Con este enlace para acortar la distancia entre productores y consumidores –que los expertos llaman cadenas cortas de comercialización–, la Sader busca que los agricultores se apropien de mayor valor en la venta de sus productos.
En este sentido, la dependencia recordó que también dentro de sus instalaciones se realiza, cada quince días, la Expo del Campo Mexicano, donde se ofrecen alimentos preparados, artesanías, textiles, productos estéticos y de higiene personal, entre otros, elaborados por productoras y productores.
En el marco del Día Internacional del Café, la Sader recalcó la importancia cultural, económica y gastronómica del cultivo del café, que celebró con la apertura de La Camfetería, que está ubicada en sus oficinas centrales de la Ciudad de México, Municipio Libre 377, alcaldía Benito Juárez.

articles.title_original: Can second-hand robots make autonomous farming affordable for smaller growers?
articles.content:
Can second-hand robots make autonomous farming affordable for smaller growers? The first generation
The first generation of agricultural field robots is slowly finding its way onto the second-hand market . This raises an interesting question: what will an agricultural robot actually be worth after 5 or 10 years, or even after 30 years?
With tractors, combines and other farm machinery, we have a fairly good idea. Age, operating hours, maintenance, brand and technical condition all provide a reasonable indication of residual value. With agricultural robots, we still have to discover how this will work. They are a new breed in the world of farm machinery, and one that has only just learned to stand on its own feet.
So when does a robot actually become old? A tractor can easily last 30 years or more, particularly older, analogue machines that are not dependent on software updates. With robots, things are fundamentally different. And that immediately creates one of the biggest uncertainties for anyone considering a used robot.
To address those concerns, robot manufacturers promise long-term software support and opportunities to upgrade their machines. Naïo, for example, can equip older Oz robots with new hardware, GPS and a modem. Other manufacturers also try to keep their robots up to date through software and hardware upgrades. In principle, a robot built in 2022 could therefore still offer almost the same functionality as a newer machine many years later.
But the opposite is also possible. Cameras, GPUs, LiDAR and AI are developing at tremendous speed. At some point, new software may no longer run on older hardware. A robot that is mechanically in excellent condition could then still become technologically obsolete. Much like a smartphone: it still works, but the latest software will no longer run on it.
A healthy second-hand market could meanwhile give robot adoption a significant boost, particularly among smaller growers. Those unwilling or unable to immediately invest €100,000 or several hundred thousand euros could get started with autonomous farming much more cheaply through a used machine. Just as generations of farmers bought their first larger tractor, self-propelled sprayer or combine second-hand.
For me, that is still the big unknown. Robots depend much more heavily on software, connectivity, service contracts and subscriptions than traditional farm machinery. Will software licences and subscriptions transfer without restrictions to a second or third owner? And will manufacturers continue supporting older generations?
And what happens if the manufacturer no longer exists ten years from now? Many robot manufacturers are still relatively small and vulnerable companies. In recent years, the sector has already seen several manufacturers disappear or run into financial difficulties. A used tractor will usually keep running regardless. But what happens to a robot that depends on its manufacturer for updates, software or cloud connectivity?
Operating hours may also take on a different meaning. Burro reports robots clocking up 20,000 to 30,000 hours in just four years. After all, autonomy makes it possible to accumulate many more operating hours in a relatively short period. But electric motors and gearboxes still wear out. A robot could therefore use up its technical lifespan faster than a tractor.
Manufacturers that continue supporting older machines, make upgrades possible and allow software to be transferred to new owners could therefore gain an important advantage. Just as with cars and tractors, a strong reputation on the second-hand market can also help sell new robots.
But ultimately, someone has to put a value on that used machine. And that makes me particularly curious about a party we rarely hear from in discussions about agricultural robots: the financier. How will a bank determine the residual value of a €200,000 or €300,000 robot that may still be mechanically sound five years from now, but for which nobody knows whether its software will still be supported?

articles.title_original: Bonsai Robotics uses AI simulation to train field robots before deployment
articles.content:
Bonsai Robotics has introduced Bonsai World, a simulation system that recreates real-world fields and operating conditions in 3D.
Bonsai Robotics has introduced Bonsai World, a simulation system that recreates real-world fields and operating conditions in 3D. By combining field data with AI-generated environments, the US company aims to train and test autonomous machines before they enter a new field, crop or working environment. This could reduce the need for extensive on-site testing and adjustments.
Bonsai World is a new component of Bonsai Intelligence, the autonomy software used on the company’s Amiga robotic platform and retrofitted machines from other manufacturers. The technology builds on more than 50 million real-world data samples collected across over 1 million acres (405,000 hectares), covering different crops, terrain, weather conditions, lighting, machines and operations.
The system starts with satellite imagery of a farm or other working environment. Using Google’s Gemini vision-language model, Bonsai World converts the two-dimensional imagery into a structured 3D environment in which autonomous machines can simulate routes and interactions with their surroundings.
The software can also generate realistic ground-level images and introduce situations that robots may encounter in practice, including dust, debris, animals, other vehicles and changing terrain. This allows Bonsai to expose its autonomy software to conditions that its machines have not yet encountered in the field. The simulations generate additional training data, supplementing information continuously collected by machines already operating in practice.
According to Bonsai Robotics, the main advantage is that autonomy software can be prepared for a specific location or application before a machine arrives. Normally, introducing an autonomous machine to a new crop, terrain or task may require additional data collection, field testing and adjustments to the software. Bonsai aims to reduce these steps by recreating likely operating conditions in advance. “Every environment we operate on expands what the system understands,” says Tyler Niday, CEO and co-founder of Bonsai Robotics. He explains that the company initially focused on difficult conditions, including unreliable GPS, limited connectivity and extremely poor visibility caused by dust. Bonsai World is intended to extend that experience to new environments without having to physically encounter every possible situation first.
Bonsai developed the system using Google Cloud and NVIDIA computing technology.
Google’s Gemini model interprets satellite imagery, while Bonsai’s own world model generates realistic simulations based on the company’s field data. NVIDIA GPUs are used to train the models and generate simulated environments. The technology is intended to support the development of autonomy across different crops, machines and tasks. Bonsai currently operates in specialty-crop agriculture in the United States and Australia and is expanding its technology into other sectors, including mining and defence.
For growers, the potential benefit is faster deployment of autonomous machines in unfamiliar fields and conditions, with less time needed for initial setup and software adjustments. However, Bonsai has not disclosed independently verified results showing how much field-testing time the new system saves or how accurately performance in simulation translates to actual field operations.

articles.title_original: RMH is working on autonomous electric feeding robot
articles.content:
Israeli machine manufacturer RMH is developing an autonomous feeding robot called Nexus.
Israeli machine manufacturer RMH is developing an autonomous feeding robot called Nexus. The electrically powered robot can independently drive to the clamp to fill the mixing tub and does not require an additional feed kitchen.
Dutch importer RMH Agri confirms that the feeding robot is being developed, but at the same time says it is still allowed to communicate very little about the robot. However, the importer exclusively confirms to TREKKER that it is a feeding robot with a 6-cubic-metre mixing tub and 2 vertical augers. The autonomous electric feeding robot navigates around the yard using RTK GPS. In the barn, the robot switches to different sensors for navigation and positioning. Exactly how this works is not yet known. In addition, the robot uses Lidar sensors for obstacle detection.
The feeding robot has a replaceable battery pack. The system used to swap the batteries has been patented by manufacturer RMH. RMH Agri also confirms that the robot’s battery pack is indeed 48 kWh and that this allows the robot to feed continuously for 2.5 to 3 hours. The robot has 4-wheel drive and 4-wheel steering.
The first prototype was recently on display at the Innov’Space livestock farming trade fair in Rennes, France. Manufacturer RMH is now further developing the robot. Importer RMH Agri is aiming for a market launch in 2028 and expects to be able to provide more information about the Nexus next year.
