articles.title_original: 🎥 Resurrect Bio reawakens plants’ natural defenses: ‘It’s very targeted, almost like personalized medicine’
articles.content:
In the evolutionary arms race between plants and pathogens, the pathogens often find a way around the plant’s defenses. Resurrect Bio has a novel, chemical-free approach to help crops fight back.
[Disclosure: AgFunderNews’ parent company AgFunder is an investor in Resurrect Bio]
In the evolutionary arms race between plants and pathogens, the pathogens often find a way around the plant’s defenses. Resurrect Bio has a novel, chemical-free approach to help crops fight back.
Rather than importing resistance genes from wild relatives or knocking out genes that make crops susceptible to disease, UK-based Resurrect Bio uses AI to map interactions between plant immune receptors and proteins deployed by pathogens and pests to suppress or evade an immune response.
It can then pinpoint precisely where partners at seed companies can make gene edits in the plant to disrupt those interactions, effectively locking pathogens out and allowing plants to defend themselves again.
The approach could enable crops to fight off threats including fungi, oomycetes and nematodes without the need for chemical crop inputs, an appealing proposition as farmers seek to reduce pesticide use and grapple with rising resistance to existing chemistries.
AgFunderNews ( AFN ) caught up with cofounder and CEO Cian Duggan (CD) at the World Agri-Tech innovation summit in London to discuss the firm’s FloraFold platform, the durability of disease resistance, and how to stay one step ahead of plant pests.
CD: We’re finding the resistance genes, the immune receptors that are naturally occurring in plants and crops, which have been defeated by pathogens and pests through evolution.
We’re discovering those, and we’re engineering or designing edits which will resurrect and restore their function, so the plant can defend itself again.
CD: In many cases, we’re looking for what we call suppressors. These are proteins from pathogens or pests that are secreted inside plant cells, and they often directly bind plant immune receptors, and they block the function of that immune receptor and stop the immune system doing its job.
The other way that it can happen is that pathogen proteins are doing something else in the cell. They’re trying to subvert the cell in some other way, and the plant has evolved a way of detecting it. But then the pathogen escapes that recognition, and we’re re-establishing that recognition.
So it can be both a positive and a negative thing that we’re trying to achieve. We’re trying to either break an interaction or fix an interaction.
CD : We start with our FloraFold AI platform , which is a protein folding tool. It enables us to try to predict protein-protein interactions, so we can scale that really nicely. The name comes from Google Deepmind’s AlphaFold [protein structure database], but it’s tailored towards plants, plant pathogens, and plant pests.
It’s quite a niche use case, but a very important use case. It’s really there to reduce the search space because there are so many plant immune receptors and pathogen proteins. We’re trying to reduce the search space so that our wet lab, which is the majority of our work, has to screen fewer things.
Then the third step in our process is the resurrection step. So that is protein engineering. We’re designing the smallest number of DNA changes possible to either break that suppression interaction or enable the redetection of a pathogen, and we license those [genome] edits to seed companies or plant breeders.
AFN : If you start trying to resurrect a plant’s natural immunity, are there any downsides/tradeoffs?
CD : Anything you do to a plant can have downsides and upsides. Conventional breeding has that, and it can have many negative effects. So they select for the rare positive ones. But actually, our technology is so specific to these resistance genes, these resistance proteins.
We screen out negative effects very early on, so by the time it gets to the breeder’s hands, the chances of any unwanted effects are extremely low. Probably the lowest out of any technology out there for this, and ultimately it’s fundamentally determined by field trials.
AFN : Can your basic approach be applied to any crop/pest interaction?
CD: So Resurrect Bio can work on any crop, most pathogens, and many pests. We’re designing a trait against potato blight or against a virus. It’s usually species specific; it’s not a one-size-fits-all. We don’t just design one trait like Bt, for instance, and put it into multiple crops. But rather, it’s a very targeted approach, almost like personalized medicine.
We usually choose a crop and a pathogen, and we develop a trait specifically for that. But a similar trait would work in other crops as well. So the technology really works across many crops. At the moment, for instance, we’re working on potato and tomato, which are very closely related, but we’re also working on soy and corn, which are completely unrelated plants, and even spinach, so we’re really not limited to any particular crop.
The only decision to make there is really a commercial one rather than a technical one.
AFN : Plants and pathogens are in this constant evolutionary arms race. Is resistance created using your approach any more durable than any other approach?
CD : It can be. The main thing, and something my cofounders—who are world-class academics in this area—like to say, is never bet against the pathogen. The pathogen will always win eventually, and that’s what we expect. It’s natural. We’re okay with that. It’s an arms race, and we’re just one step [ahead] in the arms race.
But the good news is now, thanks to technologies like ours and particularly AI, it does give us a leading edge to be able to try to predict what the pathogen is going to do next. And because we know the mode of action of how they’ve overcome these resistance issues before, we can do a pretty good job of predicting what they’ll do next. So we can try to stay one step ahead!
AFN: How does Resurrect Bio’s approach compare to others designed to build disease resistance?
CD : A lot of companies won’t have a platform. They’ll be looking at the literature and trying to find something from an academic lab. Many will look for wild resistance genes and introgress them. It’s quite time consuming, and often by the time you get it into the crop, there’s already a pathogen isolate that’s overcoming it because they’ve already evolved together.
And the other one is what’s known as loss of susceptibility. That’s finding basically a gene in a plant that is allowing the pathogen in, I call it a back door to the plant, and they knock that out.
That can be quite durable, and it can be quite broad spectrum. But the downside for me is that the back doors in buildings often have a function. They’re often escape routes, right? Fire doors. So maybe by the time you get it out to the field, in a few years, a drought comes and it dies from drought and you didn’t realize.
So I prefer to go for resistance genes because that is naturally how plants defend themselves. They don’t defend themselves with susceptibility genes.
CD : We have basically two ways of working together. One is we develop traits internally and then we out license those, and that’s usually for small upfront milestone payments, but ultimately with value sharing in the long run.
And the other way is that partners can sponsor a project from day one, and this is a really excellent way for them to get us working on something that they really care about, and it guarantees access for them of that trait at the end.
AFN : Europe has now moved forward on its new genomic techniques framework, so you’ve got a more streamlined pathway for gene edited crops. How significant is that for your business?
CD : So when Resurrect Bio started five years ago, we knew eventually the EU would adopt new regulations, but we didn’t hold our breath because you never know what’s going to happen, especially with complex bureaucracies like the EU.
So we really focused on the Americas for our product development, always keeping in the back of our mind that one day our home turf would have regulations available. And thankfully the UK came first, and more recently, and really excitingly, because it’s a large market, the EU . So we’re really excited to produce products for all of these geographies.
CD : We closed our Series A about six months ago , and we’ve been building our team and our capacity and capabilities for product development.
So now we’re really focused on executing on that product development. We’re working on soy, corn, tomato, potato, and spinach, and we’re working across several pathogens and pests in those crops. We’re focusing on those and also establishing partnerships with some big names and some smaller names as well.

articles.title_original: Equipping today’s breeders to lead tomorrow’s crop research and development
articles.content:
A three-day CIMMYT-BISA Training Workshop at Hyderabad, India, introduced wheat and maize breeders across the national agricultural research system to emerging AI-driven tools and applications in crop breeding and data management.
This hypothetical question, posed at the Training Workshop on AI-driven Crop Breeding and Data Management organized by CIMMYT-BISA in Hyderabad, gave 33 wheat and maize breeders from the National Agricultural Research System in India, including ICAR institutions and State Agricultural Universities, besides CIMMYT and BISA, reason to pause and reflect.
After few responses from participants, BM Prasanna , workshop convener and CIMMYT Distinguished Scientist and Regional Director Asia & Managing Director of Borlaug Institute for South Asia, offered his thoughts: “No. It will, however, transform crop breeding in the near future. AI’s value is in augmenting breeders’ expertise and helping them make faster, and more informed decisions using complex multimodal data. And that is what this training, a first of its kind in India, is aiming to achieve.”
Christian Werner, Quantitative Geneticist at CIMMYT , who presented CIMMYT’s perspective on the use of AI in crop breeding, put the challenge more sharply: “Breeders who adapt and learn to work with emerging technologies will be better equipped for the future.”
Behind the remark was an important distinction. The future of crop breeding is not simply about whether artificial intelligence can perform tasks once carried out by people. It is about whether today’s breeders have the knowledge, data systems and skills to use emerging technologies effectively as the science evolves.
For crop breeding programs, this is becoming increasingly important. Climate and production environments are changing rapidly, while breeders are working with growing volumes of genomic, phenotypic, environmental and management data. The challenge, therefore, is no longer simply generating data, but turning that data into better breeding decisions.
Plant breeding is always required to keep in view the needs of farming communities today and tomorrow. “Breeders must increasingly understand the complex interactions among the genotypes, environments and management, alongside socioeconomic factors,” observed P.H. Zaidi, CIMMYT maize breeder for Asia .
From drones and digital phenotyping to genomic tools, new technologies allow breeders to collect and analyse information at a scale and precision previously difficult to achieve.
Access to technology, however, is not the same as having the capability to use it effectively. “The real capability lies in knowing how to use them, when to use them and when not to use them,” Werner told participants.
Rather than treating AI as a stand-alone technology, the training placed it within the breeding cycle, connecting experimental design, field data collection and phenotyping with data management, analysis, genomics and ultimately breeding decisions.
One lesson ran through almost every stage of the training: AI is only as useful as the data and scientific judgement behind it. Sophisticated models cannot compensate for poorly designed experiments, incomplete observations or unreliable information.
The workshop, therefore, returned repeatedly to the fundamentals of experimental design, standardized information, data quality and validation before moving into more advanced applications. Sessions led by CIMMYT’s Data Science team, including Keith Gardner, Kate Dreher and Angela Pacheco , took participants through this progression, from digital field-data collection and phenotyping to centralized data management and AI-assisted analysis.
Participants worked with various platforms and tools including the Enterprise Breeding System, E-Agrology, Fairgrounds and Field Book, while demonstrations of drone-based data collection in the research fields, alongside platforms such as Hiphen and Cloverfield showed how image-based approaches can expand what breeders are able to observe and measure.
The purpose of building these capabilities is not just to create breeders who simply use a disruptive innovation like AI, but to help them make better breeding decisions. As CIMMYT Data Science Lead Keith Gardner emphasized, “this requires not only high-quality data, but systems that allow breeding information to be standardized, securely managed and transformed into knowledge.”
Through Bioflow, participants explored analytical approaches ranging from trial analysis to parental selection, while other sessions introduced applications of AI in bioinformatics, genomics and gene network modification, through specific use cases presented by Huihui Li, Professor and Director at the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences .
Together, these approaches point towards a breeding environment in which researchers can integrate complex datasets, test possibilities faster and identify promising breeding material with greater precision.
As analytical tasks become more automated, scientific judgement becomes more important, not less. Breeders still need to determine whether data are fit for purpose, whether results make biological sense and when an apparently convincing output should be challenged.
For Prasanna, that investment needs to extend beyond individual breeders to breeding programs and institutions. He described the CIMMYT-BISA training in India as a primer, with an ambition to extend the learning through future training programs, additional hands-on sessions and further demonstrations of practical use cases.
“Strengthening one breeder’s capabilities can strengthen a breeding team. Building those capabilities across institutions can help strengthen the national breeding system,” he said.
Participants were already considering how they could apply and extend the learning within their own institutions. H.B. Mahesh from the University of Agricultural Sciences, Bangalore, for example, plans to revisit the workshop lessons with his students and share what he learned with young researchers at his campus, taking the learning beyond those in the room.
Reena Saharan from the ICAR-Indian Institute of Wheat and Barley Research (ICAR-IIWBR ) described the training as particularly relevant in a rapidly changing crop-breeding environment. Several of the AI, machine-learning and data-management approaches introduced during the workshop could be directly applicable to her research, she said, while calling for future training to include even more hands-on practice.
The larger opportunity, however, extends beyond learning to use AI tools. “We need to reorient our breeding strategy,” said Prasanna stressed in his opening remarks on day one of the workshop. India, he noted, does not lack breeding infrastructure, genetic diversity or scientific talent. The opportunity is to integrate these strengths into faster, more predictive, AI- and data-driven breeding pipelines that deliver higher genetic gains and greater impact for farmers.
Seen in that context, the opening question begins to look different. The more consequential question is not simply whether AI can replace plant breeders, but whether today’s breeders are being equipped with the skills and systems they will need to lead tomorrow’s crop research and development.
The tools will continue to change, and the breeder’s role will evolve with them. But the responsibility for asking the right questions, interpreting the evidence and making sound breeding decisions remains fundamentally human.
In India, 30 Kerala Agricultural University students complete five-week research training with CIMMYT and partner scientists in Hyderabad, Telangana.
On the sidelines of the CGIAR Gender Research Conference 2023 in New Delhi, CIMMYT researchers working on gender and social inclusion across the Global South gathered to discuss pathways toward 2030 for making GESI efforts intentional and impactful.
Generating evidence and contributing to discussions and policy actions for inclusive and impactful agrifood systems, leading researchers from CIMMYT working with various stakeholders—including rural women farmers in Asia and Africa—converge in New Delhi at the 2023 CGIAR GENDER Impact Platform and ICAR Conference.

articles.title_original: When the soil moves, so must we!
articles.content:
Where did all the soil go? How do we protect the landscapes that must keep feeding families long after today’s projects have ended? What does it take for a promising practice seen on a demonstration plot to become something farmers can confidently use season after season? Most importantly, how do re
Where did all the soil go? How do we protect the landscapes that must keep feeding families long after today’s projects have ended? What does it take for a promising practice seen on a demonstration plot to become something farmers can confidently use season after season? Most importantly, how do researchers, governments, communities and development partners work together so that their combined effort makes a tangible difference in farmers’ everyday lives? These questions followed participants from the field into the meeting room during the Water and Soil Accelerator (WASA) Pause and Reflect workshop held in Salima, Malawi, from 15–17 September 2026. It was deliberately designed as three days of reflection, from taking time to step away from workplans and targets, look closely at what is happening on the ground, confront what is not working and agree on what needs to change.
The first day brought those conversations directly to the field. Farmers, researchers and implementing partners walked through sites where soil and water management practices are being put to the test. The experience gave numbers and technical discussions a human face. Across the program, demonstrations, farmer learning and landscape restoration are already underway, but the workshop challenged partners to look beyond activities toward a more coherent journey from evidence to implementation, learning, and ultimately responsible scaling.
“The real route to sustainability is to integrate what we are doing into government programming. Partnerships with the Ministry of Agriculture and Water are really important for us, as is working closely with extension services. For these interventions to be sustainable, farmers need market access, strong market linkages, and a clear economic case. The key message from the field visit is the importance of being farmer-led. No amount of technical interventions will be sustainable if communities don’t own and don’t buy into these interventions. What we are seeing in Salima today is very much that communities and farmers designing interventions based on the challenges that they share,” remarked Inga Mata-Jacobs, Strategic Program Director – Water, Growth and Inclusion at IWMI.
That connection between evidence and practice sits at the heart of CIMMYT’s contribution to WASA. In Zambia, CIMMYT provides cross-cutting technical support through the Conservation Farming Unit and Total LandCare consortia, working alongside organizations whose strengths range from farmer mobilization and extension to digital advisory services, markets and landscape management. Through the CFU partnership, that technical contribution is already visible in farmers’ fields. Between October 2025 and August 2026, activities included the establishment of 45 demonstrations, promotion of five drought-tolerant varieties and 45 mechanization promotions. The project also supported nine field staff and 15 service providers with basin diggers, alongside mechanization training, field visits, and knowledge exchange.
“A good technology alone rarely transforms a farming system. A drought-tolerant seed still needs the right agronomy, a mechanized planter needs an accessible service provider, and climate information has little value if it reaches a farmer too late to influence a decision. Beyond demonstrating technologies, we need to help farmers understand them, adapt them and decide whether they make sense for their own farms. Bringing together conservation agriculture, improved varieties, mechanization, agronomy and climate information is important, but these practices are more likely to endure when farmers, communities, extension services and local institutions understand and own them.” stated Christian Thierfelder, Principal Crop Agronomist at CIMMYT
Through the same partnership, 405 lead farmers and 38,505 farmers were trained in climate-smart agriculture, while 90 field days were conducted and more than 52,000 farmers accessed climate-smart agriculture e-messages. A clear message set the tone that partnerships are not an addition to delivery; they are part of the technology of delivery itself.
The presentations repeatedly returned to this point. Collaboration with ministries, extension services, traditional leadership, private-sector actors and farmer organizations creates the connections needed for innovations to move beyond isolated demonstrations. Implementation experience also showed that practical farmer training, demonstration plots, and farmer participation in crop evaluation strengthen understanding and adoption, while close collaboration with communities is critical to sustaining landscape restoration.
Across the wider programme, communities in Salima are working on gully reclamation and tree planting, with five villages involved in raising 50,000 tree seedlings. Demonstration plots have provided spaces where farmers can see technologies for themselves, while field days have brought thousands of people together to learn, question and exchange experiences.
The Pause and Reflect was equally important for discussing where progress has been slower. Zambia, for example, has recorded strong overall participation, but performance remains uneven across individual activities. Rather than hiding such gaps behind aggregate numbers, the workshop created room for partners to ask why they exist and what needs to be adjusted. Scaling is not simply doing more of everything, but it means understanding what works, where it works, for whom, and what supporting systems need to be in place.
For CIMMYT, the next phase sharpens that pathway, from reach, demonstrate, adopt, verify and scale. Farmer training, field days, mechanization campaigns and digital advisory services can expand awareness, but the next test is whether that reach translates into sustained adoption. Mother-and-baby trials, demonstrations and follow-up with farmers will help generate evidence around conservation agriculture, rotations, legumes, residue retention, manure and agroforestry, while trial and farmer-level data will strengthen understanding of yields, adoption and impact. The ambition is therefore not to arrive in a community carrying a single answer. It is to bring together science, farmers’ knowledge, delivery experience, government systems and market actors, and allow each to strengthen the other.
After three days in Salima, each partner had to reflect on what we can do together to keep soil where it belongs and make that soil productive enough to support the next generation. The answer will not come from CIMMYT, a farmer, an extension officer, government or any one partner acting alone. It will come from partnerships willing to walk the field together, examine the evidence together, acknowledge what is not working and adapt together. That may ultimately be WASA’s most important investment: not only better practices for water and soil, but stronger relationships capable of carrying those practices from promising science to lasting change in farmers’ fields.
WASA is helping Central Malawi’s farmers turn soil and water challenges into practical climate resilience through science, demonstration plots and farmer-led choices for lasting harvests.
An innovative pilot in Malawi is transforming poultry waste into a valuable organic fertilizer, linking smallholder farmers with chicken manure to restore soil fertility, increase yields, and support sustainable agriculture

articles.title_original: AfricaRice visits CIMMYT to deepen partnerships and advance One CGIAR’s vision for resilient food systems in Southern Africa
articles.content:
A recent visit by the Director General of AfricaRice, Dr. Baboucarr Manneh, with an international delegation to CIMMYT’s Zimbabwe office created space for a timely conversation on how stronger scientific partnerships can help accelerate the transformation of food systems in southern Africa. The d
A recent visit by the Director General of AfricaRice, Dr. Baboucarr Manneh, with an international delegation to CIMMYT’s Zimbabwe office created space for a timely conversation on how stronger scientific partnerships can help accelerate the transformation of food systems in southern Africa.
The delegation, which included representatives from Ivory Coast, Uganda, Nigeria, Thailand, Madagascar, engaged with CIMMYT scientists and regional leadership to learn about the scope and impact of CIMMYT’s research and innovations portfolio in the southern Africa region. Discussions also explored opportunities for the two CGIAR centers to bring together their complementary expertise and develop practical solutions to shared agricultural challenges in Africa.
The exchange reflected a growing recognition that crop research cannot happen in isolation. CIMMYT’s regional work increasingly connects crop improvement with climate-smart agriculture, farming systems, markets and scaling approaches to ensure that scientific innovations translate into meaningful benefits for farmers and communities.
“We deeply appreciate the opportunity to engage with CIMMYT here in Zimbabwe,” said Dr. Baboucarr. “Agriculture is changing, and our response must increasingly embrace integrated approaches. At AfricaRice, we want to draw on the best global practices to strengthen rice production and build a competitive sector that can offer a strong alternative to imports. The changing development landscape also calls on us to work together, not simply for the sake of collaboration, but around shared challenges where our combined science can deliver greater impact.”
CIMMYT Country Representative, Dr. Mainassara Zaman-Allah highlighted Zimbabwe’s important role as a regional research hub and CIMMYT’s focus on “science and innovation, productivity, inclusivity and resilience” to advance food and nutrition security. “As the funding and development landscape evolves, collaboration becomes even more important. By aligning our strengths around a shared vision, we can generate stronger science, accelerate innovation and deliver solutions that respond to the realities farmers and food systems face.”
The visit closed with a shared ambition to move beyond institutional connections towards practical scientific partnerships capable of supporting countries in achieving lasting food-system transformation
CIMMYT’s new Bambey greenhouse accelerates advanced research and breeding for key dryland crops, driving resilient and nutrition-focused innovations across West and Central Africa

articles.title_original: Para disminuir riesgos de contaminación en alimentos, se han certificado casi 6 mil unidades productivas, informó la Sader
articles.content:
Para disminuir riesgos de contaminación física, química o microbiológica durante los procesos productivos de alimentos en México, en lo que va de 2026 se han certificado 5 mil 916 unidades de producción y empaque primario que implementaron sistemas de inocuidad en sus procesos productivos. La implementación de estos sistemas brinda certeza a mercados y consumidores, …
Para disminuir riesgos de contaminación física, química o microbiológica durante los procesos productivos de alimentos en México, en lo que va de 2026 se han certificado 5 mil 916 unidades de producción y empaque primario que implementaron sistemas de inocuidad en sus procesos productivos.
La implementación de estos sistemas brinda certeza a mercados y consumidores, dado que los productores pueden acceder a mercados más rentables, al tiempo que coadyuvan a proteger la salud pública al prevenir bacterias y otros organismos causantes de enfermedades transmitidas por alimentos, informó la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader).
Del total de unidades certificadas, 68 por ciento (4 mil 025) corresponden al sector agrícola, 24 por ciento (mil 407) al pecuario y 8 por ciento (484) al acuícola, delineó la Dirección General de Inocuidad Agroalimentaria Acuícola y Pesquera (DGIAAP) del Servicio Nacional de Sanidad, Inocuidad y Calidad Agroalimentaria (Senasica).
Precisó que las unidades agrícolas certificadas se distribuyen: 3 mil 229 en Áreas Integrales, 442 en Sistemas de Reducción de Riesgos de Contaminación (SRRC), 184 en empaques, 121 en Buen Uso y Manejo de Plaguicidas y 49 en cuadrillas de cosecha.
En el sector pecuario se registraron mil 397 unidades de producción reconocidas por organismos de certificación y 10 reconocidas directamente por el Senasica.
En tanto, indicó, la certificación acuícola y pesquera comprende 318 unidades de producción, 151 permisionarios de embarcaciones menores y 15 establecimientos de procesamiento primario.
En un comunicado, la Sader puntualizó que en el sector agrícola destacan cultivos como aguacate, tomate, uva, lechuga, chile, fresa, frambuesa, cilantro, cebolla, papaya, plátano, apio y arándano, mientras que en el pecuario figuran el ganado bovino, ovino y porcino, así como huevo, miel, pollo y leche.
En la producción acuícola y pesquera están certificadas especies como tilapia, rana toro, camarón, trucha arcoíris y almeja generosa, entre otras.
Respecto a la distribución geográfica, la mayoría de las empresas certificadas se concentran en el estado de Michoacán, seguido de Jalisco y Guanajuato. En tanto que los estados de Aguascalientes, Baja California, Baja California Sur, Campeche, Chiapas y Chihuahua registran mayor número de unidades en producción pecuaria, acuícola y pesquera certificadas.
La Sader explicó que “la certificación se otorga a solicitud del propio productor o productora y, por ello, el Senasica hace un llamado al sector a implementar estas buenas prácticas y esquemas de inocuidad desde la fase primaria, para garantizar la excelencia sanitaria de los alimentos que llegan a la mesa de las familias mexicanas”.

articles.title_original: Tribunal obligado a proteger maíces nativos de trasnacionales: Acción Colectiva
articles.content:
El litigio que sostiene la Acción Colectiva (AC) contra empresas transnacionales para proteger al maíz nativo mexicano frente a la amenaza de las semillas genéticamente modificadas (GM) ha llegado a una “fase resolutiva crítica”, por lo que este organismo consideró que el Segundo Tribunal Colegiado de Apelación del Primer Circuito tiene la obligación de priorizar …
El litigio que sostiene la Acción Colectiva (AC) contra empresas transnacionales para proteger al maíz nativo mexicano frente a la amenaza de las semillas genéticamente modificadas (GM) ha llegado a una “fase resolutiva crítica”, por lo que este organismo consideró que el Segundo Tribunal Colegiado de Apelación del Primer Circuito tiene la obligación de priorizar el mandato del artículo 4o de la Constitución por encima de intereses corporativos
En un comunicado la Acción Colectiva informó que a más de una década de haber iniciado dicho proceso, esta semana se emitirá un fallo de dicho tribunal que “sentará un precedente definitivo sobre la soberanía alimentaria, la biodiversidad y los derechos de las generaciones futuras”.
La representación común de la Colectividad advierte un riesgo latente de que la autoridad competente “intente evadir el estudio de fondo de los agravios, escudándose en cuestiones de estricta legalidad formal. Limitar la apelación a un análisis superficial equivaldría a consumar una grave denegación de justicia, toda vez que, en primera instancia, el juzgado resolvió sin analizar una sola de las pruebas de la Colectividad, basando su fallo únicamente en los argumentos de la industria”.
Durante el juicio, indica, la AC se demostró el riesgo inminente para los maíces criollos, al confirmar la presencia ilícita de cientos de muestras de maíz GM en territorio nacional. Incluso, anota, “los propios estudios científicos presentados por las empresas demandadas (Monsanto, Syngenta, y las corporaciones PHI y Dow Agrosciences, hoy integradas en Corteva) operan como confesiones plenas sobre la imposibilidad de controlar el flujo génico en México. Estos documentos de la industria también admiten daños severos a la agrobiodiversidad, como la erradicación del hongo Ustilago maydis (huitlacoche), y el incremento insostenible en el uso de agrotóxicos peligrosos”.
Por ello, la AC consideró que el tribunal “tiene hoy la obligación de ejercer un estricto control constitucional, priorizando el mandato del artículo 4o constitucional por encima de intereses corporativos, dado que “este mandato supremo blinda a los maíces nativos, prohibiendo explícitamente cualquier modificación genética que supere las barreras naturales de reproducción”.
El organismo refiere que al proceso se suma “un alarmante patrón de opacidad” por parte del Segundo Tribunal Colegiado de Apelación del Primer Circuito, donde se observa el uso de “sesiones extraordinarias” —una figura eliminada de la ley vigente— para fallar asuntos en la opacidad.
“Destaca, por su gravedad, la validación por parte del juzgado de notificaciones dirigidas a la Colectividad que fueron entregadas y operadas por la representación legal de las empresas demandadas, configurando una usurpación procesal que deja a la defensa del maíz nativo en estado de indefensión”. ¡
un llamado a los poderes públicos, a las instituciones garantes de derechos humanos y a la sociedad, para observar que esta resolución histórica se dicte equilibrando el proceso, analizando el fondo de la controversia y garantizando el respeto irrestricto a la Constitución”.

articles.title_original: Ciencia verde desde la FES Zaragoza, transforman aceite de cocina usado en jabón Es-Pumita
articles.content:
Un litro de aceite desechado por la coladera puede contaminar hasta 40 mil litros de agua. Con este alarmante panorama, la investigadora Alejandra Chávez Riveros de la Facultad de Estudios Superiores (FES) Zaragoza y su equipo de estudiantes de la licenciatura de Ingeniería Química han dado vida a un proyecto que une la ciencia, la …
Un litro de aceite desechado por la coladera puede contaminar hasta 40 mil litros de agua. Con este alarmante panorama, la investigadora Alejandra Chávez Riveros de la Facultad de Estudios Superiores (FES) Zaragoza y su equipo de estudiantes de la licenciatura de Ingeniería Química han dado vida a un proyecto que une la ciencia, la sustentabilidad y el orgullo universitario: Es-Pumita.
Los estudiantes recolectan de las cafeterías del Campus II de esa Facultad, un promedio de 20 litros del insumo cada semana para luego clarificarlos: los filtran, limpian y purifican para eliminar impurezas, residuos sólidos, humedad y olores.
Posteriormente lo saponifican (proceso químico mediante el cual una grasa o aceite reacciona con un álcali, es decir, una base fuerte como la sosa cáustica), lo que permite obtener de seis a 10 litros de jabón líquido.
La relevancia de esta innovación, basada en los principios de la química y la ingeniería verdes, radica en su impacto ambiental: un solo litro de aceite o grasa desechado de manera inapropiada en hogares o empresas, por ejemplo, contamina hasta 40 mil litros de agua.
Al mezclarse con los desechos sólidos urbanos contribuye al taponamiento de los sistemas de drenaje y agrava los problemas de inundación que afectan recurrentemente a la zona oriente de la Ciudad de México, donde se ubica la Facultad. En México comemos demasiados alimentos fritos, y esos residuos (grasa) van, en su mayoría, a las coladeras.
“A diferencia de los productos comerciales, el principal ingrediente activo de nuestro jabón son las sales de ácidos grasos obtenidas por saponificación, lo que le otorga una alta biodegradabilidad. También lo hace diferente su enfoque de economía circular y educación ambiental, pues el proceso vincula a estudiantes universitarios en la recolección, transformación y aprovechamiento del residuo”, indicó la investigadora.
Nuestro desarrollo va más allá de la limpieza: integra una función social y educativa. Al final buscamos formular un artículo con la menor cantidad posible de aditivos, priorizando ingredientes simples que reducen el impacto ambiental, apuntó.
Es-Pumita tiene registro de marca y es el primer producto sostenible creado como parte de la línea de investigación a cargo de Chávez Riveros: “Ingeniería química verde y sostenibilidad”. Fue nombrado así con la finalidad de brindarle identidad universitaria y mostrar su origen y compromiso con la comunidad.
Otros ingredientes que lo caracterizan son: glicerina, EDTA (ácido etilendiaminotetraacético), vitamina E y esencias. Al inicio, el plan consistió en obtener jabón sólido en forma de “garritas” de puma y, posteriormente, “encontramos la formulación para convertirlo en líquido”. Como proyecto piloto se suministra en los baños del Campus II, aunque el objetivo es que también se utilice en el I, detalló.
Puntualizó que la capacidad del laboratorio es limitada para recolectar el aceite. Sin embargo, el interés de la sociedad en participar “nos motiva a seguir creciendo y uno de nuestros objetivos a futuro es contar con un espacio más amplio que nos permita incrementar la capacidad de procesamiento y, eventualmente, registrarnos como centro de acopio”.
De esta manera, podríamos ampliar el impacto ambiental y social al evitar que este residuo llegue al drenaje transformándolo en mercancías útiles mediante un esquema de economía circular.
A decir de Alejandra Chávez, el trabajo comenzó el año pasado con cinco alumnas de servicio social y se concluyó una tesis de licenciatura al respecto, cuya autora está próxima a titularse.

articles.title_original: 🎥 Can Picker AgRobotics’ Dr Octopus-style arms finally crack autonomous fruit harvesting?
articles.content:
"There's no gripper," says cofounder and CEO Yossi Rosenblum. "We just approach the fruit, cut the stem, and let the fruit roll through the [hollow] arm."
Can robots inspired by elephant trunks finally crack the economics of autonomous fruit harvesting?
While other orchard robotic harvesters deploy rigid arms that pick, retract, and place fruit, Israeli startup Picker AgRobotics is taking a distinctly different approach with hollow bendy arms that snake through branches, cut fruit from the stem and funnel it directly into a bin (“Snip-N-Roll”).
“All of the companies we’ve seen, they pick and place,” says cofounder and CEO Yossi Rosenblum. “They go all the way into a tree, pick one fruit, then go all the way back, and place it on a conveyor. That is a very expensive machine and not very efficient. We thought we have to do this another way.”
AgFunderNews ( AFN ) caught up with Rosenblum (YR) at the World Agri-Tech innovation summit in London to discuss why flexible robotics could succeed where conventional pick-and-place systems have struggled, the economics for growers, and its plans to begin customer pilots in 2027.
YR: Picker AgRobotics is set to solve agriculture’s number one problem, which is the labor problem. The labor problem in orchards is extremely severe. People have tried to solve this before [with robotic harvesters], but everybody has tried to do so with pick and place robotics.
All of the companies we’ve seen, they pick and place, so they go all the way into a tree, pick one fruit, then go all the way back, and place it on a conveyor. That is a very expensive machine and not very efficient.
So we thought we have to do this another way, and that’s when we figured out it has to be a very long and flexible robotic arm, and that’s how we invented Picker robotics.
YR: So the way we see it, flexible robotics is becoming much, much more common throughout the world, but it actually has done nothing in agriculture so far. We haven’t seen any flexible robotic arms there, and it doesn’t make sense because who would need a flexible arm more than a tree?
So when you look at what we’ve done, and you can see that with our patents as well, nobody has ever done a flexible robotic arm to harvest trees. Nobody has ever done a hollow robotic arm to harvest trees. So with that ability to bypass a branch and get to the fruit, I think we’re the first ones ever to do that.
YR: The farmer doesn’t need 20 different machines, each of them very expensive, each of them with autonomous capability. We have a device which is simple enough that you can tow it, you can connect it to the tractor. You can have one tractor operator or one autonomous vehicle use four or five of these at the same time and just move them to the right tree.
YR: It doesn’t pull the fruit. Actually, we don’t even grab the fruit. There’s no gripper. We just approach the fruit, cut the stem, and let the fruit roll through the [hollow] arm.
And that’s one of the perfect things about having a robotic arm that’s made of a pipe. When you have a robotic arm that’s made of a pipe, and you don’t pull the fruit, you just cut the stem and let it slide through the arm all the way to the existing farmer’s bin. So we don’t change the farm architecture. We don’t ask you to do high density or trellis or trim the trees in a very special way. The arm is just long and flexible enough.
AFN : What’s the sweet spot in terms of the type of fruit and the type of farming operation where this would make the most sense?
YR: We started training on avocados. Part of the reason was that if you can do avocados, you can pretty much do everything. They are huge trees, they’re not trimmed in a very specific way, and they’re very deep, and the fruit is green with green leaves. So if we can do that we can be sure we can do oranges, lemons, pears, and apples.
Another reason that we’re focusing on these fruits is that with this kind of fruit, we actually are coming to a farmer that has no other solution available. No other arm. These short, rigid arms [available from other robotic harvesters] can barely take 30% of the fruit, and we’re aiming for 95%.
YR: You have got to save the farmer money. You can come with great promises or great future benefits, but the farmer needs to save money from day one, so we’re saying you’re going to save money from the first day we’re in a farm.
The second thing is, we’re going to give you higher quality, and for the first time ever, you’re not going to pick blind. So far, you’ve been picking blind. You have no idea what fruit is coming from which tree, which tree has a problem, maybe there’s a deficiency. You have no idea.
Now you’re going to pick, and it’s not going to be blind [Picker AgRobotics has AI-powered, real-time vision models that make per-fruit decisions on ripeness, size, and quality, so growers can harvest what sells while generating tree-level data on what was picked and what remains]. You’re going to know what came out of each tree, what type of fruit? What size? What quality? And you could actually enhance your farm with that knowledge.
AFN : Just going back to the ROI, though, what are the key metrics that matter?
YR: I’ll give you an example. So if you go to the central valley in the United States, and you see that citrus can be harvested at $25 a 900lb fruit bin, we can do that for $20. So you’ll be saving money from day one.
And when it comes to the cost of the machine, this is very cost-effective robotics. It’s fully flexible. It’s made of very light industrial materials, so we actually don’t pay much, even if we want to extend the arm by one or two more meters, because that’s not [a major contributor to] the cost.
The cost is set in the motors and the computer, and we already know how much that costs. So we’ve actually looked at a machine that would give you harvest at 20% lower than what manual harvest costs today. And if you decide in the future to purchase that machine, it will be 50% lower than manual labor.
YR: There’s always this conflict: how do you approach the farmer? I think the answer changes over time with the specific farmer. You have to approach the farmer with a very low risk. You cannot tell the farmer who doesn’t know anything about this machine: Just put down the money, buy the machine, trust us, it’s going to be okay. That’s too much of a risk.
So we’re starting with leasing. You only lease the machine. You don’t take much risk, and you see you’re saving money from day one. Then once you see this is great, and you want 20 more units, you probably want to save more money, so you can buy the machine and still get servicing and still get upgrades. You’re still paying a service fee, but it’s much lower.
YR: We will work directly with very large growers, and we’re already in contact with many large growers today. But after that, when we want to reach mid-sized and small-sized growers, you have to use the [supply] chains that exist in the industry, and so you have to use your dealers and partners that already have the trust and the connection to these farmers.
Yossi Rosenblum: “There’s no gripper. We just approach the fruit, cut the stem, and let the fruit roll through the [hollow] arm.” Image credit: Picker Robotics AFN : How long has Picker AgRobotics been around?
YR: We’re based in Israel and we started in February 2025, so we’re kind of young, but we like to run fast. So everybody’s meeting us and saying: How many years have you been developing this? You’re already testing it in the orchard!
We say, It’s one year and a half so far, and we try to keep up with that speed and keep up with our promises. And this is part of our promise to the investors that we’re going to do this fast, simple, reliable, and get to the farmers something that they can afford and they can use reliably.
YR: So far, we’ve been testing our units in the orchard. We built four units to date. Each one of them a next generation compared to the previous one, and we’ve been testing it in the orchard. Just around the office, we have so many orchards we can use, so it’s great. We just go down to the orchard, we do the tests, we pick, then we come back home, we collect it, and we come back to the orchard for the next test. This is what we’ve been doing this year.
In January 2027, we’re going to start pilots with customers, and that means we’ll be staying there with our team until it’s just right, and then we’ll add five more units. So we’ll have six this year, starting in Israel, then going to California, and then probably Spain.

articles.title_original: 🎥 Verley progresses towards 200,000-L tanks as precision fermentation enters its prove-it phase
articles.content:
Rather than compete with commodity whey, Verley is targeting high-value applications where purified BLG can deliver distinct functionality.
French precision fermentation startup Verley is working towards production of dairy protein beta-lactoglobulin (BLG) in 200,000-liter fermentation tanks at a co-manufacturer as it prepares for commercial sales next year.
Rather than compete head-on with commodity whey protein, the firm is targeting high-value applications where purified BLG can deliver functionality that conventional dairy proteins struggle to match, from low-viscosity protein shots to high-protein yogurts.
The next hurdle, says cofounder and CEO Stéphane Mac Millan, is less about improving fermentation yields and more about optimizing downstream processing, proving repeatability at scale, and converting customer interest into sales.
AgFunderNews ( AFN ) caught up with Mac Millan (SMM) at the Future Food-Tech summit in London to discuss scale-up, pricing and what precision fermentation companies need to prove in today’s funding environment.
AFN : How are you positioning your ingredients in the market?
SMM : Whey contains several proteins, and we are making one called beta-lactoglobulin, or BLG, which plays an important role in supporting muscle protein synthesis.
So we cannot really be compared to whey protein isolate or whey protein concentrate because we are not just whey, we are one part of it, and because we are not whey, but we are BLG, the purity level is super high.
That means we can improve the functionality to a standard higher than the conventional industry can. One concrete example: We can pack 25 grams of protein in a 100-ml protein shot [while retaining low viscosity and high clarity and solubility]. That means it will cover 25-50% of your protein needs in just 100 ml. You cannot do with other proteins.
Another example: UHT drinkable yogurt is capped at 9% protein [by weight] at the very best. More than that, the texture can be sandy and awful. We’ve proved that you can go as high as 13% because we have a BLG that has been micro-particulated .
That’s the functional technology we have patented and developed. So these are one or two examples, but actually right now we have more than 20 different applications in the food and beverage industry.
SMM : Our industrial scale-up is now progressing toward 200,000-liter fermentation volumes.
The idea is to finalize this in the next months, and start commercializing next year.
AFN : Which kind of metrics do you still have the most room to improve?
SMM : On titer, yield and productivity, we are where we want. We always want more, but honestly, we are at a level that it’s not really where the focus is. Where the focus is mostly now is at the downstream processing (DSP) level. The DSP is what you call purification after fermentation: how do you extract the exact protein, and only the protein [from the fermentation broth]?
The more DSP steps you have, the more you lose product. So the idea is to recover as much as 100% [of the protein produced] if possible. So that’s what we’re focusing on right now.
AFN : On price, where do you fit in, if you’re not directly competing with whey?
SMM : Arla, the Danish company, is actually extracting BLG from milk , and right now they are selling it at more than $40 per kg, and that’s the same price as us. So we are already at price parity. But that being said, we are scaling. So with more volume coming in and further evolution as we make continued improvements [to our process], we’ll probably have the ability to lower the price.
AFN : We’ve seen whey prices go through the roof. If they come down again, does your value proposition disappear?
SMM : We don’t compete directly with whey, and we don’t compete on price. That’s not our selling point. Our selling point is the value we bring on top to the table.
AFN : Tell me about your geographical markets and your regulatory pathway
SMM : We obtained a [GRAS] no questions letter in the US in September 2025. Canada will be next, and in Europe we hope to have [regulatory approval] in the next two to three years [via the novel foods process].
So mostly we are focused on North America, Europe, and the GCC region. At some point also we want to go to Asia.
AFN : Do you think BLG will become something consumers start to recognize on a food label?
SMM : It’s funny because if you asked me that a year ago, I would have told you I don’t know. And actually now we see protein shots in the US that already have BLG on the front of the pack.
But it’s even more interesting when you see incumbents like Hilmar Ingredients, a huge dairy ingredient producer in the US. When you go on their website, you look at whey protein isolate, and as benefits, it says rich in beta-lactoglobulin, BLG.
You can also buy beta-lactoglobulin directly on Arla’s website.
AFN : You’ve said we are ‘past the time of exuberance in foodtech investing.’ What does a precision fermentation company have to prove now to raise capital?
SMM : It’s very easy. You need to prove that there is a market for what you are doing. In the past you had some startups developing products hoping that the market will follow. That is almost impossible now.
The second thing you need to prove is that you have the right product for the market, and obviously that means that you need to share samples. You need to have customers that say yes, I want that, and I want to use that.
The third thing is can you really produce it at scale? Not can you do 100 or 200 tons, but can you do thousands of tons repeatedly with the same quality, and that’s exactly what we’re doing right now.
AFN : You’re working with co-manufacturers now. Is it your hope that over time you might be able to build your own facilities?
SMM : It makes a lot of sense for a company to build its own plants for a lot of reasons. Obviously, you can design it exactly for your technology with your team operating it. And that’s why you take any big company like Cargill, ADM, or whoever, they have their own facilities.
But you cannot finance that with VC money because VC is for risk. You don’t finance a $200 million facility [with VC money]. You finance it where there is no more risk and the technology is proven and well known, the market is there, and you already have probably 80% of whatever can come out of that facility already bought for the next four years.
Once you have that, you can go and raise debt, infrastructure financing. And that exists, and a lot of people will be really happy to finance you for the next 10 years… but doing it when you don’t yet have the market, the technology, or the offtakes, is a recipe for disaster.
AFN : You raised €32 million ($36 million) earlier this year. What are the milestones that [Series A] round needs to deliver?
SMM : Produce and sell. We have the technology, the marketing, regulatory [approvals], and patents. We checked all the milestones that we needed with the previous round. What we need to deliver with this round is to produce [at serious scale] and sell [the products].

articles.title_original: Croptimal launches mounted selection robot for seed potato production
articles.content:
Croptimal has introduced a lower-cost mounted version of its Croptiscan selection robot for seed potato growing.
Croptimal, a Dutch machinery manufacturer, has introduced a lower-cost mounted version of its Croptiscan selection robot for seed potato growing.
Sold under the Croptiscan brand, the company’s self-propelled selection robots are designed to detect disease in seed potatoes. Croptimal has now added a more affordable mounted version to the range. The new Croptiscan 3000 has a working width of 3 m and is aimed at seed potato growers with a smaller acreage who still want to identify diseases at an early stage.
The mounted Croptiscan 3000 has a working width of 3 m and operates at around 5 km/h, giving it a capacity of 1.5 ha per hour. The machine can be used day and night thanks to shielding against ambient light.
Croptimal says the gross price is €95,000. In addition, annual licence costs of €4,000 apply for service and algorithm updates. For comparison, the self-propelled Croptiscan 3000 with the same working width costs €175,000. The machine has a modular design, meaning the mounted unit can later be converted for use on a self-propelled machine.
The technology behind the new mounted Croptiscan 3000 is the same as that used in the self-propelled version, which is available in 4-, 8- and 12-row models. The machine marks diseased plants, for example those affected by Y-virus or leaf roll. In some cases, it also identifies mixing with Pur-Shade sunburn oil. The diseased plants are then removed in a separate pass.

articles.title_original: FIRA USA 2026 to provide technological answers to Pacific Northwest growers’ challenges
articles.content:
In 2 weeks’ time, US Pacific Northwest growers will be joining industry experts in Yakima, Washington State.
In 2 weeks’ time, US Pacific Northwest growers will be joining industry experts in Yakima, Washington State, to find agtech and robotics solutions for their day-to-day farming operations.
After being born in California in 2022 and four successful editions, FIRA USA now moves to Yakima, Washington State to immerse Pacific Northwest growers in everything agricultural technology and robotics has in store for them. From 20 to 22 October, the premier event on agtech and robotics will enable manufacturers, researchers, investors and technology builders to show and convince growers of the opportunities and added value of their technology.
The event once again is free for growers and farm workers to attend. Co-organisers GOFAR and the Yakima County Development Association have done everything in their power to pack 40+ solutions offered by 80+ exhibitors in a compact 3-day in-field event programme. The organisers especially pride on the unique in-field aspect of the show with 3 demo zones showcasing 40+ solutions for specialty crops. “FIRA USA was built to bridge the gap between robotics and agtech solutions demonstrated at trade shows and what actually works on farms. As this remains one of the industry’s biggest challenges”, so GOFAR.
Simultaneously to moving from California to Yakima, the event is also expanding its scope from agricultural robotics to the full agtech spectrum, addressing the specific needs of growers in the Pacific Northwest. As a result, all FIRA USA visitors will be immersed in a complete programme with agtech solutions being built to serve the full diversity of Pacific Northwest agriculture: orchards, vineyards, vegetables, hops ánd berries. With technological answers and solutions to challenges including labour scarcity and costs, rising production costs and narrower working windows because of the changing weather.
If you will be one of the over 2,500 visitors expected, then you will have the opportunity to explore critical industry challenges, to address the needs of growers, and to cultivate strategic collaborations. “Through deep conversations with the region’s key players, direct involvement of Pacific Northwest commodities, and a co-construction process that brought innovative growers, commodity organisations, and industry leaders to the table from day one, this edition was shaped by the territory it serves.”
Apart from the evolvement of the event itself over the past four editions, FIRA USA 2026 will be launching the first grower-led innovation of the year award to honour farmers who shape agricultural technology. This new award is to put the spotlight on the growers behind innovation, on the farmers who test emerging technologies. And on those who work alongside developers to improve solutions, and make critical decisions about what works, what doesn’t and what is ready to scale. While nominations recently closed, the winner will be recognised during the event.
Future Farming will once again be covering the event throughout the 3 days as well as after the event. Editor René Koerhuis will be there to track and report about the newest developments, the latest news and growers wanting to share their firsthand experience with automation and robotics.
FIRA USA 2026 is taking place from 20 to 22 October at the State Fair Park in Yakima, Washington State. For more information and registration visit https://fira-usa.com .

articles.title_original: Huracanes y lluvias ayudan, pero la sequía prevalece en regiones del país
articles.content:
No obstante los fenómenos meteorológicos han generado precipitaciones en ciertas regiones de México, gran parte de su territorio continuó con déficits, sobre todo en la región noreste y la sequía observó un aumento moderado en general. De acuerdo con el reporte del Servicio Meteorológico Nacional (SMN) al 30 de septiembre de 2026, la sequía de …
No obstante los fenómenos meteorológicos han generado precipitaciones en ciertas regiones de México, gran parte de su territorio continuó con déficits, sobre todo en la región noreste y la sequía observó un aumento moderado en general.
De acuerdo con el reporte del Servicio Meteorológico Nacional (SMN) al 30 de septiembre de 2026, la sequía de moderada a extrema ocupó el 12.2 % del país, lo que representó un incremento de 1.9 puntos porcentuales respecto al 15 de septiembre del mismo año.cuando abarcó 10.3% de la superficie nacional.
En su reporte publicado el 5 de octubre, el SMN indica que durante la segunda quincena de septiembre del presente año, se registraron precipitaciones por arriba del promedio climatológico en el noroeste, sectores costeros del sur del país y zonas de la península de Yucatán. Dicha lluvias, explicó, están asociadas al monzón mexicano, los huracanes Polo y Rachel y el paso de tres ondas tropicales, favoreciendo la disminución de áreas con condiciones anormalmente secas y sequía moderada en dichas regiones.
En contraste, matiza, “gran parte del territorio nacional registró precipitaciones por debajo del promedio, los déficits fueron mayores en el noreste, asociados con la presencia de una circulación anticiclónica en niveles medios de la atmósfera.
Estas condiciones propiciaron el incremento de áreas con sequía de moderada a extrema en porciones del noreste, centro-occidente, centro, oriente y sur del país”.
Al 30 de septiembre de 2026, indica el SMN, de los 2 mil 478 municipios del país, 654 observan algún grado de sequía, 869 están anormalmente secos y 955 se encuentran sin afectación.
Comparado con el reporte del 15 de septiembre de este mismo año cuando la sequía abarcó 461 municipios hubo un aumento; en los anormalmente secos, que fueron 903, se registró una baja; mientras que los sin afectación, que eran mil 114, disminuyeron de un periodo a otro.

articles.title_original: Solo empacadoras de aguacate de exportación certificadas podrán deducir impuesto sobre la renta
articles.content:
El Servicio de Administración Tributaria (SAT) informó que las empresas empacadoras deberán cumplir estrictamente con los requisitos y medidas fitosanitarias establecidas por el Servicio Nacional de Sanidad, Inocuidad y Calidad Agroalimentaria (Senasica), para que las compras del fruto sean deducibles del Impuesto sobre la Renta (ISR). Así lo dio a conocer la Secretaría de Agricultura …
El Servicio de Administración Tributaria (SAT) informó que las empresas empacadoras deberán cumplir estrictamente con los requisitos y medidas fitosanitarias establecidas por el Servicio Nacional de Sanidad, Inocuidad y Calidad Agroalimentaria (Senasica), para que las compras del fruto sean deducibles del Impuesto sobre la Renta (ISR).
Así lo dio a conocer la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader), a través de un comunicado, en el que refirió que en coordinación con el SAT realizan estas acciones para garantizar el cumplimiento normativo y fiscal del sector, con el objetivo de combatir la intermediación informal, fortalecer la cadena productiva y otorgar certeza jurídica a las exportaciones de aguacate hacia Estados Unidos, que alcanzan un valor de 3 mil 500 millones de dólares.
La medida se publicó en el Diario Oficial de la Federación (DOF) de la Tercera Resolución de Modificaciones a la Resolución Miscelánea Fiscal para 2026 (Anexo 7), en la que se incorpora el criterio normativo 60/ISR/N, enfocado específicamente en empacadores de exportación a Estados Unidos, explicó la Sader.
De conformidad con los artículos 25 y 27 fracción I de la Ley del ISR, las deducciones autorizadas deben ser estrictamente indispensables para los fines de la actividad del contribuyente”.
El Acuerdo, que difundió la Sader el pasado 1 de octubre, “establece que la fruta fresca de exportación debe provenir exclusivamente de huertos certificados, abastecer a las empacadoras de forma directa desde dichos predios y estar respaldada por el Comprobante Fiscal Digital por Internet (CFDI) emitido directamente por el propietario, usufructuario o poseedor del huerto certificado”.
La Sader detalló que “para hacer efectiva la deducibilidad, las empacadoras deberán comprobar y conservar la documentación que acredite el cumplimiento de estas disposiciones fitosanitarias y fiscales”.
La institución responsable de la actividad agrícola en México indicó que la nueva disposición entrará en vigor el 31 de diciembre de 2026.
Otro tipo de certificación que establecieron la Sader y la Secretaría del Trabajo y Previsión Social (STPS) para reforzar la exportación de aguacate mexicano es la incorporación de las huertas al Certificado Laboral para la Agroexportación (CLA), mecanismo que acredita el cumplimiento de obligaciones laborales y de seguridad social en las cadenas de valor destinadas a los mercados internacionales.
La dependencia —encabezada por la secretaria Columba Jazmín López Gutiérrez— destaca que con el establecimiento de estos requisitos y medidas fitosanitarias se fortalecerá la competitividad comercial y el desarrollo económico de las regiones productoras y exportadoras del país.

articles.title_original: Desarrollan robot inteligente para monitoreo de cultivos en Hidalgo
articles.content:

Esto ya no es ciencia ficción, talento hidalguense está revolucionando la agricultura con el proyecto “Robot autónomo para asistencia inteligente de cultivo”. Desarrollado en el Instituto Tecnológico Superior de …
Imagina un asistente rodante, equipado con visión artificial y sensores de alta tecnología, recorriendo los campos e invernaderos para cuidar de los cultivos en tiempo real. Esto ya no es ciencia ficción, talento hidalguense está revolucionando la agricultura con el proyecto “Robot autónomo para asistencia inteligente de cultivo” .
Desarrollado en el Instituto Tecnológico Superior de Huichapan (ITESHU) y apoyado por el Fondo Hidalgo de Ciencia y Tecnología, este desarrollo tecnológico utiliza inteligencia artificial para adelantarse a los problemas más grandes del campo: detecta a tiempo plagas como la mosca blanca o la araña roja, identifica maleza y genera mapas georreferenciados para optimizar el uso de agroquímicos.
Este desarrollo es una prueba de que la robótica y la ingeniería mexicana se unen para crear soluciones reales, reducir costos y hacer más sustentable la producción agrícola.
El proyecto cuenta con un financiamiento de 250 mil pesos del Fondo Hidalgo de Ciencia y Tecnología y busca generar una herramienta tecnológica capaz de responder a algunas de las principales necesidades del sector agrícola de la entidad.
La propuesta contempla el desarrollo de una plataforma móvil equipada con sensores y cámaras de alta resolución, mediante la cual será posible recopilar información de los cultivos en tiempo real. Estos datos permitirán generar mapas y reportes georreferenciados que faciliten la toma de decisiones relacionadas con el manejo agrícola.
El propósito es contribuir a reducir pérdidas en la producción agrícola y favorecer un uso más eficiente de los agroquímicos, mediante información precisa sobre las condiciones de los cultivos.
El proyecto también busca atender problemáticas que enfrenta actualmente el sector, como el incremento de los costos de producción, la escasez de mano de obra y la vulnerabilidad de los cultivos ante factores climáticos. En este sentido, la iniciativa pretende acercar herramientas de agricultura de precisión, robótica e inteligencia artificial a los productores de Hidalgo.
El desarrollo está encabezado por el docente Luis Felipe Serna Hernández y tiene como tesista a Leslie Esmeralda Jiménez Ramírez, estudiante de la Maestría en Ingeniería Mecatrónica. En los trabajos participan también César Uribe Mejía, Pablo César Reyes Cruz y José Luis Ramírez Suárez, estudiantes del mismo posgrado.
A estas actividades se suma la participación del grupo de tercer semestre de la Maestría en Ingeniería Mecatrónica, a través de la asignatura de Prototipos Mecatrónicos, lo que permite fortalecer la relación entre la formación académica, la investigación y el desarrollo de soluciones tecnológicas orientadas a atender problemáticas reales.
Además de su posible aplicación en el sector agrícola, el proyecto representa una oportunidad para fortalecer las capacidades científicas y tecnológicas del ITESHU, mediante el desarrollo de investigación, trabajos de tesis y posibles procesos de propiedad intelectual.
La iniciativa contempla también la vinculación con productores y otros actores del sector agrícola, con el propósito de orientar el desarrollo tecnológico hacia necesidades concretas del campo hidalguense.

articles.title_original: Could GLP-1 drugs finally put a price on crop nutrient density?
articles.content:
What will persuade breeders to prioritize nutrient density, farmers to adopt practices that improve it, and food companies to pay for it?
Could the rise of GLP-1 drugs finally give food companies—and ultimately farmers and plant breeders—the incentive to tackle a problem that has largely flown under the radar but is now causing serious alarm: the steady decline in crop nutrient density?
Thanks to decades of breeding for yield over nutrient density, fertilizer regimes that boost biomass faster than mineral uptake, and continued soil degradation, we’re getting less nutritional bang for our farming bucks, notes a new report from VC firm Deep Science Ventures (DSV).
The historic challenge, says DSV, has been creating incentives for breeders to prioritize nutrient density, farmers to adopt practices that improve it, and food companies and supermarkets to pay for it.
To some extent the issue has been masked by an increase in global calorie supply. “However, we may be approaching a tipping point that requires urgent attention,” predicts DSV, which has conducted new scenario modelling showing that if GLP-1 penetration hits 15% of UK adults, driving a significant drop in calorie intake, and crop nutrient density declines a further 15%, around 5 million working-age adults could fall below safe levels of selenium, potassium and iron.
Add to this the fact that elevated carbon dioxide could cut wheat protein by up to 12.7% and zinc by 36.5% by 2050; a third of the world’s soils are already degraded; and heat and drought threaten access to nutrient-rich produce, meat and dairy while increasing reliance on starchy staples, and we’re facing a significant problem, says DSV senior associate Will Summers, PhD.
“The pathway to a future where growers see an ROI on nutrient density itself will take time,” he predicts.
But thanks to GLP-1s and concerns over ultra-processed foods, food companies are “having to think about how they compete on ‘nutrition per calorie’ basis for an increasingly large market segment, in a way that hasn’t been the case before.”
According to Summers, there is no silver bullet for declining crop nutrient density, which will require a combination of approaches.
Improving crop nutrient density is certainly not “the fix for all the world’s nutritional problems,” he tells AgFunderNews. Stepping up food fortification by adding vitamins and minerals to more staples may also be an important part of the strategy, he adds.
“What I would love to see is a coherent framework that recognizes how nutrients pass all the way from soil through to human consumption and use this knowledge to guide where the most meaningful levers for intervention are for any given problem.”
Put it this way, he says: “The best solution for zinc deficiency in teenage girls may look quite different from the best solution for vitamin C deficiency in men over 60.”
The challenge is that by focusing purely on dietary choices, we “miss a whole load of upstream and downstream factors that limit the effectiveness of those interventions and therefore deserve much more attention.”
Meanwhile, fortification with individual nutrients cannot plug all the nutritional gaps that come from decreased consumption of whole foods, he points out.
“As we increasingly uncover the chemical complexity of our food and its associated health effects… an example I like to give is there are thousands of chemicals in garlic yet the the USDA only characterizes 68… it will be impossible to plug the gaps with fortification alone.”
When it comes to commercial incentives for producing more nutrient-dense crops, food processors and retailers may end up driving the conversation, predicts Summers.
“I think that the first steps will be formulations.” With the rise of GLP-1s and increased concern about ultra processed foods (UPFs), he says, “We are already seeing supermarkets develop ranges specifically framed around nutrient density. Every UK supermarket is worried about losing business due to the drop in demand for hyper-palatable UPFs and is thinking about how to create new markets to fill the void.
“I think we are going to see a huge segment grow here with people willing to spend more on food that is nutrient-dense rather than indexing for volume. While this is the starting point, once food companies start competing on nutritional quality and density, innovations that deliver the appropriate measurement infrastructure will enable the density of ingredients to become a differentiator, thereby moving the value and demand upstream.
“I think eventually where this takes us in the long term is the scope to start valuing food in ways that haven’t been possible in the past, very much chiming with the view of groups like The First Thirty on agrihealth .”
If declining nutrient density is to be tackled at source, plant breeding is one obvious intervention point, says Summers. But most breeders are still focused on yield, disease resistance, drought tolerance and other agronomic traits. So what would make nutrient density a more important breeding target?
Policy may have a role to play, he says: “Researchers in this area are increasingly making the case that we need to better track the nutrient density of the foods we produce. Many UK policies for nutritional security such as the Healthy Start initiative are constrained in their ability to deliver maximum public good if the reward someone receives for making the right dietary choice – eating whole food – is diminished by reduced nutrient density.
“Groups like HarvestPlus [developing biofortified, climate-smart crops] have already shown in some crop groups how you can set baseline breeding targets for nutrient density, and that these can easily be achieved without compromising yield. I would love to see the government simply say a variety will not be approved for market unless it reaches this necessary baseline level, which provides a starting point.”
When it comes to farming practices that improve soil health, meanwhile, is there enough evidence that they might have a predictable and measurable impact on crop nutrient status?
It’s a complex topic, acknowledges Summers. “We need to separate out organic and regenerative ag here. There have been good reviews, especially some of Alan Dangour’s work, that show organic production does not correlate with nutritional quality . The evidence for regenerative practices appears to be stronger, but the key thing is soil health, regardless of what practices best deliver it.
“Increased biological activity aiding with nutrient bioavailability, as well as links between higher soil organic matter (SOM) content and improved retention and effectiveness of fertilizer inputs, helps support increased nutrient density. There are some nice paired farm trials that help control for crop and environmental variables that found improved soil health g ave 10-35% uplifts in density across a set of nutrients, for example.
“The challenge though is that nutrient density is dictated by a complex set of interacting factors to do with climate, soil, management practices and crop genetics. Meanwhile, the benefits of a healthy soil with ideal SOM levels can easily be undone by genetics or fertilizer practices that constrain nutrient density.”
Nevertheless, enhancing soil organic matter is likely valuable “because of the sheer extent of degraded soils globally” and the fact that it already delivers benefits such as yield resilience, he points out. “The agricultural system is already set up to value these things, while then nutrient density sneaks in as a co-benefit.
The next challenge is proving and measuring that value consistently enough to create a market for it.
“I think the key first step will be solving measurement gaps that enable food products to be differentiated on nutrient density and linked to production methods.
“This is what companies like Edacious [a startup developing a rapid testing and data insights platform to measure and map nutrient density in whole foods from meat and milk to fresh produce] are looking to solve and I think such data will help create new incentives that break from a pure yield focus.”
As to how far are we from being able to measure and verify nutrient density routinely enough for buyers to specify it and growers to be paid for it, he says, “I don’t think we’re far off. Things like hyperspectral imaging for veg and antibody based approaches for cereals are making measurement much more scalable and low-cost.
“If GLP-1s provide that activation energy for competing on nutrition per calorie, and companies like Edacious start drawing the links between nutrition and how a food was produced, I think we could suddenly see the incentives come into place that some food companies leverage these technologies to provide them with product differentiation.
“Things then potentially start to proliferate from there. On the consumer side, when we think a bit more sci-fi, I also don’t think it is beyond imagination to also picture future generations of products like meta-glasses having hyperspectral imaging included, which would unlock the scope to build embedded apps that literally enable you to look at fresh veg in the supermarket a pick out the ones that are best for you.”
