articles.title_original: Twiga’s demise underscores the need for new financing models in African agrifoodtech
articles.content:
Twiga’s administration does not signal the death of B2B food distribution in East Africa, but a changing of the guard.
The recent news of Twiga entering into administration sent shockwaves through African tech, marking a dramatic conclusion for one of the continent’s most visible ventures—and perhaps for a specific era of agrifoodtech as well.
The Kenya-based ag marketplace, launched more than a decade ago, stood as the flagship model for a generation of agrifoodtech startups: founded by high-profile entrepreneurs, backed by world-class investors, and capitalized with tens of millions before establishing a sustainable unit-economic baseline.
“Twiga is the poster child for how not to invest in food and agriculture in Africa, wasting $185 million and causing investors like Goldman Sachs, IFC, DFC, and many others to think food/ag businesses are bad investments,” author and impact investor Luni Libes wrote in his post-mortem last week.
Some lay the blame on a flawed core model, others on investors treating physical agrifood supply chains like asset-light software, and many on a combination of both.
“The trend now is to have much more patient capital and more cashflow-based businesses,” says Sewu-Steve Tawia, managing director at Africa-focused fund manager Asime Partners. “What we are seeing is the tail end of business models that were funded based on the founders’ ability to raise capital rather than the actual ability to operate in an environment that is very challenging.”
Twiga launched in 2013 connecting smallholder banana farmers and local street vendors in Nairobi. The pitch was clean: give micro-retailers access to lower-cost, high-quality produce while offering farmers predictable pricing. Business took place via an app, supported by Twiga’s own warehouses and delivery fleet.
Global investors rushed in. Goldman Sachs led a $30 million Series B in 2019 , followed by Creadev’s $50 million Series C in late 2021. Backed by additional partners like IFC and TLcom, Twiga eventually raised roughly $185 million, expanding from bananas into staple vegetables and packaged consumer goods.
Yet, as Maurice Scheepens at Dutch entrepreneurial development bank FMO notes, “fragmented supply chains, infrastructure constraints, high working capital requirements, and challenging unit economics make it difficult to scale such a model in a financially sustainable way.”
Those underlying mechanics began straining the business as early as 2022 . Twiga initiated multiple rounds of restructuring, cut hundreds of jobs, and fell behind on supplier payables—culminating in a high-profile debt dispute with cloud provider Incentro Africa over $260,000 in outstanding fees (later settled out of court ).
The most common view today is that the business never made money on what it actually did. Moving fresh produce from thousands of small farms to thousands of small kiosks means paying for collection, warehouses, trucks, spoilage and customer credit, on goods that sell for very little.
As Nairobi-based ag advisor Daniel Ochanda wrote bluntly on LinkedIn : “Technology can lower transaction and information costs; it cannot eliminate the physical economics of a tomato, banana, or onion moving through a fragmented market.”
Twiga was also competing against informal market brokers it set out to replace, who operate with hyper-local social networks, near-zero fixed overhead, and no venture benchmarks to meet.
Twiga raised its biggest rounds while capital was flowing freely, at the peak of the agrifoodtech investment boom.
While this funding built extensive physical infrastructure—including a major distribution hub at Tatu City—it also bound the company to high fixed operating costs and reliance on continuous capital raises.
When global venture markets tightened, Twiga’s planned Series D never materialized. In late 2023, Creadev and Juven backed a $35 million convertible bond, alongside $1 million in personal capital from co-founder and then-CEO Peter Njonjo. He then went on sabbatical and left the board in early 2024. F ormer Jumia executive Charles Ballard took the helm to execute an asset-light restructuring. Njonjo and Ballard did not respond to a request for comment.
In a strategic attempt to shift toward a franchise model and acquire immediate distribution scale, Twiga bought majority stakes in local consumer goods distributors Jumra, Sojpar, and Raisons. None of this helped alleviate the legacy debts Twiga still faced.
Macroeconomic pressures compounded these operational struggles. Between 2022 and 2024, the Kenyan shilling lost about 30% of its value against the US dollar as multiple factors converged: a hike in US interest rates, the Russia-Ukraine war’s impact to fuel pricing, and Kenya’s heavy debt burden.
For Twiga, this meant fuel for trucks and imported packaged goods became more expensive, squeezing both the consumers and the company. Twiga also raised money in dollars but earned in shillings, so each shilling of sales was worth less to investors, and any dollar-denominated debt became more expensive to service.
In January 2026, a creditor petitioned the High Court to wind up an affiliate, Twiga Tatu SEZ. On August 17 the main operating company, by then renamed GT Flow Ltd, was placed into administration, quickly followed by parent entity Twiga Foods Ltd (renamed Templar Field Ltd).
Scheepens agrees that “the widespread availability of venture capital, combined with the strong focus at the time on top-line growth rather than margins and unit economics, did not help” Twiga.
“It allowed Twiga to scale a very operationally intensive model and postpone some of the harder questions around sustainable profitability.”
Data from AgFunder shows that top-funded African agrifoodtech startups over the past decade have remained largely concentrated among a few established players. Preliminary figures for 2026 show sector equity funding sitting under $150 million, reflecting widespread investor conservatism globally.
“Appetite for equity has gone down because there’s literally less money,” notes Asime Partners’ Tawia. “Investors are seeing higher interest rates and want to match that, and they have shifted to later, growth-stage companies. Entrepreneurs have been building companies for the last seven to 10 years have given away so much equity they prefer to take on debt.”
Yet, Twiga’s administration does not signal the death of B2B food distribution in East Africa. Rather, it is a changing of the guard.
As post-mortems of Twiga circulate, Tanzania-headquartered East Africa Foods (EAF) has just announced a $40 million Series B equity and debt raise led by the Private Infrastructure Development Group (PIDG), Oikocredit, and FMO .
The contrast in investor strategy is telling. Where Twiga relied on fast-paced venture capital to subsidize expansion, EAF has built its foundation on DFI backing, concessional debt (including from the Schmidt Family Foundation), and direct investment in physical supply chain assets . Operating across Tanzania and Kenya, EAF sources from over 28,000 smallholders, processes and packages produce under its own consumer brands like Onja and Golden Banana , and runs its own transport network ( EA Logistics ) with over 100 trucks .
“A third of what our farmers grow never reaches anyone’s table. That is not a farming problem: it is an infrastructure problem, and it is solvable,” said EAF Founder and CEO Elia Timotheo in a press release announcing the round .
The resolution of Twiga’s administration marks a definitive turning point for African agrifoodtech. Moving forward, growth in African agrifood supply chains will depend less on asset-light venture models and more on patient capital building the unglamorous physical infrastructure required to connect farm-gate to urban vendor .
“A lot of founders, fund managers, and even LPs are looking for innovative ways to invest in companies now: dividend payment options, revenue share, milestone-based ways to finance companies with less risk and more results,” says Tawia.
“Venture capital is not the way to finance SMEs in Africa, and therefore we need to create a new asset class that is adjusted to our environment t hat takes a minimum of seven years to get to maturity, not five.”

articles.title_original: Myca raises $1.3m pre-seed to put AI agents in charge of agribusiness field operations
articles.content:
New capital will help Myca widen its geographical footprint across Southeast Asia, Latin America, Africa and India.
Myca , best known for its AI agents that coordinate agribusiness field teams, has raised $1.3 million in pre-seed funding. Kriscore Capital led the round alongside Eximius Ventures , with participation from Indigram Labs Foundation and angel investors from the agriculture sector.
The company says it will use the capital to expand its product suite, grow its engineering team, and widen its geographical footprint across Southeast Asia, Latin America, Africa and India.
Agribusinesses in the Global South still run critical operations over WhatsApp messages, phone calls and spreadsheets, so head office systems rarely reflect what is happening on the ground in real time, says India-headquartered Myca.
The company’s software takes in the messages, calls and photos field teams already produce, turns them into structured data, and uses AI agents to handle the follow-up work supervisors typically do. It sits on top of a company’s existing ERP and CRM systems rather than replacing them.
Use cases include field sales, crop surveys, procurement planning, credit assessment, and warehouse and logistics tracking. The product launched in April in India and Indonesia, and the company says it is now active in eight countries. Myca names Bayer, Olam Food Ingredients, ETG-Parrogate, BigHaat and Dayatani among its customers.
Founders Arnav Pandey, Tejas Dinkar and Seamus Tardif previously built an agritech company in Southeast Asia with more than $100 million in topline revenue, according to the company.
The team is staying focused on smallholder-heavy markets. “Some of our customers run field teams of 10 people in North America. In India they run a field team of 5,000,” Tardif tells AgFunderNews .
Agribusiness will remain the company’s focus for the foreseeable future. Pandey says that while there are “natural extensions” for Myca’s technology into fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) segments, for now the company is strictly focused on agribusiness.
“It’s a $6 trillion industry. There are so many things to solve right in here.”
The fundraising itself took longer than might be considered usual, says CEO Pandey. “Investors today are not really keen on investing in agri, at least in this part of the world. The moment you add North America to the picture, things become a little easier. But the Global South is not the most sought-after place to invest in.”
Expectations have also shifted, Tardif adds. “In 2020, 2021, people just wanted to know you’ve got a great deck and a good team. Now it’s, ‘OK, but where’s the pathway to a million?'”
Positioning was another hurdle. Myca bills itself as an AI software company with agriculture as its vertical, but investors saw it differently. As they see it, “You’re touching agri companies, ergo you’re an agritech,” says Tardif.
After several months of exploratory conversations, talks turned serious around May and June. Along the way the founders walked away from offers.
“We weren’t happy with the terms. We weren’t happy with the valuation,” Tardif says. “As founders, you have to remember that investors are buying your product. They’re not there to dictate the terms.”
Pandey describes the test the team applied to each term sheet: “Assume we don’t get a good valuation, and assume we don’t make any revenue. Would this be the paper we’d be willing to sign in that case? If the answer is no, you don’t need to sign it.”
Tardif’s advice to other founders: know when the business is ready before approaching investors seriously, keep the target list short, and don’t be afraid to walk away from a bad deal. “There is money out there. You have to have a little bit more patience for it.”
Myca expects to raise again “in the not so distant future,” he adds.

articles.title_original: 🎥 Where are foodtech investors looking next after the boom and bust?
articles.content:
Foodtech has been through boom, bust and reset — and investors are now looking well beyond alt protein. So where is the next big opportunity?
Foodtech has been through boom, bust and reset, and investors are now looking well beyond alternative protein for the next big opportunities.
For Peakbridge founding general partner Erich Sieber, some of the most compelling areas now sit at the intersection of nutrition and health, from clinically validated functional ingredients and GLP-1 wraparound support products to women’s health and AI-powered personalized nutrition.
AgFunderNews ( AFN ) caught up with Sieber (ES) at the Future Food-Tech summit in London to discuss where foodtech valuations are heading, why nutrition and health is attracting renewed investor interest, and where AI can create value across the food system.
ES : In the valuation cycle, I think we are at the bottom. On the portfolio cycle, from the funds, we’re not yet there. I think there will be more down rounds, restructuring, and some liquidations. But we’re getting there, so I would say it’s a good time to invest.
And I also think what we see is a split into capital-heavy investments and more capital-efficient ones, and the capital efficient ones are having a better time raising money on good valuations.
I’ve been investing in foodtech through corporate ventures since 2000, so I’ve seen a lot [Sieber spent many years as a partner at Nestlé’s €750 million ($844 million) strategic “fund-of-one.”]. When we created Peakbridge [in 2019] I was really thinking about where does venture capital apply to this low-margin industry?
And so we concentrated on five pillars and doubled down on three . So from the beginning we looked at functional ingredients, because exit partners in functional ingredients always have been the firms such as Symrise, IFF, etc. and even private equity knows that [space] very well.
And the next pillar was data, which we now call data AI. The third pillar was nutrition and health. As an impact fund, we also invested in alternative proteins, where I think we did some very good investments, but it just takes so much time, which for a fund is difficult.
And then we did alternative farming. There we’ve done three investments of which I’d say one or two I wouldn’t do today. But [Peakbridge portfolio co] Vanilla Vida [which grows vanilla indoors] is an amazing investment, but the time from when you do a seed early stage [investment] until you have the scale up, until you have the greenhouses, until you have the revenue and the EBIT, it’s just a very long time for a venture fund.
AFN : You’ve become increasingly focused on the intersection between nutrition and health. Where are the potential exits here?
ES : At first for foodtech startups, sustainability was in everybody’s thoughts. But actually, the consumer has always paid for health. When you buy organic, you actually buy health. Even with plant-based, people thought it was healthy. And then when the whole thing about processed food came [with some alt-meat products being framed as “ultra-processed”], that was one of the big downfalls of plant-based.
But I think health has always been a driver and a stable driver, whereas sustainability came and very unfortunately went [as a market driver].
So we see the opportunity in clinically proven functional ingredients. It can be fibers, prebiotics, probiotics, postbiotics, synbiotics… And then we think about GLP-1 companion products. GLP-1s are changing the food industry, and there is so much potential around them for companion nutrition, but also [digital] platforms [to provide wraparound support for GLP-1 users]. Because taking medicine is one thing, but then you have the side effects. And then when you get off the medicine [it’s hard to maintain the weight loss]. That’s a huge field [long-term weight loss maintenance and stabilization], and a very profitable field.
From an exit point of view, it’s also very interesting because you’ve seen that [pharma giant] Eli Lilly invested in [wearable tech co] Oura , so that’s a pharma company investing in personalized nutrition . You have Unilever buying [green supplement brand] Grüns, you have Danone buying [nutrition company] Huel …
So I think that what is interesting here [in terms of potential acquirers for startups in this space] is that you can talk to pharma companies, you can talk to AI companies… It’s a much broader segment with different margins and different M&A activity. So I think it’s a much wider, more interesting, and higher-value exit path actually than pure food.
AFN : With GLP-1s, where specifically is the opportunity for startups?
ES : One field that we like a lot is the platform that closes the loop. For example, we have invested in Ilant Health in the US, which provides GLP-1 drugs but also offers coaching. It [can offer personalized advice on] supplements, protein, fibers, and so on. So it closes the loop so the patient or the consumer is really treated [holistically]. It’s a treatment of a whole indication, like weight loss or health or diabetes, and not just one single product.
AFN : Peakbridge has also been looking closely at women’s health. Where do you see the opportunities here?
ES : I think that’s a very important category since 50% of the population is women. They decide what’s usually eaten in a household. But also their life journey has several specific indications. So first comes fertility, then comes pregnancy, then comes pre-menopause, post-menopause [where women might experience] osteoporosis or muscle [loss], and almost no drugs have been developed specifically for women with all the hormonal impacts.
Women’s health is underinvested, and most companies just do the pink thing. You know, make it pink to make it look good, right? And I think there is a real need for women to have better nutrition, and you can target it very nicely. It has very clear segments and it’s very investable. You can develop products and platforms [around women’s key life stages].
AFN : Are many of these opportunities in the dietary supplements arena, and are you seeing things that actually have strong evidence behind them in this space?
ES : Yes. So we always invest only if they have clinical trials. You have to have a clinical trial because it has to survive the physician discussion. So when you go to the physician, you say, “Oh, I heard [about supplement X].” The physician has to say, “Yes, that is true, because there’s a clinical trial.” So we only do these kind of investments, and again, it can be in specific products, but it can also be in platforms that treat the whole lifestyle challenge that women have at particular life stages.
AFN : I’ve always wondered with some of these precision health technologies whether they are for the already healthy, affluent few or something that is really going to move the needle on public health…
ES : That’s the right question. The goal is not to maximize the health of healthy people. The goal is to reach people who are at risk or have chronic diseases. And I think then the key question is, Who pays?
And what is really interesting is that from a regulatory point of view, things are moving in [the right] direction. In the US now, health insurers have codes for prevention. And so we have two or three companies like NourishedRx , where actually the insurer is the payer, and then for the whole coaching offering of nine months, it’s not the patient or the individuals that are paying. [Nourished Rx provides personalized food, nutrition counseling, digital engagement and social support, working with health plans and healthcare providers.]
And think if you do this with health, because costs are coming down for all these [personalized health and nutrition] devices, and they are integrated in the healthcare system and not a gimmick that you have to pay $100 a month for, then you can really roll them out [to large numbers of people that might not otherwise be able to afford them].
We shouldn’t forget that healthcare costs are ballooning, and with the demographics of fewer children and people living for longer, prevention is the only way to reduce healthcare costs.
AFN : AI is a growing area of focus for everybody. Where in the food value chain do you think it can create the most value today?
ES : In general, in the food value chain, we see potential to accelerate R&D and product development.
I think in personalized nutrition, what’s interesting is biomarkers, blood markers, hormone markers and other markers. If you [analyze] these with AI, you can really give [personalized] nutritional advice to individuals.

articles.title_original: User review: SwarmBot 5 scores well after 7,500 hours on Australian farm
articles.content:
Australian farmer Tom Coggan has been using two SwarmFarm SwarmBot 5 robots for five years on his 26,300-hectare mixed farming operation.
Australian farmer Tom Coggan has been using 2 SwarmFarm SwarmBot 5 robots for 5 years on his 26,300-hectare mixed farming operation. Each machine has clocked up around 7,500 hours, mainly spraying with WEED-IT technology. Coggan rates the robots on 9 practical criteria and estimates total operating cost savings of around 70% compared with conventional spraying. But keeping the robots working efficiently also requires careful field preparation and planning.
At Coggan Farms in Australia, autonomous spraying has become part of everyday farm operations. The two SwarmBot 5 machines carry out fallow and in-crop spraying, allowing staff to focus on other tasks. After 5 years of experience, Coggan is convinced of their value. The biggest benefits are consistent performance on repetitive tasks, reduced chemical use and the ability to redeploy labour.
However, autonomy does not eliminate human involvement. Field conditions, seasonal changes and maintenance still require attention.
These ratings reflect the grower’s experience after five years of operating two SwarmBot 5 robots. They are based on practical use rather than standardised laboratory measurements. Scores cover nine aspects of operation, from ease of use and reliability to costs and overall value. A lower score does not necessarily mean poor performance, but may reflect limitations or areas requiring improvement.
“The system is very simple and intuitive to learn and operate.”
The interface offers approximately 26 settings pages, all clearly labelled and easy to navigate. Operators can create a favourites menu containing their most frequently used functions.
The robots required only minor adjustments to fit into existing farm operations. However, all fields first had to be mapped and prepared for autonomous operation.
Each spraying task must be created and scheduled. Coggan says the changes to planning have also helped improve the efficiency of conventional machinery.
Under normal conditions, the SwarmBots operate independently with little intervention. However, difficult field conditions can reduce their capacity.
Both robots have accumulated approximately 7,500 operating hours and remain in reasonable condition, showing normal wear and tear.
The robots fit well into the farm’s operations. The biggest challenge is preparing them for work at the beginning of each season, particularly when field layouts have changed or adverse weather has affected paddock conditions. The robots were supplied by SwarmFarm Robotics, with attachments provided by a partner company. Spraying remains their primary task, although Coggan sees potential for future tillage and seeding applications.
The SwarmBots currently operate with 18-metre spray booms, although widths of up to 27 metres are possible. At a working speed of 9.5 km/h, Coggan reports a capacity of around 13 ha/hour and a daily output of 100–200 hectares. “Performance is reasonable. It could be better, but for the task it is conducting, it is the perfect speed.”
Based on five years of experience, Coggan estimates that total operating costs are approximately 70% lower than with conventional spraying equipment. This is his own assessment rather than a verified cost comparison.
Service intervals are 500 operating hours, with daily greasing required at approximately 14 points.
Coggan is particularly satisfied with the manufacturer’s support, rating it 10 out of 10.
Coggan estimates total operating cost savings of around 70% compared with conventional spraying, although he says calculating the exact financial benefit remains difficult.
Beyond the savings, the robots have improved work planning and helped the farm complete spraying tasks at the right time.
Seasonal changes in paddock conditions and layouts require additional preparation

articles.title_original: Vermeer Bale Hawk collects 257 bales in 24-hour test
articles.content:
Vermeer has completed a 24-hour field test with its autonomous Bale Hawk, collecting 257 round bales during the trial.
Vermeer has completed a 24-hour field test with its autonomous Bale Hawk, collecting 257 round bales during the trial. 5 years after Future Farming first reported on the concept , the latest test shows the machine moving beyond short demonstrations towards extended autonomous operation.
Vermeer is developing Bale Hawk to automate one of the more repetitive jobs in forage production: collecting round bales and moving them to a designated location. The tracked autonomous machine locates individual bales, collects them without an operator onboard and carries 3 at a time to a predefined unloading point.
In its latest field test, shown in a recently released video, Vermeer reports that Bale Hawk collected 257 round bales in 24 hours. That equals an average of around 10.7 bales per hour over the complete test period. The goal was 300 bales in 24 hours, but it turned out there weren’t any more bales on the field after all. The figure is particularly interesting because autonomy allows a relatively modest hourly capacity to be compensated for by long operating hours. Instead of assigning a tractor and driver to bale collection, the machine can continue working for extended periods while the operator carries out other jobs.
Actual capacity will depend on factors including bale density, field size, travel distance to the unloading point, field layout and obstacles.
Bale Hawk uses onboard sensors to locate bales and navigate through the field. Instead of piercing each bale with a conventional bale spear, loading tracks pick it up and move it onto the machine. After collecting three bales, Bale Hawk travels autonomously to the unloading area. The operator can define the location, direction and length of the row where the bales are placed. Vermeer says this handling method also helps maintain bale shape and density because the machine does not insert a spear into the bale.
Vermeer has now tested Bale Hawk for several years in Iowa and surrounding US states, working with different crops and bale sizes. The latest test is another step beyond the proof-of-concept machine Future Farming first covered in 2021. Remote supervision is also part of the development. Vermeer ultimately wants an operator to be able to monitor the machine while carrying out other work elsewhere on the farm.
The potential benefit is therefore not necessarily faster bale collection, but removing an operator from a repetitive operation and allowing bale collection to continue for longer periods.
Despite the progress, Vermeer has not announced a commercial launch. The manufacturer still describes Bale Hawk as a concept and states that it is not currently available for sale. The 24-hour test does, however, provide a much clearer indication of how the machine could eventually be used in commercial forage production.

articles.title_original: Producción de uva y vino tienen comportamiento positivo en México
articles.content:
La producción de uva y el vino observan un comportamiento positivo en México, por lo que la cadena vitivinícola nacional tiene oportunidad de ampliar su presencia en el mercado nacional e internacional. En el marco del Día del Vino Mexicano, que se celebra este 7 de octubre, la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader) …
La producción de uva y el vino observan un comportamiento positivo en México, por lo que la cadena vitivinícola nacional tiene oportunidad de ampliar su presencia en el mercado nacional e internacional.
En el marco del Día del Vino Mexicano, que se celebra este 7 de octubre, la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader) destacó que la producción de uva para vino en nuestro país creció en promedio 3.85 por ciento anual, entre 2023 y 2025, al pasar de 77 mil 107 toneladas a 83 mil 178 toneladas.
La dependencia detalló que el valor de la producción también se incrementó 22.8 por ciento en el mismo periodo, al escalar de poco más de mil 149 millones de pesos (mdp) a mil 412 mdp, de acuerdo con la Dirección General del Servicio de Información Agroalimentaria y Pesquera (DGSIAP).
El sector vitivinícola nacional se cultivan 9,477 hectáreas de uva industrial y se generan 300,000 empleos. Además por enoturismo, en el que se cuentan al menos ocho rutas, se generan mil 600 millones de pesos, de acuerdo con el Consejo Mexicano Vitivinícola (CMV).
Alrededor de una docena de entidades participaron en la cosecha de uva industrial en 2025, donde Baja California ocupó el primer lugar, con 30 mil 934 toneladas; le siguieron Zacatecas, con 26 mil 024 toneladas, y Aguascalientes, con 6 mil 715 toneladas. Otros estados donde se cultiva vid son Aguascalientes, Baja California Sur, Querétaro , Coahuila, Chihuahua , Guanajuato, San Luis Potosí, Sonora, Zacatecas.
Desde 2017, los vinos nacionales han escalado su participación en el mercado y cada vez se posicionan más en el gusto de los consumidores nacionales e internacionales”.
El año pasado, México exportó un millón 085 mil litros de vino, con un valor comercial de 8 mil 405 mdd en 2025, según cifras de la Secretaría de Economía (SE).
La Sader destaca que Estados Unidos se consolidó como el principal destino de las exportaciones mexicanas, al concentrar envíos por 6 mil 700 mdd y 784 mil litros en 2025. Le siguieron Japón, Bélgica, Costa Rica, Francia, España, Reino Unido, Jamaica, Suiza y República Dominicana.
Frente a estas cifras, la Sader —encabezada por Columba Jazmín López Gutiérrez— resalta que “el vino mexicano se mantiene como una de las bebidas alcohólicas más consumidas por su calidad y prestigio a nivel internacional”.
La institución refrendó su compromiso con las cadenas productivas del campo “mediante el impulso de condiciones que permitan a las y los productores incrementar su volumen, agregar valor a su cosecha y consolidar la presencia del vino mexicano en las mesas del mundo”.
El gobierno de México declaró el 7 de octubre como Día del Vino Mexicano mediante un decreto publicado el 10 de enero de 2023, como reconocimiento al desarrollo del sector vitivinícola, su contribución a la generación de empleos y divisas y compromiso para posicionar al vino mexicano en los mercados nacional e internacional.
Por ello, la dependencia remarcó que por la relevancia de este sector “contribuye al fortalecimiento de la cadena productiva mediante la coordinación con los consejos nacionales, representantes de los comités de los Sistemas Producto Vid, instituciones gubernamentales y académicas, productoras, productores y asociaciones civiles.

articles.title_original: Regen-organic food can be ‘measurably more nutritious,’ says new research from Edacious and ROA
articles.content:
The new research should act as a tool for food companies when building the consumer purchasing journey, say ROA and Edacious.
Food grown to Regenerative Organic Certified (ROC) standards can be measurably more nutritious than its conventional counterparts, according to a new report from the Regenerative Organic Alliance (ROA) and food-testing company Edacious .
Lab analysis of dozens of ROC products found more omega-3s in ground beef, more phosphorus in legumes, and a far lower omega-6 to omega-3 ratio in meat than USDA reference values, giving brands hard data to back up the long-held claim that healthier soil makes healthier food .
The new report gathers findings from year one of a four-year partnerships between ROA and Edacious, which officially launched in September 2025 and in essence is testing the nutritional value of regenerative agriculture .
Niman Ranch, Patagonia Provisions, Lundberg, and Charcutnuvo are among the brands listed in this first report. These companies and others are already pursuing ROC status and are therefore testing things beyond what ends up on a nutrition panel on food packaging.
Edacious adds “a second, independently verified layer: real measurement of nutrient density (the levels of fats, protein, carbohydrates, vitamins, minerals, and other beneficial compounds delivered) and product safety (contaminant levels, including heavy metals and glyphosate), based on primary data.”
Edacious defines nutrient density as “the relative concentration of health-promoting compounds to non beneficial compounds, per unit of measurement.”
It tests individual nutrients benchmarked against USDA reference points, presented per serving, which the report says is consistent with how FDA labeling conventions communicate nutrition to customers today.
“The data that’s come out of this is has been even better than we’d imagined,” says Darcey Howard, head of marketing & engagement at ROA. “We knew that healthy soil would create healthy food, but I think that what we were so surprised to to see was just how much healthier.”
“The biggest takeaway for me is how much more nutritious our food can be,” adds Eric J. Smith, CEO of Edacious. “Year one showed real differences in protein and fiber, which are exactly the things consumers are focused on right now. Nutrition is not fixed by the ingredient list. How food is grown and raised changes what ends up on the plate, and we can now measure it.”
Year one findings include 17 brands testing at least one ROC product with Edacious. Of those brands, 13 agreed to publicly publish their findings in the report, representing 46 products across grains and legumes, oils, meat and protein, produce, snacks, and eggs.
According to Howard, one of the biggest takeaways for different products tested was the consistently lower omega-6 to omega-3 ratio in meat products.
While how one gets to that ratio is debated (cutting back omega-6 fats versus adding more omega-3s), it is generally accepted that a lower 6:3 ratio is favorable. In conventional meat products, the ratio can go as high as 15:1.
“Nearly every” ROC product tested for the research landed between roughly 1-to-1 and 2.3-to-1, says Howard.
“The difference traces back to diet: an animal’s fat profile follows what it eats, and the pasture- and forage-based feeding standards at the center of ROC™ certification are a large part of why grass-fed, pasture-raised meat tends to skew toward a more favorable ratio than grain-fed alternatives.”
ROC ground beef in general showed higher-levels of omega-3’s, ranching from 124% to 388% higher than the USDA reference, according to the report. “While this isn’t fish-level omega-3, it is more than typical ground beef delivers.”
Elsewhere, all 10 legumes tested showed higher phosphorus content than their USDA counterparts (16% to 584% more), and some qualified as “a rich source of selenium.”
Howard says the research can function as a tool for food companies, which have to factor in the consumer purchasing journey in their products.
Right now, she says, the number of certifications on food packaging can be overwhelming to the average shopper.
“People aren’t lying awake at night worrying about soil health,” she says. “Maybe someday they will, but what is going to resonate with most people is more nutritional density, more fiber, more protein.”
The increase in GLP-1 medications, as well as a renewed focus on protein, is also leading consumers to question what’s actually in their food.
“I would love ultimately to see us finally get the nutrition panel to speak more about what’s actually in the food than how it plays to what the standard for nutrition panels is,” notes Howard. Speaking of the research, she adds, “Will it solve everyone’s problems? No. Will it actually move the needle forward for people’s purchase decisions. I think it will.”
“We want this work to push the industry to understand food quality at a deeper level,” adds Smith. “Not just what is on the label, but what is actually in the food. And we want to put more attention on the real heroes, which are whole and minimally processed foods. When people can see the difference in the data, those foods get the credit they deserve, from shoppers and from the companies that make them.”
Heading into year two of the partnership, ROC and Edacious will be bringing more ROC brands into testing and building towards the partnership’s goal of having over 200 products tested.
The companies say they will also be expanding producers in under-represented food categories “to ensure breadth and depth across food types.”

articles.title_original: Kubota and Kilter expand AX-1 robot distribution across Europe
articles.content:
Kubota and Norwegian robotics company Kilter have signed a European framework agreement to expand sales and support for the AX-1.
Kubota and Norwegian robotics company Kilter have signed a European framework agreement to expand sales and support for the AX-1 autonomous spot-spraying robot. Already commercially available in Germany and the Netherlands, the robot is now being considered for markets including France and the UK.
The agreement builds on an existing partnership between the two companies in Germany and the Netherlands. Kubota will use its European dealer, parts and service network to support a step-by-step expansion of the Kilter AX-1 into additional European markets. Kilter spare parts are already stocked at Kubota’s European Parts Centre in Thionville, France. Participating dealers can order AX-1 parts through the same system used for Kubota equipment.
The AX-1 is an autonomous field robot developed primarily for high-value crops such as vegetables and herbs. Cameras and AI-based machine vision identify individual weeds, after which Kilter’s Single Drop Technology applies small droplets of herbicide directly onto the target. Kilter claims the approach can reduce herbicide use by up to 95% compared with conventional applications, depending on conditions and application. The company says 66 AX-1 robots are currently in operation and together have avoided the use of more than one million litres of herbicide.
The European framework agreement was signed on 22 July by Kilter managing director Kristoffer Magnor and Kubota Holdings Europe president Shinichi Yamada. The companies are currently exploring further expansion into France and the UK. For Kilter, the agreement provides access to a larger established dealer and service infrastructure. Kubota, meanwhile, is adding an autonomous precision weeding system to its European smart farming portfolio.
No timetable was given for introduction into the additional European markets.

articles.title_original: Jornadas de agricultura regenerativa, gobierno y sector privado impulsan iniciativa
articles.content:
Con el objetivo fundamental de fortalecer los conocimientos del sector agrícola y promover prácticas productivas sostenibles que contribuyan a la conservación de los suelos, el uso eficiente del agua y la sostenibilidad de la producción agroalimentaria, este 8 de octubre iniciaron las Jornadas de agricultura regenerativa. En esta iniciativa, donde participan instituciones de gobierno, organismos …
Con el objetivo fundamental de fortalecer los conocimientos del sector agrícola y promover prácticas productivas sostenibles que contribuyan a la conservación de los suelos, el uso eficiente del agua y la sostenibilidad de la producción agroalimentaria, este 8 de octubre iniciaron las Jornadas de agricultura regenerativa.
En esta iniciativa, donde participan instituciones de gobierno, organismos de investigación internacionales y del sector privado, promueve acciones encaminadas a fortalecer la eficiencia en el uso del agua en el sector agrícola, informó la Comisión Nacional del Agua (Conagua).
Durante las jprnadas se abordarán temas relacionados con los principios y beneficios de la agricultura regenerativa, el manejo sostenible de los suelos, la conservación de la humedad, la eficiencia en el uso del agua, la innovación tecnológica y las oportunidades de colaboración para fortalecer la resiliencia del sector agrícola.
En un comunicado, la dependencia destacó que esto forma parte del Programa Nacional de Tecnificación del Riego que busca alcanzar una mayor eficiencia en el uso del agua en el campo y mejorar las condiciones de la producción agrícola, mediante la tecnificación de más de 250 mil hectáreas de riego agrícola en 18 distritos de riego estratégicos del país, en beneficio directo de más de 225 mil productores.
Las jornadas también están encaminadas a promover una gestión sostenible del agua en México, en el marco del Plan Nacional Hídrico y del Acuerdo Nacional por el Derecho Humano al Agua y la Sustentabilidad,
“y responden a la necesidad de fortalecer una gestión del agua que considere los retos asociados con la disponibilidad del recurso, el cambio climático y la seguridad alimentaria”.
En la iniciativa participan la Conagua, en coordinación con la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader), el Consejo Coordinador Empresarial (CCE), mediante el Centro de Estudios del Sector Privado para el Desarrollo Sostenible (CESPEDES), el Centro Internacional de Mejoramiento de Maíz y Trigo (CIMMYT) y el Consejo Nacional Agropecuario (CNA).
La Conagua detalló que la capacitación se llevará a cabo del 8 de octubre al 3 de diciembre de 2026 e incluye siete sesiones virtuales especializadas, impartidas por especialistas del CIMMYT, con la participación de representantes de las áreas de sustentabilidad de empresas integrantes de CESPEDES y especialistas del CNA.
En estas jornadas, puntualizó, participarán más de mil representantes de los distritos de riego, agricultores, productores, instituciones de gobierno y entidades regulatorias, así como integrantes de los sectores empresarial y académico.

articles.title_original: Garantiza gobierno de México abasto de maíz blanco en Guerrero: Sader
articles.content:
El estado de Guerrero cuenta con reservas suficientes de maíz blanco para garantizar el abasto local, además que el gobierno federal fortalece alianzas con la industria de la tortilla mediante el Acuerdo Nacional Maíz-Tortilla, asegurando un precio competitivo de 6 mil pesos por tonelada. Así lo informó, en un comunicado, la Secretaría de Agricultura y …
El estado de Guerrero cuenta con reservas suficientes de maíz blanco para garantizar el abasto local, además que el gobierno federal fortalece alianzas con la industria de la tortilla mediante el Acuerdo Nacional Maíz-Tortilla, asegurando un precio competitivo de 6 mil pesos por tonelada.
Así lo informó, en un comunicado, la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader), quien explicó que en la entidad guerrerense se registró una cosecha récord en el ciclo agrícola 2025 —que alcanzó un millón 564 mil 134 toneladas, de acuerdo con la Dirección General del Servicio de Información Agroalimentaria y Pesquera (DGSIAP)—.
De esta producción, puntualizó, Alimentación para el Bienestar “acopió a pequeñas y pequeños productores un volumen histórico de más de 80 mil toneladas, lo que permite fortalecer las condiciones de abasto del grano en la entidad y atender las necesidades de la población más desprotegida a través de las Tiendas del Bienestar”.
La Sader detalló que 80 por ciento de la producción de maíz en Guerrero se destina al autoconsumo y solo 20 por ciento ingresa al mercado regional y local. Por ello, la industria de la masa y la tortilla recurre de manera habitual al suministro proveniente de otras regiones del país, principalmente del Bajío y Sinaloa.
Ante este dinámica de mercado, puntualizó, el gobierno de México ha reforzado las estrategias para garantizar la disponibilidad del grano en los establecimientos dedicados a la elaboración de masa y tortilla, por lo que 123 comercios se encuentran adheridos al Acuerdo Nacional Maíz-Tortilla, lo que les permite acceder al maíz de Alimentación para el Bienestar a un precio preferencial de 6 mil pesos por tonelada.
Otra estrategia que ha implementado la Sader “ha sido promover contratos directos para la próxima cosecha con comercializadoras del Bajío, donde se anticipan condiciones productivas favorables para el presente ciclo primavera-verano”.
De manera paralela, con el objetivo de mejorar la distribución del grano y generar mayores condiciones de certidumbre para el abasto, se mantienen mesas de trabajo con la Secretaría de Agricultura, Ganadería, Pesca y Desarrollo Rural de Guerrero (SAGADEGRO) para habilitar almacenes estratégicos de maíz distribuidos de acuerdo con la demanda de cada región, expuso.
La Sader destacó que a través de la red de Tiendas Bienestar se mantiene la venta directa a comunidades a un precio de 6 pesos por kilogramo y, de esta manera, se asegura que el grano básico permanezca accesible en el hogar de las familias guerrerenses.
Respecto al ciclo agrícola en curso, la dependencia refirió que se han documentado afectaciones por estrés hídrico debido a la sequía intraestival (canícula); sin embargo, el impacto total en las cosechas se precisará una vez que concluya la etapa de recolección.

articles.title_original: US spray drone market “very much in flux” as firms attempt to navigate evolving landscape, says ASDC
articles.content:
The challenge has been compounded by a recent FCC proposal that could ban sales of existing foreign-made drones as well as new models.
Ten months after the FCC’s bombshell decision to ban sales of new models of foreign made drones and critical components in the US, the US ag spray drone market is “very much in flux” as firms attempt to navigate the evolving landscape, says the American Spray Drone Coalition (ASDC).
The challenge has been compounded by a recent FCC proposal to crack down on foreign-made “military grade” drones that could effectively ban sales of existing foreign-made models from top Chinese players such as DJI that have already been approved, says the ASDC.
The changes follow a turbulent couple of years in a market that has already been roiled by import restrictions on shipments from DJI that have been periodically blocked by US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) on the grounds that DJI may be using forced labor. DJI says these claims are “ categorically false .”
Largely thanks to CBP’s interventions with DJI shipments, sales of new spray drones in the US fell by 60% in 2025, said ASDC president Eric Ringer.
“What we’ve seen is that this [the blocks on DJI shipments] come in fits and starts,” he told AgFunderNews . “Sometimes they get blocked and caught up in the ports, and sometimes they don’t. And anecdotally, talking with some [US spray drone] operators, they’re buying up any available existing DJI models [that are not caught up in the ban] because they don’t know what they can expect yet from the American options as far as reliability and capability.
“So I think overall, as an industry, it’s just very much in flux. A lot of the established operators don’t quite know who to trust for a tool that they rely on for their businesses. We’ve still got a number of operators that are like: What is the solution that I need to buy?”
While other Chinese companies such as XAG, EAVision and Talos were able to pick up some of DJI’s slack, and US firms are beginning to build domestic manufacturing operations alone or in partnership with overseas firms, demand still exceeds supply, he said.
“We went from 8,950 spray drones sold in 2024 to 3,711 in 2025. That was not because of a lack of demand. That was because of a lack of supply. I think a lot of us had hoped that US manufacturers would be able to pick up more of the slack, but it doesn’t show in the 2025 data. In 2026, we may see a greater increase, but I’ll hold off on commentary on that until I see the data [which the ASDC is currently collecting].”
The FCC did provide guidance for US firms on how to apply for temporary exemptions to the ban on new foreign-made models and components. However, there is still a lot of confusion in the market as to what is allowed, said Ringer, who recently cofounded a new firm called American Autonomy Inc, which develops software for US drone makers.
“What we’re finding in talking with some of the US drone manufacturers is that they’re only getting clarity when they can engage with the FCC directly through the conditional approval process. And even then, it’s very hard to make bill of materials decisions, for example trying to figure out which LiDAR system they need to use.
“So when they’re comparing a US-made version versus a Chinese made version, there’s real trade-offs, and they’re having to continually go back to the FCC and get clarification on what am I allowed to do here? Can I use this [Chinese component] for the next year and then switch, or is that just off the table? Do I just need to go with the US version?”
Meanwhile, US-sourced components such as batteries and motors are “orders of magnitude more expensive” than Chinese-sourced products, he noted. This makes it very hard for US firms to compete with existing Chinese models that for now at least are still permitted in the US.
“US drone manufacturers are still trying to figure out how to produce drones at a cost that will work for the market.”
According to Ringer, “The additional challenge that we’re now dealing with is this FCC proposal that came out in July to limit the import and marketing of foreign-made drones that are over 55lbs that use LiDAR.”
The proposal is framed as targeting “military-grade” drones, he said. However, the FCC’s definition includes previously authorized foreign-made drones with thermal imaging, LiDAR sensing, swarming drones, drone docking stations, drones weighing 55lbs+ on takeoff, and aerosol drones capable of dispensing “economic poison.”
The latter is defined as “any substance intended for preventing, destroying, repelling, or mitigating pests, viruses, or intended for use as a plant defoliant, or drying agent.”
This, claimed DJI in its comments on the proposal, “is a roundabout way of describing every agricultural drone that can spray pesticides or spread seeds.”
While it is still just a proposal at this stage, “It’s one that we take real seriously, because I don’t think that we’re yet at the stage where US drone manufacturers are able to fully replace the Chinese options,” added Ringer.
“We agree that we need to establish our own US-made drone capability for national security reasons, and for global competitiveness reasons, but we disagree with the approach.”
To make the switch to US-made drones work, he said, there needs to be a transitional period whereby US drone makers get support to help them transition and US farmers that have come to rely on foreign made drones are not put at a disadvantage vs their counterparts in other countries, who still have access to cheap, effective, Chinese-made drones.
“We need to make sure that US farmers can remain globally competitive. Adoption of drones in Brazil in ag is now outpacing the US and we run the risk of being left behind.”
In comments seen by AgFunderNews , the ASDC urges the FCC to “exclude FAA Part 137 agricultural spray drones from its proposed “military-grade” prohibitions and provide a structured, multi-year off-ramp. Safeguarding national security requires protecting food security by ensuring domestic supply can realistically scale before foreign alternatives are cut off.”
The ASDC added: “Survey data reveals that 49% of agricultural operators are unwilling to pay a price premium for US-manufactured hardware. To bridge this cost gap, the FCC should coordinate with federal partners to direct tariff revenues from foreign drone imports into a direct-buyer rebate program for compliant US technology.”
While sales of spray drones plummeted last year primarily due to CBP’s blocks on DJI shipments, registrations of ag spray drones rose 45.6%, and the amount of US acreage sprayed rose by 58.7% to 16.4 million acres, according to a new report from the ASDC.
The discrepancy reflects the fact that registrations typically lag sales, such that sharp declines in sales in one year often don’t show up in the registration data until the following year, noted the ASDC, which represents leading distributors in the ag spray drone market.
“DJI’s share of annual spray drone registrations fell from 83.8% in 2023 to 52.4% in 2025, as Chinese competitors XAG, EAVision, and Talos — the latter two entering the registered fleet for the first time in 2025 — gained significant ground.”
One other notable trend Ringer expects will also show up in 2026 data is a move towards larger tanks, increasing a drone’s productivity.

articles.title_original: Sudan: Rethinking Agricultural Advisory to Improve Food Production
articles.content:
As conflict continues to disrupt livelihoods across Sudan, the Sustain Sudan Project is helping farmers rebuild food production by improving access to quality fertilisers, improved seeds, and agricultural services. The project supported the importation of 86% of the fertiliser used in Sudan during t
As conflict continues to disrupt livelihoods across Sudan, the Sustain Sudan Project is helping farmers rebuild food production by improving access to quality fertilisers, improved seeds, and agricultural services. The project supported the importation of 86% of the fertiliser used in Sudan during the 2025 winter season, reaching more than 100,000 farmers across 10 states. While access to essential agricultural inputs has improved significantly, many farmers still lack the technical guidance needed to use these resources effectively and maximise their harvests.
To address gaps in Sudanese farmers’ knowledge and skills on fertiliser use and soil fertility management, the Sustain Africa Initiative and CIMMYT organised an Agri-Advisory Content and Dissemination Development Workshop in Nairobi from 3-4 September 2026.
The workshop brought together farmers, extension specialists, representatives across national, states and irrigation scheme levels, agrodealers, communication experts, and digital media influencers and content creators, Agricultural Research Corporation (ARC), Universities, and experts from Sustain Africa and CIMMYT to identify information gaps and develop practical, evidence-based advice on good farming practices, focusing on improving fertiliser-use efficiency.
“Farmers need more than seeds and fertiliser to succeed. They need access to reliable information and skills that help them make the best decisions for their farms,” said Dr Kamaluddin Tijjani, CIMMYT’s Cropping Systems Agronomist. “By strengthening agricultural advisory services, providing practical guidance on fertiliser use, and improving how information reaches farming communities, we can help farmers increase production, reduce losses, and improve their incomes,” he elaborated.
In New Halfa, the Sustain Africa Initiative and CIMMYT are helping farmers improve soil fertility and fertiliser use through hands-on demonstrations of sorghum and pigeon pea production. These learning sites allow farmers to test different practices, compare results, and make better farming decisions.
“We thank Sustain African and CIMMYT for organising this important workshop, which enhanced our understanding of agricultural extension and the roles of different actors in the system,” said Mr Mohamed Buami, Head of Agricultural Extension and Knowledge Transfer, Sudan Ministry of Agriculture.
“This will help ensure extension services are more responsive to farmers’ needs and better able to influence their decisions.”
Participants also explored how to share this information through channels such as print, SMS, radio, video, social media, and digital platforms. The workshop produced validated advisory content and a dissemination plan to help farmers access timely and relevant agricultural guidance.
“At Alzeree Alsudani, we use digital tools, knowledge platforms, and AI-powered chatbots to make agricultural information more accessible to farmers. We also work with the General Administration for Technology Transfer and Agricultural Extension to strengthen extension officers’ digital skills and help them reach more farmers through video and social media,” said Mr El Amin Jaafer, founder of the Sudanese agricultural community Alzeree Alsudani (AZAS).
Gaffer further added, “We believe digital transformation is not about replacing extension officers but empowering them to reach more farmers and deliver specialised agricultural knowledge in a practical and accessible way whenever it is needed.”
This effort builds on the achievements of the Sustain Sudan Project, which has played a vital role in supporting food production during Sudan’s ongoing conflict. Through a market-based approach, the project has helped farmers access quality agricultural inputs essential for restoring local food production.
“Farmers need more than inputs to succeed. They need reliable advice and practical skills to improve soil fertility and use fertilisers effectively. These skills help increase incomes, strengthen communities, and support sustainable farming for future generations,” said Ms Basma Suliman, a leading woman farmer and entrepreneur from Sennar State.
While addressing the closing ceremony of the Agri-Advisory Content and Dissemination Development Workshop, Sudan’s Ambassador to Kenya, H.E Kamal Gubara, noted that Sudan appreciates Sustain Africa and CIMMYT support for agriculture in Sudan. “Sudan is one of the largest agricultural countries in the world, and we appreciate your efforts to equip and train farmers on modern cultivation technologies,” he noted.
During the first phase of implementation, the project facilitated the importation of 48,500 metric tons of fertiliser and 5,200 metric tons of certified seed potato, reaching more than 100,000 farmers across 10 states. Project-supported fertilizer accounted for approximately 86% of Sudan’s total fertilizer imports, helping farmers continue producing food despite the severe challenges created by the conflict.
While access to quality inputs is critical, farmers also need the knowledge to use them effectively. By strengthening agricultural advisory services and expanding access to practical, evidence-based information, we can help farmers improve productivity, enhance soil health, and contribute to Sudan’s long-term food security and resilience.
CIMMYT proposes actions to respond to the deteriorating food crisis catalyzed by the ongoing civil war in Sudan.
In conflict-torn Sudan, women farmers are equipped with new skills and sustainable techniques to cultivate hope and abundance—doubling yields and empowering communities toward self-sufficiency.
In conflict-affected Sudan, access to quality seeds and fertilisers is helping farmers save the season.

articles.title_original: Seeing the whole farm: 35 researchers from India and Nepal train in systems approaches
articles.content:
A three-day course in Jaipur, part of the CGIAR Sustainable Farming Program, gave scientists, postgraduate students and practitioners practical tools to analyze complex farming systems and use the evidence to guide more sustainable, context-specific solutions.
How can researchers better understand what farm households really face, and use that evidence to design farming systems that last?
Smallholder farms in South Asia rarely produce just one crop or keep just one kind of livestock. They combine crops, animals, labor and income, and all of it is exposed to climate change, volatile markets and limited resources. Improving these farms means understanding how the parts interact. That was the focus of an international training course on systems approaches for integrated analysis of agricultural systems, held in Jaipur, India, from 14 to 16 September 2026.
As part of the CGIAR Sustainable Farming Program, CIMMYT organized the course with the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), through the Indian Institute of Farming Systems Research (IIFSR). The Rajasthan Agricultural Research Institute (RARI) and Sri Karan Narendra Agriculture University (SKNAU) hosted it. The course brought together 35 scientists, postgraduate students and development practitioners from India and Nepal, building a regional group of researchers who can apply systems thinking across very different farming contexts.
Opening the course, SKNAU Vice-Chancellor Dr. P. S. Chouhan and Dr. Ummed Singh, Director (Research), SKNAU, Jobner, said integrated approaches are essential for helping farm households cope with complex challenges such as climate change and market volatility. Dr. Surendra Singh, Director, RARI, Durgapura, welcomed the collaboration between the partners in delivering the course.
Led by Santiago Lopez-Ridaura, principal scientist at CIMMYT and the course coordinator, the course covered four skills:
Hands-on work took up much of the time. Dr. A. K. Prusty of IIFSR led participants through building farm typologies in RStudio and introduced FarmDesign. Dr. N. Ravishankar, coordinator of the All India Coordinated Research Project on Integrated Farming Systems, showed how integrated models are assessed against performance indicators. He then took participants to RARI’s integrated farming systems prototype to see crop and livestock components working together in the field. Dr. Powell Mponela, Scientist, Climate Adaptation, Landscape and Agricultural Water Management, Nepal, and Dr. Maxwell Mkondiwa, Scientist, Spatial Economist, CIMMYT-BISA, New Delhi, India, of CIMMYT presented tools for technology targeting and risk modelling.
Participants valued the practical group exercises and hands-on sessions most. They said the real-world examples and classroom discussions made it easier to carry the methods into their own work. They saw the skills in systems analysis, indicator selection, and multicriteria assessment as directly relevant to the agricultural challenges they deal with.
The main limitation they identified was time. Participants felt a week-long program would have allowed a deeper dive.
Participants asked for further learning, especially advanced training in machine learning for systems design and sustainability assessment. They plan to apply the new skills in their own regions.
Stronger skills in characterizing farming systems, assessing sustainability, modelling trade-offs and targeting technologies mean better regional capacity to produce the evidence behind more context-specific, sustainable agricultural development. That is the kind of change the Sustainable Farming Program exists to support.
“It is important to strengthen the capacity of national partners to use systems analysis to develop, adapt, and scale context-specific agricultural innovations for greater sustainability. NARES are often siloed into specific disciplines, and integrated systems analysis needs to be strengthened. Targeting graduate and postgraduate programs will be the initial step in developing future scientists with strong skills in systems science,” said Dr. Santiago Lopez-Ridaura.
In India, 30 Kerala Agricultural University students complete five-week research training with CIMMYT and partner scientists in Hyderabad, Telangana.
Florence Bangwaya began with motor vehicle mechanics. One training course later, she was repairing the machines that keep farms and rural businesses moving.

articles.title_original: Science-based farming practices improve wheat productivity and resource efficiency in Mexico’s Yaqui Valley
articles.content:
Results from wheat fields in the Yaqui Valley show that combining conservation agriculture, soil-informed fertilization and more efficient water management can increase yields while reducing resource use. Through their collaboration, Grupo Trimex and CIMMYT are generating evidence to help wheat farm
Sonora, Mexico, 2026. Producing more wheat is no longer the only challenge farmers are facing in the Yaqui Valley. The amount of water, fuel and fertilizer required to produce each ton of grain has become a critical factor in a region where water scarcity, soil degradation and rising production costs are putting increasing pressure on farmers’ margins.
In response, Grupo Trimex and CIMMYT are working with farmers in Sonora to bring science-based solutions into the field, adapting them to local knowledge and production conditions. Results from the 2025–2026 fall–winter growing season provide early evidence of the approach’s potential. Across the innovation modules evaluated, improved farming practices reduced average fuel consumption by 42% and water use per unit of grain produced by 26%. Nitrogen use per ton of wheat declined by 34%, while yields reached 4 tons per hectare, compared with 3 tons under conventional management, representing a 27% increase.
These results are not the product of a one-size-fits-all approach. Throughout the growing season, farmers and technicians worked with a portfolio of six broad innovations and 18 specific practices that can be adapted to the economic and agronomic conditions of individual fields. The options being evaluated include conservation agriculture, permanent raised beds, crop residue management, soil testing, fertilizer applications tailored to crop needs and growth stages, pest monitoring, land leveling and improved irrigation management. Decisions about which practices to implement are made following an assessment of each field.
Field assessments help document the results of the practices implemented and generate evidence of their performance under real farming conditions.
This approach marks an important shift for an agricultural system that has relied on intensive production methods to achieve high yields for decades. For Grupo Trimex, whose relationships with farmers are part of a value chain connecting agricultural production with the milling industry, the challenge is also to create the conditions for proven practices to reach a growing number of wheat producers.
Roberto Miramontes, Head of Wheat Procurement at Grupo Trimex, explains that concerns over declining soil organic matter, water scarcity and production costs prompted the company to explore ways to expand the use of practices that some farmers had already begun adopting.
“Working with science-based evidence allows us to rely on objective information, focus on what has been proven to work and demonstrate the results to farmers,” he says.
The initiative began during the 2024–2025 growing season with 17 farmers, covering 527 hectares. By the following season, participation had grown to 22 farmers and 1,078 hectares. Across the two growing seasons, the initiative reached a cumulative 1,605 hectares, with three demonstration modules and 11 extension areas. Conservation agriculture and integrated nutrient management are among the practices with the highest adoption rates.
Improving nitrogen use efficiency is particularly important. The results show that nitrogen use per ton of wheat can be reduced by 34% without compromising yields. The next phase will focus on strengthening soil testing and mapping to provide more precise nutrient recommendations, addressing an input that offers considerable opportunities to reduce costs and improve efficiency.
The initiative examines water, fertilizer and fuel use, alongside soil management, to identify approaches that can help sustain productivity.
The findings also highlight the limits of what agronomic improvements alone can achieve. Despite gains in productivity and resource-use efficiency, farm profitability remains under pressure from wheat prices and production costs, underscoring the need to continue improving how inputs are used.
Against this backdrop, producing each ton of wheat with fewer resources is becoming increasingly important. In Sonora, the collaboration among Grupo Trimex, CIMMYT and local farmers is helping connect scientific research with the decisions made in the field each growing season and the needs of a wheat value chain adapting to changing conditions.
The evidence generated is helping refine farming practices while laying the groundwork for successful approaches to reach more producers over time. Although the results from this growing season do not eliminate the pressures facing wheat production, they offer an early indication of how farming systems can evolve to meet these challenges.
At CIMMYT’s Sanjaya Rajaram Experimental Station in Toluca, advances in genomics, accelerated breeding, disease resistance, physiology and agronomy are helping scientists anticipate emerging threats and develop solutions for wheat farmers in Mexico and around the world.
CIMMYT and CREA unite to develop innovative, climate-resilient wheat varieties that strengthen global food security and empower sustainable agriculture from Mexico to the Mediterranean
Success stories witnessed in India, Pakistan, and Nepal underscore the transformative potential of this approach, offering a beacon of hope for agricultural communities in South Asia and beyond.

articles.title_original: Producción de huevo, motor dinámico del sector pecuario en México
articles.content:

México es el primer consumidor de huevo del mundo, con 24.8 kilogramos, es decir, cada mexicano consume, en promedio, 410 huevos cada año. Además, nuestro país ocupa el sexto lugar como productor de este alimento, por lo que se ha consolidado como uno de los motores más dinámicos del sector pecuario.
De acuerdo con la Secretaría de Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural (Sader) la producción de huevo registró un crecimiento de 6.1 por ciento en volumen y 18.8 por ciento en valor, al cierre de 2025.
Este alimento indispensable de la canasta básica y aliado estratégico para la soberanía alimentaria del país alcanzó, en 2025, una producción de 3.4 millones de toneladas (t), un aumentó de 199 mil 524 t, en relación con los 3.2 millones de t de 2024, refieren cifras de la Dirección General del Servicio de Información Agroalimentaria y Pesquera (DGSIAP), organismo dependiente de la Sader.
Este rubro genera un alto valor económico y empleos para México. El valor de la producción de huevo pasó de 96 mil 675 millones de pesos a 114 mil 881 millones de pesos, lo que representó un repunte de 18 mil 206 millones de pesos.
En tanto, el sector avícola reportó que en 2025 la producción de huevo generó 616,567 empleos totales, de los cuales 88,081 directos y 528,486 indirectos.
La Sader indicó que si bien las 32 entidades participan en la actividad avícola, la producción de huevo se concentra en cinco estados que aportan el 80.6 por ciento del total nacional: Jalisco, un millón 789 mil 061 toneladas; Puebla, 496 mil 846 toneladas; Sonora, 204 mil 768 toneladas; Yucatán, 165 mil 272 toneladas, y San Luis Potosí, 142 mil 820 toneladas.
En un comunicado, la dependencia apuntó que “para proteger el bolsillo de las familias y garantizar el acceso continuo a productos de primera necesidad, el gobierno de México reafirma su compromiso a través del Paquete Contra la Inflación y la Carestía (PACIC), acuerdo impulsado por la Presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo, que contribuye a mantener precios estables en alimentos esenciales como el huevo”.
La Sader, cuya titular es Columba Jazmín López Gutiérrez, reiteró que “el desempeño registrado ratifica la solidez de la avicultura mexicana en ese periodo, y estimó que su producción se mantendrá a un ritmo constante y sostenido en este 2026”.
Lo anterior, agregó, porque las cifras preliminares muestran una producción de un millón 422 mil 420,toneladas a mayo, es decir, 40 por ciento de la meta programada para el cierre del año en curso.
